en: *Tattvabodhavidhāyinī* 69–133 (*Īśvarasvarūpavāda*).

Here, those who maintain that the world was created by Īśvara say: "It is rightly said that the teaching was composed by an omniscient one, and because it was composed by him, it is authoritative. However, this is incorrect: [the definition] 'Jinas are those who have conquered enemies such as passion and hatred' applies only to ordinary yogis other than Īśvara; it does not apply to Īśvara, the creator of the entire world including the teaching and so forth. And thus says Patañjali:

"The Lord (Īśvara) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions (kleśa), karma, its maturation (vipāka), and latent dispositions (āśaya)" [Yoga-sūtra I.24]. By this aphorism, it is established that the Lord is naturally devoid of the six afflictions characterized by passion and so forth; it is not, however, that his afflictions and the like have been destroyed through the practice of cultivating their opposites, such that the statement "he has conquered passion and the rest through his own effort" would be meaningful in reference to him. Thus, it has also been said by others:
"Whose knowledge is unimpeded and whose sovereignty belongs to the Lord of the World..."

Anticipating the objection that "dispassion (*vairāgya*) and merit (*dharma*) are established together as a fourfold set," he says: "of those who have conquered existence" (*bhavajinānām*). Existence (*bhava*) is *saṃsāra*, so called because living beings "exist" (*bhavanti*) within it by way of the states of hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods. Because they are the cause of that [existence], passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions] are intended here by the term "existence" through figurative usage (*upacāra*); those who have conquered that are the "Conquerors" (*jināḥ*). The purpose for resorting to this figurative usage is to demonstrate that it is impossible to effect the conquest of *saṃsāra*, which is their effect, unless passion and the other afflictions—their complete causes—have been destroyed.

Furthermore, the means for conquering passion (*rāga*) and other afflictions, which serve as the causes of existence (*bhava*), has already been set forth previously. Through that means, by way of conquering the opposing passions and so forth, the conquest of existence—which is their effect—is possible, and not otherwise. For the attainment of the goal (*upeya*) does not occur apart from the means (*upāya*); otherwise, since the goal would be causeless, there would be no fixed determination of place, time, or nature, and consequently, either all living beings would be lords (*īśvara*), or none at all would be. And this point has already been established:
"A thing must be either eternally existent or non-existent, because a causeless entity does not depend on anything else."

"For the occasional occurrence of entities is possible only through dependence [on other causes]," as stated by Dharmakīrti in the passage beginning with *PV I 35–37*. Therefore, it is not logical that the Lord’s freedom from afflictions such as passion occurs by his very nature.
[This concludes the incidental discussion on the afterlife.]

[The prima facie position: An objection regarding the next world] Here, those who follow the doctrine of Bṛhaspati, considering that the Jaina—who is attempting to establish the non-existence of the *sthāṇu* (the cosmic pillar) which is presided over by a collection of attributes such as knowledge that is naturally perfected—has actually rendered us assistance, say: "It is rightly stated that there is no Lord (*īśvara*) endowed with the perfection of knowledge and other qualities that are naturally perfected; however, this which has been asserted—that 'living beings are born in this world with the nature of undergoing transformations into the forms of hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods'—is incorrect."

Because there is a lack of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of another world. To explain: the Jaina must accept that the proof establishing the existence of another world is either perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*), since he does not accept any other as being a valid means of knowledge. Nor should it be said here: "What is your own proof for rejecting that [other world]?"—for we do not establish its non-existence by means of a proof that rejects it; rather, we merely perform a critical inquiry into the proofs put forward by the opponent. For this very reason:
The Cārvākas have stated: "All the aphorisms of Bṛhaspati consist solely of interrogations.

This interrogation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) put forward by another consists of an investigation—by means of questions and so forth—of that person's own acceptance [of those means], and not of the presentation of a means of valid cognition established for oneself; otherwise, you too would be subject to an interrogation from our side such as: "How can a means of valid cognition, which functions by rejecting supersensible objects, function at all, given that it is vitiated by defects such as the unestablished nature of its locus (āśrayāsiddhi)?"

For this very reason, having first caused the opponent to accept the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the next world, an investigation is conducted regarding that acceptance in the following manner:

In this regard, perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which acquires its own existence through the operation of the sense organs such as the eye and which has as its object specific, proximate things like visible forms—does not, first of all, function as a prover of the next world. Nor can it be said that supersensuous yogic perception functions there, because that too is unestablished, just like the next world and so forth.

Nor does inference preceded by perception attain its operation there, because when perception does not operate, inference—which is preceded by it—likewise does not operate there. Now, even if inference arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*) whose invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has been apprehended through perception does not operate there, nevertheless, inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) will operate there; that too is not tenable.

For is that [inference] also produced from a mark whose necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been understood through general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), or is it arisen from a mark whose necessary connection has not been understood? If the position is that it is produced from a mark whose necessary connection has not been understood, that is not tenable; because that which originates from such a mark is invalid due to its deviation from its own object, like the conceptual construction of obtaining a kingdom that arises immediately after seeing a horse.

Now, suppose the position is taken that [the inference] proceeds there by means of a mark (*liṅga*) whose connection has already been apprehended; that too is not tenable, because the apprehension of the necessary connection itself is impossible in that case. To explain: since perception lacks the cause for apprehending the connection of the mark therein, one would have to admit that inference is what grasps the connection of the mark.

In this regard, if that very inference which makes known the existence of the other world were to grasp the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and its producer by means of an object intended as its own subject, then there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). If, on the other hand, it is accepted that it arises from another inference whose connection has been grasped through a mark, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, all inference is unestablished for us. Thus, the *Bṛhaspatisūtra* states:
"Inference is not a valid means of knowledge."

Thus, by this, the presentation of the thesis (*pratijñā*) has been performed; since it presents an unascertained object, the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—namely, "like the so-called means of valid cognition of one who has already established [the object]"—are to be inferred.

Alternatively, the validity of inference is untenable when analyzed in terms of its objects: for if one were to prove either the property (*dharma*), the substratum (*dharmin*), or both independently, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Therefore, it is the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) that must be proven. A means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) attains its status as a valid means only by producing a cognition characterized by a specific object of knowledge (*prameya*). Furthermore, in this context, the object of knowledge is a composite whole delimited by its constituent parts; and with respect to such a whole, not even a single characteristic, such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*), is established.

For the nature of the reason does not belong to the collection [of the subject and the property], nor is there positive or negative concomitance with the collection; rather, when there is the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) with respect to the mere locus (*dharmin*), and pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to the property-to-be-proved (*sādhyadharma*), it is secondary (*gauṇa*). And it has been said:
"Because the means of valid cognition is not secondary, the ascertainment of an object through inference is difficult to obtain."

Even in the apprehension of the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and its nature (*dharmatā*), the avoidance of figurative usage is not achieved, because the distinction between the figurative and the primary is to be considered in relation to what is actually perceived; and yet, the whole (*samudāya*) is what is perceived. Furthermore, the three-fold form (*trairūpya*) is untenable even by resorting to a single part, because pervasion (*vyāpti*) would remain unestablished. For an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is not a prover merely by its existence, but rather when it is cognized; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And that [cognition] is difficult for one who is not omniscient to ascertain without perceiving all similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). As it has been said:
"Must a mortal necessarily possess cattle simply because he possesses a cow? Must he likewise possess horses?"
Furthermore, because the diversity of entities is understood through differences in place, time, and state, there is no certainty. As it has been said:
"Of states, places, and times... [Vākyapadīya, Prakīrṇaka-kāṇḍa 32], and so forth. And it is further stated:
"Because the relationship of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva) is impossible to grasp... [ ].

And as for [the statement]: "Because of the non-existence of a universal as its object, because the distinction between inference for oneself and for others is impossible, and because of the contradiction with contradictory inferences everywhere..."

Therefore, that web of refutations beginning with "because of [the possibility of] occurrence" and "in some cases, because of the non-deviant contrary" need not even be voiced; for, since it fails to establish an ascertained object, once the invalidity of inference has been established by the statement "inference is not a valid means of knowledge," the remaining web of refutations is like killing what is already dead. Consequently, since inference is invalid, how could it function to establish the existence of the other world, which is beyond the senses?

Now, if it is claimed that this very birth is not possible without another previous birth, and thus the existence of a "hereafter"—characterized by such other births—is sought to be established, is this a case of *arthāpatti* (presumption), or rather an *anumāna* (inference)? It cannot first be *arthāpatti*, because its defining characteristic is absent; for *arthāpatti* is defined as: "That which is seen or heard is not otherwise possible" (*Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* 1.1.5, Śābarabhāṣya).

Thus, its lack of defining characteristics (alakṣaṇa) is asserted by the wise. However, it is not established that this birth is impossible without another previous birth, because it arises solely from the causal complex of mother and father; and if it were caused by that alone, the postulation of anything else would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

[Objection: But since wisdom, intelligence, and so forth are observed at the beginning of a life to be preceded by practice, how could they be without such a cause? For smoke, which is not preceded by fire, is never observed to occur without being preceded by it. [Response: That too is incorrect.

Because the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), characterized by pervasion across space and time, cannot be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—for direct perception is observed to have as its cause the apprehension of only that which is immediately present—it is not logical to claim through perception that "smoke is impossible without fire in all places and at all times."

Therefore, it is not established by means of perception and non-perception that smoke is preceded by fire in all cases; how, then, can the existence of another life and a future world be proven by such an example? Consequently, some [qualities] such as wisdom and intelligence are preceded by similar practice in a previous state, while others are preceded by the bodies of parents. Furthermore, wisdom and the like do not appear as objects of cognition with a nature distinct from the body, and since the body alone is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance of those qualities, how can one justify a different arrangement?

Now, how can there be a body distinct from those of the parents without the influence of previously acquired *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit)? But surely, by this very fact, a deviation [from the rule] is observed; for it is not always the case that the effect must strictly correspond to its cause. Therefore, even if the offspring's body arises from a body of the parents that is dissimilar [to itself], yet differs from them in terms of wisdom, intelligence, and so forth—if at other times that body were to arise imitating their form, what contradiction would there be in this? Just as in some cases a lotus-root (*śālūka*) arises from another lotus-root, and likewise in some cases [a creature] arises from cow-dung.

Conceptual construction arises from instruction, or for some, from the perception of an object possessing that form. Now, if conceptual construction arises even from perception, how could it occur without the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of prior conceptual constructions? In that case, one must also ask: how can a lotus (*śālūka*) arise even from cow dung without [prior] lotuses? Therefore, this is merely a matter of the relationship between cause and effect.

Furthermore, since there is no restrictive rule in that regard, consciousness might arise from the bodies of the parents rather than from [the previous] consciousness; or, just as one conceptualization arises from another even when separated by an interval, so too it might arise from the very body of the parents despite the separation—we see no difference between these cases. And just as multiple offspring can be produced from the body of a single pair of parents, so too all progeny could arise from a single Brahmā; thus, no one would ever take on a different species of birth, and the existence of a future world would not be established.

For the mere relationship with one's mother and father is not the next world, as that would contradict the acceptance of what is desired [in the scriptures]. Now, if it is argued that the next world is established by relying on a self that is without beginning or end—since no mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*) is possible apart from a single experiencer, and such synthesis is never observed in the case of different experiencers—that too has been refuted;
for there is the statement: "Due to the absence of one who goes to the next world, there is an absence of the next world."

For the self, which is without beginning or end, is not established by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it were established by inference (*anumāna*), there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the self would be established once the invariable concomitance (*avinābhūtatva*) of the conceptualization of synthesis (*anusandhāna-vikalpa*) with a single form is established; and the synthesis would have its invariable concomitance with that [self] established once the self is established. Thus, because of the existence of this mutual dependence, neither of the two is established. And what is unestablished cannot be proven by that which is unestablished.

Furthermore, since perception and recollective synthesis (anusandhāna) occur in a temporal sequence of cause and effect as established by direct perception, how can the existence of a self (ātman) be proven on the basis of that recollective memory? Moreover, since there is no cognizer residing within the body, how could there be a transition into the body of another birth? If it is argued that this transition occurs through a continuity of an intermediate state body (antarābhava-śarīra), even that does not differ from the case of the next world.

Furthermore, no transition [of the self] is observed during one's lifetime in this world; that it will occur at the time of death is difficult to ascertain, so the existence of another world is not established. Alternatively, even if another world were established, since the connection between specific actions and their fruits remains unproven, the proof of the existence of another world through inference would be entirely futile. If, however, the connection between specific actions and their fruits is established through scripture (*āgama*), then the existence of another world is likewise established by scripture alone; what, then, is the use of the exertion of inference?

Nor can the existence of another world be established through scripture (*āgama*), because its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not proven. It is not reasonable to accept another world and so forth when it is established by what is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), for that would entail the same acceptance of its non-existence as well. Therefore, without first demonstrating a means of knowledge that establishes another world, it is not reasonable to state an etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word "existence" (*bhāva*) that touches upon its actual meaning. However, if this is done in the same manner as the etymological derivation of words such as "cow" (*go*) and so on, then we too shall not direct our minds toward questioning the means of knowledge that establishes it. This is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

[The Counter-Argument – The Establishment of the Other World] To this it is said: Regarding what was stated—that "we are merely making an inquiry"—it must be addressed: Is this inquiry being made by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or without a valid cognition? If it is by means of a valid cognition, that is untenable; for as to that effect which is the valid cognition, is it perception (*pratyakṣa*), or is it inference (*anumāna*) and so forth? If it were perception, that is untenable, because perception, by its very nature of non-investigative [immediacy], lacks the skill required for the composition of an investigation into the nature of an inquiry.

Furthermore, it is not logical for even perception (*pratyakṣa*) to possess the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), because according to your own admission, its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is impossible. That impossibility arises because a defining characteristic must be a property that establishes the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the thing defined]. In this regard, one must admit that the property establishing the essential nature of perception’s validity is the characteristic of non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*). And that non-contradiction must be admitted as being invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with the validity of perception; otherwise, the validity of perception could not be established from that [non-contradiction] if it were otherwise.

Alternatively, if [the probans] were established by any means whatsoever, then anything undesirable might also be established, which would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, that invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) must be understood through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for if one were to apprehend another object based on a connection that has not been understood, then even a resident of the Coconut Island (*nālikeradvīpa*) would apprehend fire from smoke, since he too would have an unapprehended connection. Moreover, the understanding of invariable concomitance must be accepted as being established by a means of valid cognition through a pervasion across all places and times.

Otherwise, if this [reliability] were understood only in that specific perceptual instance where consistency and validity are apprehended, then validity would be established only for that instance due to its non-discrepancy, and not for other instances, because it is not apprehended there. Furthermore, an individual instance whose relationship between the definition and the definiendum has been apprehended does not persist across different places and times, because that specific perceptual instance perishes at that very moment and does not extend to other instances.

Alternatively, in the case of a universal (*anugama*), it lacks the nature of a particular (*vyakti-rūpatā*), because that which is pervasive is by definition a universal (*sāmānya-rūpa*), and you do not admit such a thing. Or, if you do admit it, then it is not logical to reject it by demonstrating the absence of an object for inference characterized by a universal.

Furthermore, if the cognition of the pervasion and inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the definiendum (*lakṣya*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is admitted to arise from perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is incorrect; for you admit that the function of perception consists solely in the manifestation of its own proximate object.

Now, if—in one particular individual instance—through perception one understands the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between those two, namely non-contradiction and validity, then even in another case, by means of perception itself, there is an understanding of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) through the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the definition and the definiendum, in the form: "Perception of such a kind is valid. Why, then, should there not likewise—in other cases—an understanding of the invariable concomitance of the effect-definition reason (*kāryahetu*) with its own probandum through universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), in the form: "An effect characterized by such cognition arises from a cause characterized by such cognition"?

By means of this, the refutation you have leveled against the proponent of inference—namely, that "inference is not a valid means of knowledge because the relationship of invariable concomitance cannot be grasped through pervasion"—is rendered untenable. Furthermore, the property characterized by non-contradiction, which establishes the definition of the validity of perception, must be ascertained as being dependent upon perception.

Otherwise, the establishment of the definition and the definiendum of validity (*prāmāṇya*) would not occur in that very case, because for something unrelated to anything else, there is an absence of both proximity and distance; consequently, it would follow that such an establishment could occur elsewhere as well.

And if this is accepted, then just as the property characterized by "conformity" (*saṃvāditva*) is apprehended as being related to the perceptible subject (*dharmin*) even when the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) is not yet apprehended, so too smoke is apprehended as being related to that location even when fire is not yet apprehended in one part of the mountain. How then can it be said that "the whole [mountain] is the probandum (*sādhya*), and in relation to that, the presence of the reason (*pakṣadharmatva*) must be understood; and that without the cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject, there can be no cognition of that location as qualified by the probandum-property, namely fire"?

Alternatively, would there not be the following objection: "If [the reason] is understood through practice (*pratipatti*), then the pursuit of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth is useless, because that [reason] has already arisen prior to such understanding. Even if one understands that it is a property of a subject which is a part of the whole—since the whole is metaphorically designated as the 'probandum' (*sādhya*)—there is no fault in understanding it as a property of the subject; yet, if the reason were thus merely metaphorical (*upacarita*), inference would become secondary (*gauṇa*). Since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be secondary, the determination of an object through inference would be impossible. Is this not the occasion for such a challenge?

Even when defining the validity of perception (*pratyakṣa-prāmāṇya-lakṣaṇa*), this [same argument] has been established as being equally applicable to all [cognitions]. And when it is accepted that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the definition of non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*) and the objects characterized by the validity of perception through a universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), and when the property (*dharma*) of non-contradiction—which establishes validity—is admitted therein according to the previously stated reasoning, then how is it that inference (*anumāna*) is not likewise accepted as a means of valid cognition? For instance: "Whatever is perceived..."

"For that knower of the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), that [reason] is the indicator of that [object] wherever such a relation exists"—this much alone is the definition of inference as well. And this is accepted by the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Mīmāṃsaka), who accepts the definition of the validity of perception. Likewise, the validity of inference is indeed accepted, because the very same characteristic of non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*) which constitutes the validity of perception also constitutes the validity of inference. As it has been said:
"In the absence of an object, there is no existence; therefore, validity exists even in the case of perception. (S. 73)
"When the non-existence of that which is dependent [on another] is its cause, both are equal" (PVin I 3).

Since the non-existence [of perception] when the object is absent is the nature of its correspondence (*saṃvāda*) and the basis for its validity, and since this is the same for inference—which arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*) that does not exist when the object to be proven is absent—why is its validity not also accepted?

Furthermore, this Cārvāka, who maintains that perception is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), if he explains the definition of perception to others who do not understand it, from what means of valid cognition does he ascertain their possession of cognition? It cannot be from perception, because the mental states of another's mind cannot be known through perception; rather, having ascertained for himself through a means of valid cognition that activity and speech are preceded by cognition, he infers it in others as well upon seeing such [activity and speech] in them.

One understands its relation to that [object], and consequently, one communicates it through those [means]. And if this is accepted, then the fact that the signs—such as activity and speech—are invariably concomitant with their own probandum, characterized by a relation to cognition, and that they possess the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), are thereby admitted. Thus, how could the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) of the object that gives rise to inference be unestablished? For we do not reject inference; rather, we reject that which is called a "sign" (*liṅga*) by proponents of inference when it lacks these three characteristics.

The statement, "That which is accepted does not constitute a valid definition," does not merit praise—given that, for the purpose of establishing the definition of perception, you have necessarily established the acceptance of the three-fold mark of the logical reason (*trirūpa-hetu*) upon accepting the thorough knowledge of the mental states of others? Or rather, [it is said] to us: "We also accept perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, in formulating its definition, the acceptance of the validity of inference (*anumāna*) is inevitable. Thus, [the objection] is directed at us.

You might argue: "The statement that 'perception alone is the only means of valid cognition' is made with reference to the perception of worldly common practice (*loka-saṃvyavahārin*) which is not characterized by the definitions of the technical treatises (*tāntrika*). For this very reason, in the textual sequence beginning with 'inference is not a valid means of cognition,' the lack of validity is established for inference that is preceded by a perception defined by those technical definitions, and not for that which is proficient in the conventions of ignorant people such as cowherds."

The claim that the cognition of fire arises merely from the perception of smoke is not tenable; for even that [cognition] is, in reality, shown to be preceded by perception as defined by the experts, since it is produced by the force of smoke—which is a property of the subject (the mountain) whose connection with its own probandum has been ascertained through a means of valid cognition operating upon a locus such as a kitchen (the example).

"This is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and this is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this smoke"—since such conventional usage is of no consequence for the foolish world, including cowherds and others, and since the non-contradiction of perception is the definition of its validity, which has been established by those who maintain that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥprāmāṇya*) in whatever way it occurs, this has already been shown in the commentary on that term and is not stated again.

Thus it is established: according to your own view, there is no possibility of a defining characteristic that establishes the validity of perception; or, if such a characteristic were to exist, the validity of inference would also be established. Therefore, perception cannot serve as the basis for raising an objection.

Nor does inference and the like serve to challenge [the opponent], because we do not accept inference and so forth as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, even if we do not accept inference and the like as valid means of knowledge, nevertheless, since the opponent accepts them as such, a challenge is directed at the opponent by means of that which is established for him; [this is what is meant].

Now, is that [cognition] for the opponent established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that is, is it an object of his acceptance as being valid—or is it not established by valid cognition? If it is established by valid cognition, then it would likewise be an object of valid cognition for you yourself; for it is not logical that an acceptance established by valid cognition should belong to one person and not to another.

Now, if the opponent accepts inference and the like as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) despite their being invalid (*apramāṇa*), then it is not proper to subject them to scrutiny by means of that which is invalid; for that which is invalid lacks the capacity to do so, just as it lacks the capacity to establish the existence of another world (*paraloka*). Alternatively, if he has accepted their validity because he does not understand the definition of a valid means of knowledge, then one may indeed employ those very means—established for him—to scrutinize the means of knowledge he intends to use for proving the other world and so forth.

Surely, that [object] is intended by another as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to ignorance; and a thing, being perceived as something other than it is through ignorance, does not conform to the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it. Otherwise, even a great medicine or the like, which is considered poison by the ignorant, would be capable of performing its own function when given to them by one desiring to kill them.

Alternatively, we do not subject the means of valid cognition that establish the next world to an inquiry by means of inference and so forth—whether through a validity established independently or through a validity understood as accepted by the opponent; rather, if the opponent accepts such supersensible objects as the next world and so on, then he must state the means of valid cognition that establishes them, for the determination of the object of knowledge is dependent upon the means of valid cognition, and because that means of valid cognition lacks the necessary characteristics and so forth.

The objection is made in the form of an inquiry characterized by such an investigation as "the non-existence of even that which is intended as its object"; thus, for those who follow the doctrine of Bṛhaspati, there is no room for defects such as the failure to establish the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) in the presentation of an independent inference (*svatantrānumāna*). [Objection: Even so, by this very method, you yourself have, in your inquiry regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes supersensible objects such as the next world, effectively set forth an inference known as a *prasaṅgasādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) and its contrapositive form.

For instance—by stating that "the determination of the objects of cognition (prameya) is based upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)," you have demonstrated that the establishment of the objects of cognition has the means of valid cognition as its very cause. And this is an argument by reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasādhana), which is characterized by showing that when the relationship of pervader and pervaded (vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva) is established, the acceptance of the pervaded is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance of the pervader. Therefore, you must demonstrate that the establishment of the objects of cognition is pervaded by the operation of the means of valid cognition.

Otherwise, the determination of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) would occur even without the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, why would there not be a determination of the next world and so forth, even when one subjects the means of valid cognition that establish the next world and such to critical inquiry? Furthermore, if one accepts the means of valid cognition that apprehend the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), how can one reject the operation of the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) or the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) as they function to establish the next world and so forth? For when a means of valid cognition exists that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*), the operation of inference is established without effort.

If there is an absence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would also be an absence of the determination of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) which is based upon them; this is the contrapositive of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*). And that [contrapositive] consists in the nature of an inference arising from the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), namely: "In the absence of the pervader, there is also the absence of the pervaded."

This inference, which takes the form of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) and its contrapositive, operates only when the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) has been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, you have yourself, by your own words, given the final seal of approval to the validity of the means of cognition that establishes pervasion and to the inference obtained through its grace; therefore, we shall not exert ourselves further in establishing the validity of inference and the like.
Consequently, the statement that "all the aphorisms of Bṛhaspati consist merely of challenges" appears, according to the reasoning already stated, to be devoid of any meaningful content.

As for what was said—that perception, by virtue of having only proximate objects as its domain, does not function to apprehend the next world and so forth because it arises from the eyes and other [senses]—that is not a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, as for the statement that "supersensuous yogic perception does not exist either, because like the next world, it is unestablished," that is merely the word of one whose memory has failed, since it was demonstrated immediately prior that yogic perception is indeed inclined toward the apprehension of supersensuous objects.

Furthermore, the claim that inference does not operate in the absence of what has been previously perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is inconsistent. For it is observed that inference regarding an imperceptible object, such as fire, proceeds only after the relationship [between the mark and the object] has been grasped through direct perception; this same logic applies to the proof of the next world (*paraloka*) by means of inference. Why, then, should it be considered unobserved or defective? To illustrate: whatever is an effect is produced from another effect, just like an effect characterized as cloth and so forth. And this birth is an effect. Therefore, the existence of the next world is established by this reason. To explain further:
"Existence or non-existence would be eternal, because [an eternal entity] does not depend on anything else for its cause;
for it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of things is possible. [PV I 35–37]

First of all, it is not unestablished that this birth is an effect; for if it were not an effect, being independent of causes, it would follow that it must either exist eternally or not exist at all. Now, one might argue that the occasional nature of things arises from their own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), since the dependence on a causal relationship has never been perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) such that its absence would cause [the effect] to cease; for indeed, the causal relationship itself is not established by direct perception.

If this is so, then since the causal relationship with an external object is likewise unestablished, there would be non-duality insofar as there is only self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). However, if that too is absent upon investigation, it follows that everything is empty, which entails the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of all worldly activity (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, just as the dependence of the self upon an external object is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—for otherwise even this present world would not be established, since it is impossible for something to be a grasper if its nature as being produced by that [object] is not cognized through direct perception; [so too must the external object be admitted].

Thus, just as perception must be accepted here as a means for achieving the goals of this world—since it establishes its own connection with its object through its own nature—in the same way, that very same thing is the means for achieving the goals of the next world; therefore, the existence of the next world is established by inference. And just as the dependence of perception upon external objects is proven by its occasional occurrence, and just as smoke is proven to be dependent on fire, so too the occasional occurrence of this present life proves its dependence upon another birth.
Consequently, just as in the case of fire and external objects, inference is established regarding the next world as well.

In this case, it is indeed logical that this present birth occurs only occasionally, since it arises merely from the causal complex of parents who existed in a previous birth. But if that were so, then the occasional occurrence of the perception of smoke and its direct awareness would result solely from a specific causal complex consisting of a particular location and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); consequently, the cognition of fire as an external object would not be established, leading to the absence of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

If, then, the existence of fire as an external object is established solely from a specific difference in form that is possible without being otherwise, then likewise, the existence of one's own previous birth distinct from one's parents is established here simply from a specific difference in form such as wisdom, intelligence, and so forth.

Likewise, it is ascertained that this very specific form of cognition—which is distinct from the cognitions of those suffering from ophthalmia and the like—cannot exist for perception without an external object; otherwise, since no external object would be established, there would be nothing but the non-dual consciousness (saṃvedanādvaita) asserted by the Buddhists, and consequently, there would again be an absence of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). In the same way, let it be ascertained through inference that a specific form belonging to this life is connected to a specific cognition existing in another birth, on account of the specific nature of the cognition produced in this life.

Now, if one were to maintain that determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) itself is indeed [the means of knowledge] from the perspective of ultimate reality for the cognizer—following the argument of the Mīmāṃsakas and others beginning with the verse, "Thereafter, the object is [cognized] again through its properties" (ŚV 4.120)—then this would serve as proof that the cognition of a pillar or other objects standing before one while awake, which arises from smoke, is preceded by external fire. By accepting this, proponents of the existence of a future life consider their own position to be established without effort, according to the maxim: "What is perceived is not untenable. (S. 75)

For just as the proof that one is born from parents is established through a form of certainty, so too here, the proof that one is connected to a previous birth—established by the specific forms of cognition and other factors in this life that are distinct from the conditioning of this present life—would likewise be ascertained by direct perception; thus, there is no loss of the next world.

Furthermore, a cognition of certainty does not transcend the status of inference during the stage of non-habituation, because—due to its similarity to previous forms—it is established as such and does not escape being an object of inference (anumeya), according to the principle: "Because [the following] is perceived during the stage of non-habituation, namely the pursuit of positive concomitance (anvaya), negative concomitance (vyatireka), and the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā); and because during the stage of habituation, the pursuit of the property of the subject and so forth is not experienced elsewhere either, it is established that the next world is known through inference."

If it were argued that inference does not exist at all in such a case due to the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), [we reply: if that were so, then because all distinctions would be absent, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be annihilated. Since one who desires worldly transaction cannot accept such annihilation, inference must necessarily be accepted by one seeking to engage in transaction. By this, it has been established that inference possesses validity even in the absence of being preceded by perception. Nor does the fault of mutual dependence apply even when inference is preceded by inference, for that very fault of mutual dependence is refuted through the actual engagement in worldly transaction.

As for the argument that inference cannot function because it would lead to an infinite regress if it were preceded by another inference, that too is incoherent. For if that were the case, then even regarding an object grasped by perception, there could be no removal of doubt or conflicting views without the operation of inference; since perception would thus have no scope regarding external objects, the consequence would again be either non-duality (*advaita*) or emptiness (*śūnyatā*), resulting in the cessation of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, by the force of worldly transaction itself, that very infinite regress is avoided.

This has been stated as a concessive argument (*abhyupagamavāda*); otherwise, perception (*pratyakṣa*) functions for the sake of establishing external objects. Likewise, for the purpose of proving the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) demonstrated [in the inference], according to the view of some, it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), while according to others it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and produced by the operation of the sense organs such as the eye; according to yet others it is mental (*mānasa*); according to some it is a cognition useful for grasping exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); and according to others it is a form of indirect valid cognition (*parokṣapramāṇa*) called "inference" (*ūha*), which arises from the power of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) and is devoid of logical marks (*aliṅga*). In that regard:

Since [the opponent] maintains that [the relation] is established through activity, how could you urge against the proponent of the afterlife the faults of infinite regress and mutual dependence regarding the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) by means of inference?!!!20

As for what was stated—that "all inference is unestablished as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for us," and so forth—that too is incoherent. For, do you intend to establish the invalidity of inference in general through the passage beginning with "inference is not a means of valid cognition," or is it a rejection of the definitions provided by the experts (*tāntrika*), or rather a refutation of inference regarding supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*)? First of all, the negation of inference in its entirety is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence of the total cessation of worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*).

For the learned, upon seeing a certain object, necessarily understand some other object, but there is no comprehension of everything from every [perceived] thing. And it has been said by Ānanda: "One who has departed from his own home ought not to return to it again."

Now, having observed something, one must postulate a mark (*nimitta*) for the cognition of another thing; and that [mark], which possesses an invariable concomitance (*niyatasāhacarya*) and is designated by the term "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*), has been postulated by the Naiyāyikas and others. And the cognition of that [concomitance] is apprehended through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) aided by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*). Because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is apprehended by way of universals (*sāmānya*), spatial deviation and the like do not constitute a sublation, nor does the infinity of individuals, since in both cases the universal is one.

And just as in mental perception there is the manifestation of all individual instances drawn in by a universal—such as in the cognition "one hundred" where, by the delimitation of the number one hundred, there are objects that were previously apprehended and are drawn in as qualifiers of the scope of that number—one indeed has the cognition, "These are one hundred. Furthermore, the existence of the universal is established by its being the object of a recurring, non-sublated cognition.

Thus, in this way, the perceived [reason], by establishing another object with which it has an invariable concomitance, brings about the proof. And perception necessarily belongs to that which is situated somewhere; that itself is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Then, upon the recollection of the connection, there follows the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*).

But for one who does not encounter an obstruction, how is it that there is no comprehension of everything from everything? Or, if you accept [the existence of a relation], then the consequence would be comprehension even when the relation has not been apprehended? To say "because of the absence of prior perceptions which produce the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the cognizer" is no answer, because if the relation is not apprehended, the production of the cognizer's impressions is impossible. Furthermore, an impression born of perception, if unmanifested, is not conducive to comprehension by its mere existence alone.

Nor does its existence occur without memory; nor is memory ever based on the destruction of an experience, because that would be impossible without a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and because destruction cannot be causeless. Even in cases where, regarding a familiar object, the cognition of another thing follows immediately upon seeing a different thing, there too the comprehension of that other thing occurs by relying on a prior sequence.

However, this is the distinction: in one case, because it has not been practiced, there is an awareness of memory in the interval; in the other case, due to practice, there is a lack of awareness even though [the memory] exists.

Some, however, assert that the perception of a yogin is the grasper of the relationship (*sambandha*), because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is understood through the inclusion of all [instances]; thus, the objection that there would be no manifestation of individuals scattered across space and time—expressed as "wherever... wherever"—is untenable. Therefore, for one who grasps the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the state of being a yogin exists in a single moment. This is not different from the previous [view]. Consequently, when logicians reflect upon the cause for the firm cognition of one thing from the sight of another thing in the world, they formulate [the requirements] such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*).
Thus, even if the technical definitions [of the logicians] are rejected, [our position remains valid].

If it is argued that while those cognitions which have already arisen possess validity, those cognitions yet to be produced—namely, the inferences regarding supersensible matters such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), the next world (*paraloka*), and the omniscient being (*sarvajña*)—are to be rejected, that is incorrect. If this is said with reference to cognizers who have not yet grasped the [logical] relation (*sambandha*), then the same applies to smoke and other such signs. Alternatively, if it is said because the appearance of supersensible things like the next world does not arise even for those who have grasped the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), that too is incorrect.

For those who have grasped the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of a specific effect with its specific cause, they indeed understand the afterlife and so forth from that [effect]; therefore, it is not understood by what qualification the inference of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*) is rejected? Even though the concomitance (*sāhacarya*) is no different, it is the necessity residing in the pervaded (*vyāpya*) that is the operative factor, not that residing in the pervader (*vyāpaka*); hence, even in the case of co-extensive (*samavyāptika*) relations, comprehension occurs solely through the medium of the pervaded.

Furthermore, when certainty is attained regarding the necessary connection (*niyatatā*) and another object is understood, there is neither sublation (*bādhā*) nor obstruction (*pratibandha*), because it is impossible for a single entity to possess distinct forms (*rūpabheda*). Consequently, what was stated—that the "contradictory-to-the-particular" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) and the "non-deviating-contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) are possible—is also refuted, since contradictory inferences and oppositions occur everywhere, and the non-deviating-contradictory occurs in some cases.

This is because the relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) cannot be grasped, due to differences in state, place, time, and so forth; thus, according to the aforementioned principle, the status of inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is untenable.

When the cognition of an imperceptible object occurs through its general form based on something else—a process well-known in the world—the Buddhists nevertheless postulate a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by causal relations and the like as the basis for that cognition. As it has been said:

"Or from the relation of cause and effect, or from an essential nature (*svabhāva*) which acts as a restrictor; the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is established through non-observation [of the contrary], not through observation," and so forth. [PV I 31–33]
Likewise:
"Otherwise, what necessity would there be for another [cause] to be determined by others?
Or [if it were] a property caused by a different object, it would be like the dye on a cloth. (PV I 32–34). And: [as stated in the same passage].

For instance: if smoke, being perceived in a certain place such as a mountain, were to exist even without fire, then its status as an effect of that [fire]—which was established through specific perception and non-perception (*viśiṣṭapratyakṣānupalambha*) by way of following the properties of the burner—would not exist at all. Since it would lack a cause, it would not be perceived anywhere; or else, it would be perceived at all times, in all places, and in every form, because that which lacks a cause must exist at all times.

And if intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were to exist apart from the entity (*bhāva*), then, because the entity would consequently fall into being devoid of intrinsic nature, it would follow that intrinsic nature itself does not exist. Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for that [intrinsic nature] is precisely perception (*pratyakṣa*), which—though designated by the term "specific perception and non-perception" (*viśiṣṭapratyakṣānupalambha*)—is subsumed under the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*); this was demonstrated during the discussion on ascertaining the necessary connection of the reasons that establish an omniscient being. As for the "essential-reason" (*svabhāvahetu*), however, the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against its contrary is the nature of the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

However, some accept a specific [type of] perception. In any case, one must admit a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between universals and individuals—either by way of the universal itself or by way of the individual's nature as excluded from what is not that [universal]; otherwise, if one thing were understood from another without such a connection, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes this connection must necessarily be accepted.

Otherwise, even if one were to understand one thing from another based on a connection that has not been grasped, the same undesirable consequence would persist. When that object whose connection has been grasped is perceived, it brings about the establishment of the probandum; its "property-of-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) consists in its being a property of that [subject], and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends this is either perception or inference. As Dharmakīrti stated:
"The ascertainment of the property-of-the-subject occurs through perception or through inference. (cf. *HB* 2.12f)

Therefore, since there is no difference between that which is established by worldly consensus and inference characterized by tantric definitions, the capacity to prove supersensuous objects such as the next world belongs to that [worldly consensus] alone; thus, if its validity were not accepted, it would follow that even this present world could not be accepted.

Furthermore, it is not necessary here to deliberate whether it is non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), yogic perception, or inference (*ūha*) that determines the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*); nor is it relevant to consider whether that concomitance is characterized by a fixed coexistence or consists of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and so forth. For, just as fire is understood from smoke, the existence of another world—whose nature is the consciousness of one's own previous births—is established through the specific effects of cognition, such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and intelligence (*medhā*).

Therefore, the web of arguments set forth by the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) in order to demonstrate the invalidity of inference (*anumāna*) should be regarded as refuted; it is not criticized word for word here for fear of making the treatise too voluminous. (S. 77)

As for what was also said—that because perception does not operate regarding the next world, the existence of the next world is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone, namely by the fact that this present birth would otherwise be inexplicable—that too is not correct; for it has been demonstrated that every determinate cognition functions by following its antecedent, and thus possesses the nature of inference (*anumāna*). If it is argued that there is no inference here because the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) cannot be grasped, [we reply]: in that case, who could address faults to whom regarding that very non-duality or emptiness?

Therefore, since the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) occurs through perception or through inference (*ūha*) as employed in conventional practice, how could the existence of the next world not be established by means of inference? As for the argument that the present birth arises solely from the causal complex of mother and father, and thus it is not logical to prove a "next world" consisting of elements distinct from that birth—that too has already been refuted. For, since the cognition of perception occurs merely through the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), external objects are not established by perception—just like cognitions in dreams and so forth—and thus the position favored by the Buddhists would follow as a consequence, which is undesirable.

As for the argument advanced—that because perception has only proximate objects as its domain, it lacks the capacity to grasp a logical connection (*pratibandha*) through the pervasion of space and time—that too is of no consequence; for if this were so, perception would function only with respect to its own immediate nature due to having an extremely proximate object, and thus it would follow that it is merely self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) as asserted by the Buddhists and others, which results in the total destruction of all worldly transactional activity (*vyavahāra*), as has already been demonstrated.

"Therefore, because the operation of inference proceeds from the apprehension of the necessary connection (pratibandha) of a reason possessing the aforementioned characteristics—either through the power of non-conceptual perception capable of initiating worldly transaction, or through the means of valid cognition called *ūha* (presumptive reasoning) by way of universal pervasion across space and time—the present subject is not contradicted. This [objection] is also refuted by the passage beginning with "some [faculties], such as wisdom (*prajñā*), etc. and so forth.

Nor is the objection that "wisdom, intelligence, and so forth are not included within the nature of the body," and so on, tenable; for even if they were included therein, a solution is possible through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Since those [qualities] are produced from the bodies of the parents, and since the production of the offspring's wisdom and so forth from the parents' bodies is established by these two methods, there is no difference [in the offspring] despite the difference in causes. Let this further fault belong only to the follower of Bṛhaspati’s doctrine, who does not accept a difference in the cause even when there is a difference in the effect.

For us, however, the distinction between consciousness—which is subject to numerous contradictory properties such as joy and sorrow and which possesses an inward-turned aspect—and that which is to be known, such as the body and its like (which is characterized by numerous contradictory properties occurring sequentially, such as form, taste, smell, and touch, or the successive states of childhood, youth, and old age), is indeed established as distinct from what is apprehended by the cognitions arising from the external senses. For the superimposition of contradictory properties and the difference in causes are the differentiators of entities.

Since that [distinction] certainly exists between the body and consciousness, just as it does between water and fire, how can there be no difference between them? If they were non-different despite such a difference, it would entail the doctrine of the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaitavāda*); consequently, the four principles beginning with earth would cease to exist, resulting in the total collapse of worldly convention. Alternatively, if this effect [the body] is produced from the same causal complex as its mother, father, and previous birth, then there is no fault even in the position of non-distinction between consciousness and the body.

It was also stated previously that, even from something dissimilar, consciousness may arise from the bodies of the mother and father through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); for it is not the case that an effect must possess the entire form of its cause. That [objection] is also incorrect; because we do not say that an effect cannot be dissimilar to its cause, but rather that its status as an effect of that [cause] is established by its following the positive and negative concomitance of that [cause].

For instance: it is established that whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of a modification of something is the effect of that thing. For example, smoke—which follows the positive and negative concomitance of the fragrant scent and other qualities residing in the fire that burns substances such as *aguru*, camphor, and wool—is established as its effect. Likewise, how could subsequent cognitions, such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and intelligence (*medhā*), not be the effects of that [prior cognition], since they follow the positive and negative concomitance of the properties of the preceding cognition which is itself refined by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the teachings and so forth belonging to a single continuum?

Is this accepted? If it is not accepted, then even in the case of smoke and the like—which are well-known effects of fire and so forth—there would be no established proof that they are such effects; thus, once again, all worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) would be destroyed.

Therefore: "The mind necessarily follows the impression (*saṃskāra*) of that very [object]; the mind is inseparable from that, and for this reason, it is dependent upon the mind. (PV II 78) [Note: The phrase "XE '[PV II 78 Abweichung]' [PV II 78 Abweichung]" appears to be a metadata or editorial marker indicating a variant reading or deviation in the edition of *Pramāṇavārttika* II, verse 78.]

Furthermore, the specific relationship between cause and effect has already been established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by those who provide the word-commentary for the phrase "the eradication of false doctrines" (*kusamayavisāsaṇaṃ*) in the proof of the Omniscient One; thus, it is not stated again here.

As for the argument of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) based on the example of the lotus-root (*śālūka*)—just as a lotus-root may arise from cow dung, while some arise from a lotus-root of the same species, so too some [qualities] such as wisdom and intelligence arise from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), whereas others arise from the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*). (S. 78)

Others claim that it arises solely from the specific nature of the parents' semen and blood; this too is not correct, because even in that case, the possibility of a prior habituation to similar types exists. Otherwise, even when the use of elixirs and the like is common to both twins, there would be no fixed rule as to why one of them possesses wisdom, intelligence, and so forth in some respect while the other does not, since the application of the elixir is shared equally by both.

Furthermore, there is no distinction in the case of wisdom and the like when they arise from elixirs (*rasāyana*) and so forth; however, a distinction is observed between a lotus stalk produced from a lotus root or cow dung and one produced from something else. Moreover, since the phenomenon of recollecting past lives (*jātismaraṇa*) is observed, it is not logical that the specific effects such as wisdom and intelligence should arise solely from visible causes, namely the bodies of the mother and father.

Nor is there absolute dissimilarity in the case of cow dung and lotus roots, which have been presented as instances of deviation [from the rule]; for both are undifferentiated insofar as they are transformations of matter (*pudgala*) possessing color, taste, smell, and touch.

Furthermore, because consciousness and the body are established as being absolutely distinct—due to their respective orientations as inward and outward, their status as objects of apprehension for self and others, and their being experienced through cognitions produced by self-awareness and external sense organs respectively, which are based on the superimposition of numerous mutually contradictory properties—the relationship of material cause and its effect (upādānopādeyabhāva) is not tenable.

As for the observation of the relationship between material cause and its effect—characterized by the increase of consciousness and so forth corresponding to the increase of the body—which is put forward [as proof], that is inconclusive because it fails even in the case of large-bodied beings such as elephants or pythons, whose consciousness is minimal; thus, it does not establish that relationship.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the property of being its effect is established by the observation of changes in consciousness following changes in the body, that too is unproven, because among those of a virtuous nature (*sāttvika*) or those whose minds are directed elsewhere, no change in consciousness is perceived even when bodily changes such as cutting or wounding are present.

Furthermore, it is observed that even from a specific auxiliary cause (*sahakāri*) such as water, soil, and so forth, a distinction arises in the sprout and other effects produced by the material cause (*upādāna*), which is the seed. Thus, although the body and other factors serve as auxiliary causes, a distinction characterized by growth is not impossible for consciousness—which has as its material cause the prior cognition acquired through the distinctions gained from the refinement of learning and the like—when there is the consumption of specific food and so forth during the stage of youth.

As for what was also said—that even within a beginningless succession of parents, since such a consciousness exists even in remote ancestors, the occurrence of specific qualities such as wisdom and intelligence is indeed logical through the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—that too is incorrect; for it is generally possible for the wisdom of immediate parents to be awakened [in their offspring] as well.

Consequently, if self-awareness produced by the instruments such as the eye, or visual cognition itself, were to arise either simultaneously or sequentially, there would follow a recognition of the form "this was perceived by me alone" even with respect to the cognitions of other mental continua or their offspring; yet, no one ever perceives a recognition of their own offspring or others based on the perception of the parents' cognition.

By this, the production of progeny from a single Brahmā is refuted; for if all living beings originated from one source, there would follow the undesirable consequence of mutual recognition among them, just as there is between the visual and tactile cognitions arising within a single continuum.

As for the claim that "the next world does not exist because the self is not perceived," that is incorrect, because such non-perception is unestablished. For instance, the self is indeed directly perceived through the cognition of "I" as distinct from the body, the senses, objects, and so forth. Nor is it reasonable to argue that it cannot be the object of a perceptual cognition produced by the sense-faculties—such as the eyes—because they lack the capacity to generate knowledge regarding a supersensible (atīndriya) self; this is because we accept that the self is grasped by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

For instance, in one who has withdrawn all activity of the sense organs and is situated in darkness, the cognition "I" arising in all living beings is experienced as self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*). And in that state, even though the body and so forth do not appear, the essential nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*) manifests as distinct from them. Nor can this cognition, being experienced, be denied; for if even what is being experienced were to be denied, it would lead to the absurd consequence of universal denial.

Nor is it the case that this [cognition] does not arise at all, for that would contradict its occasional occurrence. Nor does it originate from the operation of the external sense organs, because it arises even in their absence. Nor is it produced by causes such as words or logical marks (*liṅga*), since it is observed to arise even when those are absent. Furthermore, this is not invalid on account of being sublated, because the existence of a sublater in that regard is unestablished. Nor is it invalid due to being conceptual (*savikalpaka*), since conceptual cognition will also be established as being valid knowledge.

And sometimes, even at a time when the external senses are active, when one perceives an object such as "I know the jar," one perceives one's own self as well. For instance, in that case, just as there is the manifestation of the object as the object of action (*karman*), so too is there the manifestation of the self as the agent (*kartṛ*).

Nor can the body and so forth possess the status of a knower; for just as objects such as jars appear as distinct from the body by virtue of being objects of cognition—such that one thinks, "The jar and so forth are mine, I am the knower of the jar and so forth"—likewise, one thinks, "The body and so forth are mine, I am the knower of the body and so forth. Thus, because the aggregate of the body and so forth is equal to jars and other objects in its status as an object of cognition, it cannot be the knower.

Nor is there an appearance of the knower (*jñātṛ*); for if that were not appearing, there could be no such appearance as "these things appear to me and not to another. And if the manifestation of that [knower] were denied, how could even a jar or similar object be cognized? However, this much is the distinction: one [the jar] is the object of cognition, while the other [the self] is the agent of that cognition; yet it is not the case that [the self] does not appear. Therefore, since the manifestation of the self exists independently of signs (*liṅga*) and so forth, how can it be said that it is unperceived?

How could there be non-perception of that? For it is not reasonable to establish the invalidity or the nature of memory for this cognition—which is free from sublation, has an object not previously known, appears with a form as certain as the manifestation of an object produced by the senses, and appears in a form that is beyond doubt; therefore, even in this cognition, it is logical that what appears possesses immediacy itself, rather than being cognizable through another means of knowledge.

As for what they say here: "This appearance exists, but its status as perception (*pratyakṣatā*) is to be examined. For perception is knowledge arising from the operation of the sense faculties. And you have stated: 'Perception is the arising of cognition when there is contact with an existing object' (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.4). The status of the object as perceptible is due to its being the object of perception, but not directly, because it does not arise from the sense faculties themselves. In that regard, the perceptibility of jars and the like is established by the consensus of all people through their being objects of external sensory cognition; however, it is not so for the self."

Now, it might be argued as follows: "The self does not possess perceptibility in the same manner as a jar or similar objects, for that [perceptibility] is established in the case of a jar and so forth by virtue of being an object of sensory cognition (*indriyajajñāna*); however, the self is not an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How then is it perceptible? It is not perceptible because it is an object of cognition, but rather it is called 'perceptible' because it appears in a non-mediated (*aparokṣa*) manner."

Furthermore, that which was previously established as the proof for the existence of consciousness alone, or as being included within the cognition of jars and the like, is also untenable. For what is the meaning of "proof for the existence of another"? Does it mean the existence of the nature of consciousness itself, or its operation toward its own cognition? If the existence of the nature of consciousness itself is called its self-illumination, then an illustrative example must be stated.

Nor should it be doubted here that one need not seek an example for something directly perceived, since in such a subject of dispute, the seeking of a well-known example is observed. Furthermore, the lamp and the like are not the intended examples; for in those cases, some have established self-luminosity (*svaprakāśakatva*) on the basis of independence from light of the same class for its own cognition, but not on the basis of being ungraspable by the senses.

If they were ungraspable, then lamps and the like would be self-luminous, which would entail that even those blind from birth—who lack sight—would perceive them; therefore, lamps and the like are not self-luminous. As for the claim that they do not depend on another light, this merely means that a certain causal complex illuminates a particular object; it does not follow that because something is observed in one instance, it must necessarily apply elsewhere. Now, as for the second position, that too is untenable.

Precisely because [the self] is not perceived—indeed, no entity whatsoever, whether in the form of an agent or an instrument, is ever observed to possess an activity within itself as it does toward its own object. How, then, is there cognition of the self even when it is inferable, given the absence of another cognizer? There is no fault here, for when a single entity undergoes differentiation through distinct states by depending on instruments such as logical marks (*liṅga*), [the distinction between subject and object is established].

Furthermore, what is the meaning of this statement that [the self] possesses immediacy even while being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If you say it is "manifesting by its own nature as the knower," then are objects such as a jar not also perceived as having their own distinct natures? Therefore, since whatever is the nature of a thing is determined even when that thing is an object of valid cognition, the cognizer is not an object of cognition. To explain: his state of being a knower is his essential nature as the subject (*pramātṛ*), whereas the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) or the state of being knowable for a jar and so forth is the nature of the jar and so forth.

Therefore, just as that [cognition] is not non-perceptual because it appears in its own form (*svarūpa*), so too it must be accepted for the self (*ātman*). Otherwise, one would have to state a definition for the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of the self and so forth—which is indeed perceptual—that is distinct from the definitions of perception and the rest; and in that case, there would be a contradiction regarding the limited number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since self-awareness whose object is the self and so forth would not be included by any of the definitions of perception and the rest.

For this reason as well, it has been stated that there would be the undesirable consequence of having to admit consciousness in the result (the fruit) just as one does in the case of the cognizer. If it is argued that there is no fault because such an admission is made, it has been said accordingly:
"Consciousness is to be known only as consciousness itself, not as an object of cognition."

This has already been refuted previously: it is not the case that there is a lack of being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when there is the manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, if this were postulated, two internal cognitions would have to be imagined—one as the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpa*) and the other as the object; and that is improper, because since the manifestation of the object is established by a single [cognition] alone, what is the use of imagining two? If it is argued: "Imagination applies to that which does not manifest, but in the case of the two cognitions, there is a manifestation just as there is of a jar and so forth, therefore there is no imagination [of them]," [we reply:]...

If such appearances are established as valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), then even the cognition of an instrument—such as "I see the jar with my eye"—must be considered a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), just like the cognitions of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the result (*phala*).

Furthermore, that cognition of an instrument which some have described as being of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is also not at all consistent with reason.
