For instance, in the awareness "I see the jar with my eye," does the eyeball (*golaka*) constitute the eye, or rather something distinct from it? If the eyeball were the eye, no one would ever be blind. And as for something distinct from it, such as a ray of light (*raśmi*), that is not admitted [by you].

Or, even if it were admitted [that the word exists], it would not be an object of cognition; at the time of the cognition of a jar, one merely utters a sound. Thus, the utterance of the word is determined to be nothing more than that which pertains to the cognizer and the result [of the action], and not the two [the jar and its cognition] as objects of cognition, unlike the case of the instrument. For thus the logicians maintain: when the operation of the sense organ occurs, there is the manifestation of the object alone, as distinct from the body.
When questioned as to what its manifestation is, they offer silence as the answer, because it is impossible to designate it; therefore, the manifestation of the subject is untenable.

Surely the cognition "I am" is witnessed by all the world and cannot be denied. If it is not denied, is it with an object or without an object? How could cognitions that possess an uncontradicted form be without an object? Even if they have an object, if the knower does not appear [in the cognition], of what would this cognition be the object? It is not that the cognition is denied, nor is it without an object; rather, the Self—which appears as the subject—is not its object, nor does it appear as the knower [in the sense of being a mere instrument].

To this it is said: what, then, is the object? We reply that it is the body. For it is observed that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) between [the notion of self] and cognitions based on the body and so forth, such as "I am thin," "I am fat," and "I am fair."

But surely, in this way, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is also in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with cognitions such as "I am happy" or "I am suffering"; therefore, its object is not the body. As for the objection that it has the body as its objective support because we observe such coreferentiality as "I am fair," that too must be examined: it is observed that qualities such as fairness—which are distinct from the body and so forth—are not the locus of the ego; likewise, it is logical to establish that those qualities residing in the body and so forth are also not the locus of the ego.

And thus it has been stated by the author of the *Vārttika*: "For there does not arise in this seer the cognition, 'I am that which is my fair form'; rather, he indicates it in this way only by eliding the possessive suffix *-mat*. This is the meaning: the sense of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*) with respect to the body is metaphorical, not real; just as the sense of "I" is figurative when applied to something else that performs its function and is extremely close, as in "this which is here, that is I," so too is it with the body.

From this cause, this notion of "I" (ahaṅkāra) arises with respect to that which is not-self in nature—which is common to both [the self and the body] and is the object of the cognition of "this-ness"—and for that very reason, it also arises with respect to the body. However, the notion of "I" whose object is the Self is not metaphorical, because it manifests as a cognition of "I" that is not conflated with the cognition of "this"; thus, the cognizer is distinct from the body and so forth.

How is this so? Because of the apprehension that "this body is mine," and because of the absence of the apprehension that "this self is mine. [Objection: Is it not the case that the apprehension "this self is mine" does occur? [Reply: We say it does not occur. How then is it said thus? Only the word is uttered, but there is no possibility of such an apprehension. Even here, since the manifestation of the apprehension of "mine" is not observed, who can prevent the mere utterance of the word?

Is it now maintained that pleasure and so forth belong to the body? Not so; because of the absence of a connection with pleasure and so forth, this notion "I am happy" is a false cognition (*mithyā-pratyaya*), and it does not have the body as its objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore, it is established: since no appearance of a cognizer is observed, or rather, since the body appears as the cognizer when there is an appearance, the object of the notion of "I" is not something distinct from the body and such.

Furthermore, even though the body appears as the knower, its status as the locus of false cognition is established by valid means of knowledge due to the denial of its connection with intelligence (*buddhi*); however, if that [body] were insentient, no other knower could be established as an object of the means of perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), and so forth—this too is inconsistent.

Therefore, let it be that for the followers of Jaimini—who maintain that perception is defined by the sūtra "perception is the arising of cognition when there is contact of a person's sense-faculties with an existing object" (MS 1.1.4)—the fault of the cognition "I" not being perception due to its not being produced by the sense-faculties does not apply to us who follow the doctrine of the Jina. For according to us, perception is not exclusively that which is produced by the sense-faculties; rather, whatever clear cognition occurs with respect to an object, whether caused by the sense-faculties or the non-sense-faculties (the mind), that is perception in that regard.

Because it is accepted [by the scriptures], as stated by the primary authority: "That [perception] has the sense organs and the mind as its causes" (Tattvārtha-sūtra 1.14). Therefore, just as a jar or similar object is considered perceptible because it is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), what contradiction is there in the self also being directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)? For this very reason, it is said that while the perceptibility of a jar and so forth is established by virtue of being grasped by a distinct cognition, the self possesses perceptibility because it appears as non-external (*aparokṣa*).

And since that "proof by another" (*aparasādhana*)—whether as something independent or as included within the cognition of a jar and so forth—was previously established, what is the meaning here of the term *aparasādhana*? Having raised two alternatives—namely, whether it is the existence of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), or whether it is its operation toward the cognition of the object—the first position is refuted as follows: if it is said that the very existence of the nature of consciousness is what constitutes its self-illumination, then an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) must be stated; however, that is rejected, because it is improper to seek an illustrative example for an object that is perceived through direct experience (*adhyakṣapratīti*).

Now, even when a matter is perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), it is well known in the world that one still seeks an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*); therefore, such an example must be stated here as well. Thus, there is indeed an example characterized by a lamp or the like, in order to prove that cognition does not depend on another member of its own class for its own manifestation. To explain: just as the light of a lamp or similar source does not require another light for its own apprehension, so too cognition does not require a cognition of the same kind for its own apprehension.

The light serves as an illustration merely in this respect; however, its status as cognition is not thereby attained, such that one might urge the objection that—because it is not grasped by the sense organs—it would follow that it is perceived even by the blind, just as it is by those with sight. For it is not proper to attribute all the properties of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) to the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*); otherwise, the properties of sound, such as "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), would also follow for a jar, which would entail the absurd consequence that a jar too must be perceivable by the sense of hearing.

Nor can it be said that an object established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) remains unestablished in the absence of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); otherwise, when the living body is to be proven as possessing a self (*sātmaka*), its establishment through [the reason] "possessing breath and so forth" would not occur, because there is likewise an absence of a well-known similar instance.

If, on the other hand, even in the absence of a similar instance, the establishment of that [property] occurs there by the force of pure negative concomitance (*kevala-vyatireka*)—since there exists a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) such as a jar—then [it follows that]: wherever there is no self-luminosity, there is also no luminosity of objects. (S.

Since there exists a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) such as a jar and the like, why does consciousness not achieve the proof of self-luminosity through the reason characterized by the illumination of an object? As for what was said—that a certain causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for a certain object produces an illumination that appears in the cognition apprehending itself independently of any other illumination—that is indeed correct; for just as lamps, light, and so forth, arising from their own respective causal complexes, do not require another light of the same kind, [so too is the case for cognition].

While appearing in a cognition that apprehends itself, [objects] depend upon it; however, the consciousness arising therefrom through its own causal complex—which has the nature of illuminating its own object—does not depend on another cognition for its own apprehension, because the potencies of entities, whose births are dependent upon their own causes, are specifically determined.

As for the argument that things such as the light of a lamp, though independent of another light of the same kind for their own manifestation, nevertheless depend upon cognition for their apprehension—this is logical because they are of the nature of non-cognition, whereas cognition is by its very essence the opposite of that; thus, it is established that the position of the opponent is devoid of substance, for it is not reasonable to attribute a nature established in one instance to something else.

Now, if it is argued that the apprehension of light is an apprehension independent of anything else in between, then by the force of that example, the apprehension of cognition must also be independent of another cognition; however, this is not so, because such is never observed and because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.

Now, even if an object is thus perceived, if one were to claim that it is unperceived and that there is a contradiction [between perception and its existence], then for the Buddhist who asserts that cognition does not apprehend external things such as jars—just as it does not apprehend itself—because they are unperceived and because an insentient thing cannot be luminous, no crookedness of speech arises. For he too is capable of saying this: "An insentient object does not manifest by itself, like consciousness; otherwise, it would follow that its insentiency is lost."

Nor does it manifest from another, because consciousness—which would have to be distinct from blue, pleasure, and so forth—is non-existent due to its lack of being perceived. Now, if one argues that "the manifestation of blue" implies a manifestation of blue and the like that is distinct from the manifesting consciousness itself—otherwise, if there were a distinction between them, the perception of consciousness would not involve the appearance of that [object]—we reply: indeed, a separate appearance of the blue and its cognition is not possible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because blue and the like are experienced as inseparable from the light of manifestation, and because consciousness does not appear as something distinct from that.

Furthermore, it is not logical to maintain a distinction between blue and its cognition when they are not perceived as distinct by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the failure to perceive a distinction is the basis for the misconception of non-distinction, just as in the case of the nature of blue itself. Even if conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) delineates a distinction between blue and its cognition—such as "the experience of blue"—is it not the case that even non-distinction can be constructed as a distinction, as in "the body of a stone statue" or "the nature of blue"?

Now, if it is argued that non-difference (*abheda*), being established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is the sublater [of difference] and thus the mention of difference is not real, then since non-difference between blue and its cognition is likewise established by direct perception, the conceptualization of a difference between them cannot be real. Thus, it is established that blue and so forth, as well as pleasure and so forth, appear as self-luminous in nature; for there is no existence of a light distinct from them, since such a light does not appear.

Or, let it be granted that cognition (*bodha*) is distinct; even so, it is not logical that blue and other objects are its objects of apprehension. For instance, is cognition the illuminator of those objects at the same time as they exist, or at a different time? If it is at the same time, is it imperceptible (*parokṣa*) or self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*)? First, it cannot be imperceptible, because we shall refute this position while establishing the self-cognizability of knowledge through such arguments as: "For one whose apprehension is not perceived, the seeing of an object is not established. Nor...

It would be cognizable by another cognition, because the defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*) will be demonstrated against this position. However, in the view of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), just as consciousness, remaining internal, appears as self-cognized, so too at that same time do blue objects and the like appear as having a self-luminous nature while being connected to external space; since blue and its cognition appear simultaneously and independently, there can be no relationship of the cognized and the cognizer between them, just as in the case of the left and right horns of a cow.
Even if cognition were the apprehender of blue despite being simultaneous with it, it would follow that blue is also the apprehender of that cognition.

Although there is no difference in their simultaneous appearance, [the opponent claims] that cognition is the apprehender because it effects the grasping of blue and so forth, whereas blue and the rest are the objects of apprehension (*grāhya*). This too is not tenable; for no act of grasping appears as distinct from the cognition of blue. To explain: while cognition resides within as the locus of pleasure, blue and the rest appear clearly with their forms manifesting externally; however, no other act of grasping appears as an object of manifestation.

And if that [action] is not manifest, it is not logical for blue and so forth to possess the status of an object (*karman*) by virtue of being pervaded by it. Or, let there be an action distinct from the cognition of blue; even so, is that action itself perceived through itself, or through something else? In that regard, if the act of apprehension appears through itself, then—since the three factors, namely the cognition, the blue, and the act of apprehension, would appear simultaneously while submerged in their own intrinsic nature—there could be no linguistic convention regarding agent, object, and action. Alternatively, if the act of apprehension appears through something else;

[Objection: But surely, even there, another act of apprehension must be admitted—otherwise, its status as an object of apprehension would not be established—and yet, for that too, another act of apprehension must be admitted as the basis for its being an object; thus, there would be an infinite regress. [Reply: That is not so, because there is no further act of apprehension, since its own nature does not manifest [as an object]. Consequently, both internal self-awareness and external objects such as blue are indeed self-luminous.

If the doctrine of self-awareness alone (*svasaṃvitti-mātra-vāda*) is superior, then consciousness, being hidden within, would not be the cognizer of blue and so forth, but rather it would be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) itself. This being the case, there could not arise the cognition characterized by the adherence to the relationship of object and agent in the form "I know blue," because the relationship of object and agent would be absent in the case of the object. But surely, even in the absence of an object, a cognition is indeed observed, such as the apprehension of silver in mother-of-pearl?

Now, one might argue that this [cognition] is an error because a sublation arises later, whereas in the case of blue and so forth, there is no sublation of their status as objects and so on; therefore, they possess reality. But surely here too, there exists a sublation consisting in the perception of independence regarding the pair—the cognition and the blue—which are inherently connected in their own nature, [namely] the delineation of the relationship between object and agent. Well then, what is the cause of this error? For even an error does not arise without a seed. Is it not the case that a preceding error itself is the cause for the subsequent apprehension of the relationship between object and agent?

Since even the state of being an object and so forth from a prior delusion is itself another prior delusion, there is an beginningless succession of delusions; thus, the state of being an object and so forth is not the ultimate reality.

Alternatively, the cognition "blue," which determines only that much, is distinct; the thought "I," carrying an internal reflection, is different; and the cognition "I know" is yet another. Consequently, these three mutually unconnected cognitions appear in succession, and there is no relationship of object and agent, because such a relationship is impossible between two things existing at the same time, and since they do not even appear simultaneously when occurring at different times, the understanding of [the blue] as an object and so forth is in no way possible.

Furthermore, it may be argued that although the blue object exists prior to its perception, it does not appear then, whereas it does appear when that perception arises; thus, it possesses the status of an object (*karmatā*). This, however, is not at all sound. For the prior existence of the object is not established. Since the object is apprehended by the perception within the limits of its own time, it is indeed the blue that appears at the time of the perception, but not prior to it. How, then, could the prior existence of the object be established, given that the perception is absent at a time preceding it? Nor does the perception at that [present] time manifest the prior proximity of the object, for if it did, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that object appearing at all times.

If, however, the object is cognized prior [to its own perception] by another perception, then surely the existence of that object prior to that perception must also be determined by yet another [perception], resulting in an infinite regress. Therefore, since everything such as blue and so forth appears only at the time of its perception, its existence prior to that is not established.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the existence of the prior object is established by the determination "I see what was seen before," because it is impossible for the object currently being seen to attain identity with what was previously seen without the existence of that prior object—then by which [cognition] is their identity apprehended? Is it by the present seeing, or by the previous seeing? It cannot be by the previous seeing, because in that case, the object appears only as delimited by its own [past] time.

For by that [present cognition], the pervasion of the object appearing within it by the time of its present observation is not determined, because at that time, the present observation and so forth [of that past object] do not exist. Nor does what is non-existent appear, for that would entail the falsity of the observation. Furthermore, the pervasion of blue and so forth by a previous observation and the like is not determined by a present observation, because at the time of that [present] observation, the time of the previous seeing has already ceased.

Furthermore, perception does not engage with a contact involving a previously perceived appearance and so forth, precisely because that would entail the consequence of its being false. Therefore, every object is grasped by vision as being divested of connection with that previous seeing and the like; as for the state of having been previously seen, memory merely delineates it, and that [connection] is discarded, since there is no delineation of what was seen [in the present act of seeing]. Nor is the cognition "this is that very same thing" a single [undivided] entity; for "that" is the form of memory, while "this" is the own-nature of vision. Since these two cognitions possess the forms of the remote and the immediate respectively, they do not have a single nature; how, then, can there be an establishment of identity?

If it is argued that the prior existence of an object is established through inference—on the grounds that its subsequent perception would be impossible without prior existence—that too is incorrect; because the connection between subsequent perception and prior existence is not established, since prior existence is not proven in any way whatsoever. Nor is subsequent perception established as being pervaded by an unproven existence, such that the latter could be proven from the former.

Therefore, if perception were to arise independently of an external object, then, in the absence of any regulating factor, it would occur everywhere, at all times, and in every form. This objection is not valid, because the restriction of cognition is determined by the awakening of specific latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For instance, in the state of dreaming, a restriction regarding place, time, and form is observed for perception due to the power of latent impressions; thus, this same principle is appropriate for perception during the waking state as well.

However, the existence of the object is not established, nor is there a restriction of cognition based on its differentiation; therefore, the variety of cognitions does not arise from it. Consequently, the existence of blue and so forth prior [to cognition] is not established in any way whatsoever.

Now, what is the proof for the absence of prior existence? Is it not non-apprehension itself that serves as the proof? For if blue were of a nature connected with a previous time, it would be apprehended in that very form; yet it is not so, because it appears at all times only as existing at the moment of perception.

And whatever appears in a certain form exists in that very form; for example, blue, appearing as the nature of blue, exists exactly as such and not as the nature of yellow or other colors. Furthermore, every perceived form appears only as belonging to the present time, not as belonging to the past or other times; therefore, there is no existence of an object in the past. (S. 83)

Now, [the opponent argues: "Blue appears even when one's own vision has ceased, provided there is another's vision; therefore, because it is common [to both], blue is the apprehended object (*grāhya*). Consciousness, however, is the illuminator (*prakāśaka*) because it is not common. This too is not tenable; for the appearance of blue is not established as being common, since through perception one understands only its own manifestation. Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to the effect that "blue appears in another's vision," because as long as another's vision is not apprehended, the fact that blue and so forth are cognized by it cannot be apprehended.

Now, it might be argued that the commonality of blue and other objects is established through inference—namely, that just as there is an activity for the sake of grasping blue upon seeing it within one's own continuum, so too, because activity is observed in another continuum, an observation having that [blue] as its object is inferred. But this is not the case either; for by means of inference, the oneness of blue and so forth, which constitute the observations of oneself and others, cannot be established.

For that [cognition], arising from the observation of a similar convention, would establish the similarity of what is seen by another to what was previously seen by oneself; just as, from the observation of another smoke, one is able to apprehend a fire similar to the previous one, but not that very same fire created before, because the connection is determined through a universal. Therefore, even by means of inference, there is no identity of the apprehended form.

But surely even its difference is not established? For when there is a difference in manifestation, how could it be unestablished? [Otherwise] it would be impossible for it to distinguish—by excluding the manifestations of others—the manifestations of itself, and by excluding the manifestations of itself, the manifestations of others, as having a nature of differentiation. Therefore, although blue and other objects perceived by oneself and by another are treated identically in conventional practice, there is indeed a difference due to the difference in their manifestations;

otherwise, because one observes effects such as a mass of horripilation that are similar [in both cases], pleasure and so forth existing in one's own and another's continuum would have to be identical in reality.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the distinction between pleasure and so forth arises from the distinction between their respective continua (*santāna*), then one must ask: does the distinction between continua also arise from another distinction? If so, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Alternatively, if the distinction of the continuum is due to a distinction in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then let that same principle apply to pleasure and so forth as well; for otherwise, their distinction cannot be established. Indeed, one thing is not rendered distinct by the distinction of another, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Since blue and other objects appear both to themselves and to others, there is a distinction in their appearance; therefore, they are not a single unity.

Now, if it is argued that there is oneness because of the oneness of location, [we reply: surely oneness is not tenable even for a location, since—according to the reasoning just stated—it is seen by both oneself and others. Therefore, like the form of the apprehender, blue and other objects, appearing to each person, are indeed distinct. And that [object], because it is perceived at the same time [as the subject], is self-luminous, just like the apprehender.

Now, it may be argued that the aspect of the subject (*grāhakākāra*) is the cognizer because it is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), whereas the aspect of blue (*nīlākāra*) is the object (*grāhya*) because it is insentient (*jaḍa*). To this, it is replied: what is this "nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpatva*) of cognition? If it is its own immediate (*aparokṣa*) nature, then that too exists for blue and so forth; thus, they would not be insentient. If, on the other hand, the immediate nature of blue and so forth arises from something else and is therefore the object, then surely the entire nature of cognition also arises from the sense organs and so forth, and thus it too would be an object. If you say that what is an effect of the sense organs and so forth is not the cognized, then let blue and so forth also be an effect of the eyes and so forth, yet they would still not be objects.

Furthermore, if it is argued that consciousness is eternal because its nature is consciousness, whereas blue and other objects are non-eternal because their nature is to be manifested, that too is incorrect. The form of a pillar or similar object arises as something immediate through the power of the eyes and other senses; let that pillar be non-eternal, but how can it be the "grāhya" (the apprehended object)? For that which is produced from something else cannot be the object known by that [cause], as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, pillars and other objects, being of a non-mediately-apparent nature, are self-luminous; however, consciousness—whether eternal or non-eternal—merely manifests at that time, but it is not the knower, because otherwise both would incur the status of being the grasped and the grasper toward one another. Now, if it is argued that consciousness is the grasper because it is directed toward the blue, what is this so-called "being directed toward" on the part of consciousness? If it is its existence at the time of the blue, then since that [existence] belongs equally to the blue at that time, the blue too would be the knower of consciousness. If, on the other hand, this directedness is something else, then that which shines while immersed in its own nature would have to be a third nature.

For instance: its being directed toward that [object] is its activity (*vyāpāra*). If that activity were to operate upon the blue, then there would be another activity with respect to that [first activity], leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it does not operate [upon the blue], then by virtue of that [activity], consciousness would not possess the status of a grasper (*grāhakatva*), nor would the blue and so forth possess the status of the grasped (*grāhyatva*). If it is argued that the activity possesses the nature of operating toward the blue even without depending on another activity—because it has that very nature as its form—then surely the blue also possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*); thus, it would follow that it must have an activity of grasping toward consciousness.

Furthermore, if by means of cognition (*bodha*) the act of grasping toward blue is produced, is that [act] different from the blue, or non-different? If it is different, then blue cannot be its object (*grāhya*) precisely because of that difference. If, on the other hand, it is non-different, then blue and so forth would possess the nature of cognition, because they are produced by cognition, just like a subsequent moment of cognition. Alternatively, there might be such a power belonging to cognition alone, by which it has the status of the grasper (*grāhaka*) with respect to blue, while blue and so forth have the status of the grasped (*grāhya*) with respect to it.

Now, if it were established that consciousness is the grasper and blue and so forth are the grasped, then the postulation of a capacity (*śakti*) would be appropriate, since a capacity is to be inferred from its effect; but if that [distinction] is not established, such a postulation is inappropriate, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). (S.

For instance: since the specific capacity of consciousness is established through its status as the apprehender of blue, and the establishment of that [status] depends on the establishment of that capacity, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, the establishment of consciousness as the apprehender of blue is not possible; consequently, even if one accepts that consciousness is distinct [from the object], self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is logical because of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*).

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, only this much appears: that pleasure and so forth, as well as blue and so forth, are directly perceived; since a formless cognition (*nirākāra-bodha*) is not observed even in a dream, its existence is not established—how, then, could it possess the capacity to apprehend an object?

For this very reason, they offer the following proof: "In this world, whatever appears is indeed what enters the path of conventional usage as an existent thing, just as pleasure whose form is manifest in the heart does not exist at that time as a pain that is not manifesting; and it is consciousness alone that appears to all embodied beings in the form of blue and so forth"—this is a *svabhāvahetu* (reason based on essential nature).

Thus, since the capacity to apprehend an object is unestablished, and because being insentient (*jaḍa*) is contradictory to luminosity (*prakāśa*), even the capacity to apprehend an object is not tenable from the Buddhist perspective.

Furthermore, since even insentient objects such as blue and so forth, which are connected with external regions, are experienced, it is not unestablished that the manifestation of blue and so forth possesses the capacity to apprehend them; nor is it logically consistent to raise an objection regarding the contradiction of an insentient pillar or similar object being an object of manifestation while it is being experienced.

Regarding an entity whose nature is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), an inference that purports to reveal a nature contrary to it is a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*), because it arises from a reason (*hetu*) afflicted by the fault of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), as it is employed immediately after the object has already been sublated by perception. Furthermore, a contradiction is not established with respect to a nature that is not established by perception; otherwise, even consciousness would incur a contradiction with its own nature as consciousness.

Now, in this way, since even the cognition of blue and so forth is experienced within the mind as being the object of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), its self-knownness (*svasaṃviditatva*) is not unestablished; nor is the objection regarding the contradiction of an action upon itself logically tenable, for no contradiction is established in that which is being experienced. Furthermore, the same applies to the argument put forward to prove that knowledge is not self-cognizing: because its subject matter (the thesis) is refuted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it lacks the power to establish the probandum.

Furthermore, if self-cognizing knowledge (*svasaṃviditajñāna*) is not admitted, then regarding the cognition "this object is connected with an external location," since that cognition which establishes [the object] would itself remain unestablished due to its non-cognition, the object to be established could not be established either; for nothing such as a donkey's horn, which is itself unestablished, is ever observed to be the establisher of anything.

Now, if it is argued that even though cognition is not itself cognized, there is no lack of stability because it is established by an infinite series of cognitions inhering in the same object, then—since even that subsequent cognition inhering in the same object as the first would not be established by another such cognition—it could not establish the cognition that establishes the object; thus, yet another such cognition must be admitted to establish that [prior] cognition, resulting in an infinite regress.

Now, if it is argued that the cognition which establishes another cognition is established by itself through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and thus this fault does not apply, then why is it not likewise accepted that the cognition which establishes the object is also so? For the logic is the same. Alternatively, if it is argued that a cognition, even if not itself cognized, establishes another cognition, then the first cognition would also establish the object even if it were itself unestablished; this would contradict the saying: "There is no cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) without the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) having been apprehended."

How would it not be wavering? Because when the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)—namely, "the object" (*arthaḥ*)—is apprehended, it is accepted that the apprehension of the qualificand occurs even if the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of that apprehension is not understood.

Furthermore, if it is accepted that a cognition—which is itself apprehended by another cognition inhering in the same object—is the grasper of that object, then, because successive cognitions would arise incessantly with the nature of perceiving each preceding cognition, there would be no transition of cognitions to other objects; for even when another object is present, the object characterized as the preceding cognition—inhering in the same object and being more intimately proximate due to its internal nature—would still exist.

As for the one who says: "Since the object qualified by the cognition is established when there is the mere apprehension of the cause, namely the perception of the object, there is no infinite regress"—this does not even cohere, because self-cognizing knowledge (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*) is not admitted; and this has already been demonstrated.

Furthermore, the Naiyāyika, who maintains the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*), accepts that perceptual and verbal cognitions have the same object. Consequently, just as in the case of perceptual cognition, there would be no difference in the mode of apprehension when that very same object—neither less nor more—is comprehended through verbal cognition as well; thus, verbal cognition too, like perception, would possess a clear manifestation (*spaṣṭa-pratibhāsa*). Now, even though the object is one and the same, it might be argued that there is a difference in the mode of apprehension regarding the verbal object due to the absence of a connection with the sense organs.

Now, surely the true nature of the object must be manifested by the sense organs as well; and if that same nature is also displayed by verbal cognition, then why is there not a clear manifestation of the verbal cognition even in the absence of a connection with the sense organs? For it is not logical that there should be a difference in the manifestation of cognitions without a difference in their objects; otherwise, the determination of the difference between objects could not arise from the difference in the manifestations of the cognitions.

Indeed, even in the case of external objects, we perceive no basis for establishing difference other than the perception of a distinction in their manifestation. Furthermore, even in the case of direct perception, the object is not capable of being known in its own nature through a direct connection with the sense organ—since that [connection] is beyond the senses—but rather through the effect, which is the manifestation of its own nature. If the nature of the thing manifests in verbal cognition just as it does when the effect is complete, then why is a connection with the sense organ not likewise admitted in that case as well? (S. 85)

Now, if it is argued that this [object] is not inferred because there is no clear manifestation (*spaṣṭapratibhāsa*) therein, [we reply]: surely its absence is due to the lack of contact with the senses, and the lack of such contact is due to the absence of a clear manifestation; thus, this is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayadoṣa*). Therefore, one must admit that the determination of the difference in the manifestations of cognitions is based solely on the difference in their objects; and that [difference] is not compatible between verbal and perceptual cognitions if they have a single object.

Now, even though an entity appears in verbal cognition (*śābda*), there is no appearance of all its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*); thus, that [verbal cognition] has an indistinct manifestation. But surely, in this way, since the particular (*viśeṣa*)—which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākṣama*) and which appears in perception—is not manifested therein, this very fact constitutes the difference in object (*bhinnaviṣayatva*) between verbal and perceptual cognitions, both of which consist of the nature of consciousness (*jñānātmabhūta*). But surely, in this case, when an object connected with the sense organs (*akṣasambaddha*) is being manifested, the simultaneous manifestation of clarity (*spaṣṭatva*) would result in the manifestation of the cognition itself.

Because the cognition produced by a distinguished causal complex possesses clarity, and because at the time of the appearance of blue connected with the sense organ, there is—according to your own admission—no other possible cause for the manifestation of that clarity apart from the manifestation of that [cognition] itself.

Moreover, let it be granted that the conventional usage of "clarity" (*vaiśadya*) in that case refers solely to the appearance of clear cognition; nevertheless, the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedita*) of that cognition is not established, because such conventional usage is possible even when [the cognition] is known by another cognition inherent in the same object. As for the conventional usage of simultaneous appearance, however, it is caused by the non-perception of succession due to the rapid functioning of the mind, like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals.

Now, if this were the case, then even the appearance of five fingers in a single cognition would—despite occurring as a sequential appearance—be characterized by a non-perception of that sequence for the same reason. Consequently, in the proof of an omniscient being based on the syllogism: "Every existent and non-existent phenomenon is directly perceived in a single cognition of someone, because it is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), like the five fingers," there would follow the fallacy of the example being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

Likewise, is the self grasped by all-cognizing consciousness (*sarvavijñāna*), which apprehends all existent and non-existent phenomena, or not? If it is not grasped, then, since it possesses the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), the reason characterized by that very *prameyatva* would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*). If, on the other hand, it lacks the status of being an object of knowledge, the reason is unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddha*). Now, if the self is also grasped by the omniscient cognition (*sarvajñajñāna*) which apprehends all categories of things, then the reason is not inconclusive.

Now, if this were the case, then just as the knowledge of God, despite being knowledge, apprehends itself by itself and there is no contradiction regarding an action upon itself, so too the knowledge of "non-existence" (asat) and the like will be the same; thus, there would be no contradiction whatsoever. Furthermore, if one accepts this, then in the formal argument—"Knowledge is apprehended by another knowledge, because it is an object of cognition (prameya), like a jar"—the reason "because it is an object of cognition" is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to the knowledge of God, since although that knowledge is an object of cognition, it is not apprehended by another knowledge.
This is the reason: therefore, since multiple defects would arise if cognition were apprehended by another cognition, cognition must be admitted to be self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*).

Furthermore, the Self is of the very nature of cognition; otherwise, because of the existence of distinct cognitions, it would lack the status of a knower, just like space. Nor is it reasonable to say that cognition inheres in the Self alone—and not in space and so forth—while being distinct from space, because inherence (*samavāya*) will be refuted later.

Since it is established that cognition is self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), and since the self is not distinct from it, that [self-cognition] is also established for the self. Thus, how could it be that the self is not established by the perception of self-cognition? Therefore, the first position is not defective.

As for what was said regarding the second position—that no entity whatsoever, whether in the form of an agent or an instrument, is ever observed to possess an operation within itself as if it were its own object—that too is inconsistent; for it has been demonstrated that the self, as the agent, and cognition, as the means of knowledge, are self-cognized even in the absence of any separate operation.

Just as you yourselves accept, without contradiction, that a single entity can possess both the status of a knower (*pramātṛ*) and the status of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) according to its different states—depending on whether it is considered the instrument of cognition (*liṅga*) and so forth—why do you not likewise accept that for a single self (*ātman*), even at one time, the statuses of knower, means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and object of knowledge are non-contradictory? For there is no contradiction, since the fact that it possesses those respective natures is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through its connection with those various attributes.

As for what was said—namely, "What is the meaning of this statement that [the Self] is immediate even though it is not an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? and so forth—that too is without substance; for it has been established that its own nature manifests both as the knower and as the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, while the nature of a jar or the like is grasped by a distinct cognition, the nature of the cognizer and the means of valid cognition is grasped by a non-distinct cognition; this is because their nature is established as being of the essence of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), whereas the nature of the jar and such is established as being the opposite of that.

Nor is there a failure to include within its definition the perception that apprehends the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*), for such a defining characteristic has already been demonstrated. Furthermore, the objection raised—namely, that this leads to an over-extension (over-inclusion) by the statement "I see the jar with my eye"—is also irrelevant; for while the insentient eye is not self-cognizing, it is not logical that the knower and the cognition, which are of the nature of consciousness, should likewise be non-self-cognizing, since it is impossible for them to possess a different essential nature [than consciousness].

As for what was said—that when the sense-faculties are active, there is the manifestation of the object alone, strictly distinguished from the body—that is utterly incoherent; for the awareness of that manifestation has been established just like the object itself, and in its absence, the manifestation of the object would not occur at all.
Therefore, the manifestation of the cognizer is indeed logically established.

Nor can it be established that this cognition has the body as its objective support, because the cognition "I am thin" or "I am fat" arises through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the body; for even when the body is not perceived due to the absence of the operation of the sense organs such as the eyes, the cognition "I" is observed to arise with pleasure and so forth as its coreferential terms and as having a clearly manifest appearance. Therefore, it is not logical to determine that its objective support is the body.

Furthermore, if the cognition "I am emaciated" is erroneous, it would be logical that the cognition "I am a knower"—which arises in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [first] cognition—would also be erroneous. Otherwise, if the cognition of fire in the boy in the expression "The boy is fire" were erroneous because its object is metaphorical, then the cognition of fire in actual fire would also have to be erroneous due to its metaphorical nature.

Therefore, since the grounds for metaphorical usage—such as the characteristics of being clever or tawny—exist there, a metaphorical cognition arises in that case; yet [the opponent claims] that no such basis for metaphorical usage exists here, which is also inconsistent. For even though the transmigrating self is distinct from the body and so forth, a metaphorical cognition based on that [distinction] occurs with respect to one's own servant and the like who are extremely beneficial, such as the cognition: "I am this servant."

Nor can it be said that the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya), which arises in coreferentiality with pleasure and so forth, has only a figurative object; for, like the notion of fire in relation to fire, this notion is primary in this context due to its being uncontradicted and its non-erroneous nature. On the other hand, qualities such as whiteness are properties of the person (pudgala) and are perceivable by the external senses; therefore, they cannot be the objects of the inward-looking, non-sensory "I-notion."

Furthermore, it is not logical for the body—which is the substratum of qualities such as whiteness and which is admitted by us to be disintegrating moment by moment—to be the object of a cognition experienced as having a stable referent, such as: "I, who previously saw my friend, am the very same I who now touches him after an interval of five years or more. Otherwise, that [cognition], being experienced as having color-form (*rūpa*) as its object, would have taste (*rasa*) and other qualities as its referent.

Furthermore, we perceive no subverting argument against the view that the self has as its object a self whose nature consists in the manifestation of pleasure and so forth, such that this [self-cognition] would be erroneous by virtue of having that as its object. Nor is there any faltering nature in it with respect to that [object], which would justify the assumption that it is metaphorical, like the cognition of a cow in a *vāhīka* (a forest-dweller). Therefore, because it is apprehended by the "I"-cognition, which is both uncontradicted and non-faltering, the self is not unestablished. As for the remainder of the opponent's text, it has been set aside, as it is devoid of substance and does not merit a rebuttal.

Nor is it appropriate for a follower of the Buddhist view to say here: "The self is not apprehended by the notion of 'I' because that notion is conceptual and thus not a form of perception," since conceptual perception itself will be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); moreover, even if [the self] were an object of perception, inference would still have its scope when a disagreement arises.

Furthermore, the recognition (*anusandhāna*) that is dependent upon the self’s unity is not established merely by the proof of that unity; nor does the unity of the self follow from the establishment of that recognition, for such would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Rather, the unity of the self is established through the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which is of the nature of direct experience (*pratyakṣa*), in the form of the cognition: "I, who previously saw the jar, am the very same one who now touches it."

And this objection should not be raised here: "Does the form of the self as seer appear through its entry into the form of the toucher, or without such entry? If it is by entry, then because the form of the seer has entered into the form of the toucher, there is only the form of the toucher and not the form of the seer."

And likewise, how can there be a single recognition such as "I am the seer who touches," from which the establishment of that unity [of the self] would follow? If, on the other hand, it occurs without mutual penetration, then because of the difference between the appearances of seeing and touching, how could there be a single recognition? For there is no unity when there is a difference in appearance; otherwise, there would be such unity even for the appearances of a jar and a cloth.

Now, if it is argued that here the difference belongs only to the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and not to its object, the self (*ātman*), then from what source does the non-difference of that [self] arise? It cannot be from the non-difference of the appearances, because their distinctness has already been established. Nor can it be from itself (*svataḥ*), because even now it remains a subject of dispute. If it is further argued that this fault does not apply because the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), which is the substrate of those states, remains non-different despite the difference between the states of seeing and touching, that too is inconsistent.

Because, through the appearance of the state of seeing, only that form of the substratum (*avasthātṛ*) connected to it is apprehended, and not that which is connected to tactile cognition; for in that case, since that state has not yet arisen, it does not appear. And when that [state] does not appear, the substratum also does not appear, because it is pervaded by that state. Nor is the pervasion of the substratum by the state of seeing understood through the appearance of tactile cognition, because seeing, having perished, does not appear in tactile cognition.

Furthermore, if [the entity] were to appear, there would follow the consequence of the appearance of an infinite succession of prior states. Moreover, if a prior state appears, it is impossible for the substratum of those states to be apprehended as being pervaded by that state. And whatever appears in a certain form must be accepted as existing in that very form; just as blue, appearing in the form of blue, is accepted as such.

Furthermore, since the state-endurer (*avasthātṛ*) is apprehended as being connected to itself precisely through the cognitions of seeing and touching, it must be admitted to be of that very nature; thus, how can there be a proof of a state-endurer?

For this can be said even regarding the appearance of blue: does the manifestation of the atoms of one cognition of blue appear by entering into the manifestation of the atoms of another cognition of blue, or without entering into it? (87)

If [the atoms] enter [into one another], then because the appearances of the atoms of the cognition of blue enter into one another, the cognition of blue would have the nature of a single atom; and since that [single atom] is not experienced, how can the cognition of the cognition of blue be established? If, on the other hand, they do not enter [one another], then because the appearances of the atoms of the cognition of blue appear like iron rods, how could there be a single, gross cognition of blue, given that it would be distinct for each appearance of an atom of the cognition of blue? Furthermore, if...

Even though there is a distinction in the manifestations of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), there is no distinction in that manifestation, namely, the cognition of blue (*nīlajñāna*). Now, from what does the non-distinction of the cognition of blue arise? Is it from the non-distinction of its self-cognition, or from itself? If it were from the non-distinction of its self-cognition, that would be incorrect, because a distinction between those [manifestations] has already been established. If, on the other hand, that non-distinction arises from itself alone, that too is incorrect, because that [non-distinction] remains unproven even now.

Likewise, if the state of touch does not appear during the state of seeing, then the pervasion of that state cannot be apprehended by the cognition of seeing with respect to the substratum. But if that [state] does not appear, how can its non-pervasion [of the substratum] also be apprehended by it? For if that does not appear, it is likewise impossible to apprehend even this: "this form of the substratum is excluded from that."

Nor is it reasonable to say that its non-pervasion [of the object] is already grasped simply because there is an appearance distinct from it; for if that [object] does not appear, the very thing distinct from it cannot be apprehended. Nor is it reasonable to argue that since non-pervasion is the very nature of that [object], the cognition of perception—which grasps its nature—must also grasp that non-pervasion because it is non-different in nature from it; for this same logic applies equally even if there were pervasion. Furthermore, the oneness of the self, which is the object of a single uncontradicted cognition, is not unestablished.
Furthermore, there is no sublation whatsoever of this determination of oneness, because any means of valid cognition that might be suspected of sublating it will be refuted in its proper place.

Or, let it be that the proof of that [self's] unity is established from the reason characterized as the cognition of synthesis (*anusandhāna*); even so, there is no fault of mutual dependence here. For synthesis is not ascertained by way of a positive example (*anvayidṛṣṭānta*) as being necessarily bound to unity—which would entail this fault—but rather, because synthesis is impossible in the case of multiplicity, synthesis is pervaded by unity through its exclusion from that [multiplicity]. Thus, its establishment occurs even through inference, since synthesis such as recollection and so forth is observed within a single continuum.

Furthermore, a synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of cognitions such as perception and memory is not possible if there is a difference [between them]; otherwise, Yajñadatta would have a synthesis consisting of memory and so forth regarding an object experienced by Devadatta.

Now, if it is argued that there is no synthesis because Devadatta and Yajñadatta lack a single continuum (*santāna*), whereas where there is a single continuum, synthesis certainly occurs even though the preceding and succeeding cognitions are absolutely distinct—[we reply: if the continuum is distinct from its constituent members (*santānin*) and yet possesses unity, then that is simply the self (*ātman*) expressed by another name, to which synthesis is bound.

Now, if the continuum (*santāna*) is non-different from the members of the continuum (*santānin*), then, because the preceding and succeeding moments of cognition—which are denoted by the term "continuum"—are absolutely distinct (just like the cognitions of Devadatta and Yajñadatta), the continuum, being non-different from them, must also be distinct. In that case, how could it serve as the basis for a synthetic connection (*anusandhāna*)? Alternatively, if it is argued that those preceding and succeeding moments of cognition belonging to a single continuum possess the status of a single continuum despite their mutual distinction, on account of their being in a cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and that the cognition of synthetic connection is thus appropriately based upon that [causality], then [the opponent] is not...

There is no causal relationship between the cognitions of Devadatta and Yajñadatta; therefore, the absence of recognition (*anusandhāna*) in that case is caused by the absence of a single continuum (*santāna*) based upon such a [causal] connection. [Objection: But when Devadatta’s cognition is inferred by Yajñadatta through the force of signs such as his purposeful activity (*vyāpāra*) and speech (*vyāhāra*), then that [cognition] becomes the producer of Yajñadatta’s inference. Consequently, there would follow the contingency of recognition being based on a single continuum, which is itself grounded in a causal relationship.

Now, [it may be argued that] there is no such fault because within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtati*), there is a relationship of producer and produced (*janyajanakabhāva*) among cognitions by way of the relation of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*), whereas in a different continuum (*bhinnasaṃtati*), that relationship exists by way of being a cooperative condition (*sahakāribhāva*). But what, then, is this "material causality" (*upādānatva*), in the absence of which there is a lack of recollection (*anusandhāna*) in a different continuum? That which produces an effect upon the cessation of its own continuum is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*); for example, a lump of clay, ceasing itself, produces a jar, and thus it is the material cause in the production of the jar.

Alternatively, another [definition]: that which, when an effect arises from multiple [causes], imparts its own specific quality [to that effect] is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*); however, the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) is not like this. But [one might object]: since things are disintegrating at every moment and there is no existence of moments possessing a single nature established in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior, the very relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) cannot be established among these moments.

To explain: when producing a subsequent cognition, does the preceding cognition produce it while being destroyed, or while not destroyed, or while possessing both natures, or while possessing neither nature? It cannot be while being destroyed, because even that which has been destroyed immediately prior is non-existent—just like that which was destroyed long ago—and thus its capacity to produce something is contradicted. Nor can it be while not destroyed, for that would entail the collapse of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Nor can it be while possessing both natures, because it is impossible for a single entity to possess two contradictory natures simultaneously.

Nor is it of the nature of neither, because for things whose definitions consist in mutual exclusion, the negation of one is inseparable from the affirmation of the other; thus, a nature that is neither is impossible.

Now, if it were admitted that a cause produces an effect through the operation of an activity (*vyāpāra*), then this fault would indeed arise—namely, that since an operation is impossible for what has already perished, how could there be the production of an effect? But when the cause's status as a producer of an effect consists merely in its prior existence, then from where would there be occasion for this fault? [Objection: But if this [mere prior existence] is accepted, when an effect arises from many preceding factors, from where does this distinction [between which factor is the cause and which is not] come?

Is it that "this is the material cause here" and "this is the auxiliary cause," because both follow the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the effect? Or, even though both follow the positive and negative concomitance, one produces as a material cause while the other does so otherwise? But surely, this very status of being a producer by way of being a material cause is difficult to ascertain for something whose specific nature is not continuous, based on its mere prior existence alone.

Now, it might be argued: "Since the definition of being a material cause (*upādānakāraṇatva*) has already been stated, how can it be difficult to understand upon its comprehension? True, it has been stated; however, that [definition] is not possible unless some common form (*rūpa*) is present as an underlying factor (*anugama*). Nor is it possible to ascertain it [without such a form].

For instance: as for that which was stated to be the nature of a material cause (*upādāna*), namely, the conferring of its own specific qualities—does this mean the conferring of only some of its own specific qualities, or rather the conferring of all its specific qualities? In this regard, if the first position is held, it is not tenable; for it would follow that our own cognition, by imparting its own form to the cognition of an omniscient being, would thereby become its material cause.

Likewise, it would follow that matter (*rūpa*) is also the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the cognition of matter, because that [matter] too imparts certain specific qualities inherent to itself [to the cognition]; otherwise, since a formless consciousness (*bodha*) would be indistinguishable with respect to all objects, there would be no determination of the object for each respective action—such that this [cognition] is the grasper of matter alone and not of taste and so forth—and consequently, the restriction of [cognitions] to their respective objects would not exist. Furthermore, if cognition has matter as its material cause, the funeral libation of water would have been offered to the next world [as the continuity of rebirth would be severed].

Furthermore, if [the object] were the material cause (*upādāna*) by virtue of imparting only a few particularities, then by admitting that a single moment of cognition is connected with multiple properties—both those that follow from its effects and those that exclude them—the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) would be undermined. And thus, just as a single cognition is admitted despite the superimposition of many simultaneous contradictory properties, why should it not be admitted as one even when associated with many such properties occurring sequentially?

If [the cause] is that which bestows all specific qualities, then the arising of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) from non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) would not occur. Nor could such a relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyatva*) exist even between two non-conceptual cognitions; and if that were so, how could there ever be the arising of a cognition with the form of taste or the like—though intended as its effect—from an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) having the form of color?

Now, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because one accepts a multiplicity of consciousness-streams (vijñānasantāna)—such that everything arises from its own similar [precedent]—then, in this view, there follows the undesirable consequence of a plurality of cognizers even within a single stream. Consequently, there would be no subsequent synthesis by one person regarding an object seen by another, when those two belong to different streams, just as there is no synthesis for one person regarding what was experienced by Devadatta or Yajñadatta belonging to their respective streams. Yet, we observe: "I knew the cow previously, and now I know the horse. [ŚV Ātmavāda 122]

Furthermore, since it would be utilized in its entirety within the momentary cognition that is to be produced—there being no other nature remaining unutilized if it were to impart all its own specific qualities—the yogic consciousness and such things as form, which belong to the same causal complex, cannot function as its cooperative causes. Consequently, in the absence of cooperative causes, there can be no production of any other effect distinct from the momentary cognition to be produced.

Now, let this [objection] apply to those for whom the cause itself transforms into the effect; it does not, however, apply to us, who accept that causality consists merely in prior existence. But even in this view, by which very nature does consciousness produce another consciousness as its material cause—is it by that same nature which is included within the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), or by a different nature? In that regard, if it were by that same [nature], then form (*rūpa*) too would become a material effect of consciousness, because it is produced by that same nature.

It is like the subsequent moment of cognition. Now, if it were by way of a different nature, then the cognition intended as the material cause would result in having two natures. Just as there is a connection with the two natures of being a material cause and a cooperative cause, so too, in relation to other effects produced by other things within the three worlds, its non-productiveness is also a nature.

And therefore, just as the unity of a single moment of cognition is accepted despite its being superposed with multiple contradictory properties—such as being a producer of its own material cause (*upādāna*) while not being a producer of its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)—so too must the unity of that continuum (*saṃtāna*), which consists of various manifestations such as joy and sorrow, be accepted. Now, if it is argued that those properties, such as being a producer of material and auxiliary causes, are merely constructed by the artifice of conceptualization (*kalpanā*);

Since its unity is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), it cannot be removed by those [arguments]; such is the view. Then, in the case of the self as well—which is established by the direct perception of self-awareness and is known by the term "continuum" (*santāna*)—its unity should not be subject to removal by the properties of being a producer or a non-producer dependent on [conditions] inferred from the observation of successive effects such as joy and sorrow. Therefore, according to your own admission, it is not consistent that the definition of a material cause (*upādāna*) consists in being the substratum of all its own inherent properties.

Nor does it have the nature of producing an effect through the continuity of a stream (*saṃtāna*); for if that were accepted, the consequence would follow that there is no future life due to the mere continuity of a stream of cognitions.

Now, if it is said that being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) constitutes being the material cause (*upādāna*), then it is as follows: *sama* means equal; *anantara* means immediate, i.e., uninterrupted; and *pratyaya* means a producer.

And since this [effect] does not arise from a different continuum, there is no possibility of a connection between them. Now, one might object: "In this case too, if the condition is the material cause (upādāna) by virtue of its equality with the effect, then it must be stated: is the equality total, or only partial? If it were total, that would be impossible; for if the cause and effect were identical in every respect, then just as the cause exists prior [to the effect], the effect would likewise have to exist prior [to itself]."

And thus, because cause and effect would exist at the same time, there could be no relationship of cause and effect; for a causal relationship does not exist between two things that are simultaneous, just like the left and right horns of a cow. Likewise, that which is considered a cause would itself have its own cause at the same time, and that too would have its own cause at the same time; consequently, the entire world at this moment would be devoid of any causal continuum. Therefore, there is some degree of parity [between our position and yours]. If that were the case, even the cognition of a yogi, when taking the cognition of someone like us as its object, would share the same causal continuum with it by virtue of having that same form, and so forth.

The refutation is exactly as stated previously. Now, if "immediacy" (*anantaratva*) is defined as "being the material cause" (*upādānatva*), then indeed, under the view of absolute momentariness, since the world arises at the intended moment immediately after every moment of the entire world, all [preceding moments] would be material causes; thus, the world would constitute a single continuum (*ekasantānatva*). In that case, spatial proximity (*deśānantarya*) is irrelevant, because it is accepted that even a mind separated by space—such as the mind at death in this life—is the material cause of the mind in a future birth.

But being a condition (*pratyayatva*) is not the same as being a material cause (*upādānatva*), because even in the case of a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), the status of being a condition exists; therefore, even the status of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyayatva*) is not the same as being a material cause. Furthermore, since entities perish at every moment, it is not possible for them to possess the capacity to produce [an effect] in any way without some single continuity (*ekānvaya*); how much less so can there be a distinction between material causes and other types of causes? We shall explain this on the occasion of establishing the refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

Regarding this, some state the reason why, even though the capacity to produce is equal, consciousness residing in one's own continuum (*svasantāna*) and consciousness residing in another's continuum (*parasantāna*) differ in their status as material causes (*upādāna*): "Cognition that has been cognized within one's own continuum produces another cognition, but it is not so in the case of another's continuum. Therefore, since there exists a ground for being a material cause distinct from the mere capacity to produce, the determination [of the relationship between cause and effect] proceeds from such a causal relation. This too is an untenable ground for determination, for a cognition that is not itself cognized cannot attain a determined status.

For the self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) of cognitions is held to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*); and that [self-awareness] is the same with respect to a cognition occurring in another continuum as it is for one occurring in one's own continuum. Furthermore, since the Buddhists do not admit that a cognition is necessarily cognizable by another cognition, this [objection regarding] over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is not avoided. Nor is it established that even within one's own continuum, a cognition is preceded by a self-cognized cognition, because such a state is not perceived in the case of a cognition arising after a period of unconsciousness (*mūrchā*) or similar conditions.

Since disputants disagree even regarding the fact that [the world] is preceded by consciousness (*vijñāna*), how much more so regarding its being preceded by self-cognized knowledge (*samvidita-jñāna*)? To this, one might say: "How can there be disagreement when the fact of being preceded by consciousness is established through inference? And it has been shown that "from that which belongs to a certain class, that which belongs to that same class arises. This is incorrect; for we observe the arising of entities even from what does not belong to that same class, as in the case of smoke and the like.

As for those who say that this objection does not apply because it is impossible for entities to arise from a dissimilar cause due to the distinction between the similar and the dissimilar—for them too, the discrimination between the similar and the dissimilar is not within the range of perception for an ordinary cognizer; even when investigating the effect, the discrimination between those two is difficult to obtain. Therefore, this is no solution.

Furthermore, as for those who assert that everything arises from a homogeneous material cause (*upādāna*), we do not understand how even the atoms existing within the wood—which are established as the material cause of the first moment of smoke—possess homogeneity. For is the homogeneity of form and so forth due to their being preceded by form and so forth, or due to their being preceded by parts characterized as "smoke-ness"? In the former alternative, there would no longer be production from heterogeneous causes, since even a cow could be produced from a horse.

Even regarding the latter alternative, is the "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) of the parts contained within the wood-worldly or technical? First of all, this is not the domain of technical convention; for even in common worldly usage, there is no practice of treating those parts established in that form as "smoke. It is proper for a logician (*tārkika*) to follow the conventions well-known in the world. Therefore, there is no production from a homogeneous cause.

And as for what is said here: "If consciousness were absent in that state, then upon emerging from that state at a later time, such a cognition would not occur—namely, 'nothing at all was perceived by me'—for this memory is preceded by experience. Therefore, one must necessarily admit the existence of that [consciousness] in that state, by means of which experience, while existing, nothing was perceived. This is poorly argued; for when one says, "nothing was perceived by me," either the non-perception of an object is being stated, or...

Or is it the cognition of its own nature? If there were no cognition of the object, a total negation of everything would not be tenable. As for the cognition of its own nature, that is utterly discarded if one accepts self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, it is precisely now, through the operation of the mind, that the cognition of all things occurring in that state is experienced.

Or, even if consciousness exists in that state, there is still no specific operation distinct from its status as a producer; for if one were to admit an operation over and above its status as a producer in the case of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), it would follow that there is a real distinction between those two. And if that were so, it would not be possible for that which constitutes the status of being an immediately preceding condition within one’s own stream of cognition to be the very same thing that constitutes the status of being a producer as an object of support (*ālambana*) within another’s stream.

Now, if properties such as being a producer (*janakatva*) and immediate succession (*samanantaratva*) are merely conceptual (*kālpnika*), while that which is non-conceptual—the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*)—is the ultimate reality (*tāttvika*), and that [nature] is of the form of consciousness (*bodharūpa*); then, do entities arise from a conventional form? No, it is said [they do not]. Or, how can they be conceptual? If it is argued that "immediate succession" is stated as something distinct from "being a producer," then how can there be a systematic determination (*vyavasthā*) based upon that?

For instance: although the consciousness belonging to another continuum possesses the same capacity for production as that within a single continuum, the establishment of a single continuum is made by accepting a specific mode of production based on its status as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). However, when even the basis for such an establishment is merely conventional (*saṃvṛta*), it is difficult to maintain that the establishment effected by it possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*). This fault belongs to the Buddhists (*Saugata*) and not to the Jains, because it has already been previously established that knowledge is preceded by [another] knowledge, and that the nature of knowledge is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedya*).

Furthermore, the argument that the production of entities is observed even from things of a different class—just as smoke and the like [arise from fire]—is also not tenable.
