For we do not deny that production from what is of a different class occurs, since smoke is indeed seen to arise even from a fire that possesses different characteristics; rather, the basis for our acceptance of something being an effect is its conformity to the properties residing in the cause, and this has already been demonstrated in the case of cognition.

Furthermore, there is not an absolute dissimilarity between the two, as in the case of fire and smoke or the body and consciousness, because both are similar in being transformations of the *pudgala*. If there were absolute similarity, it would follow that the relationship of cause and effect could not exist, since they would attain identity. As for the fact that the distinction between the similar and the dissimilar is difficult to discern even when defining an effect—in such a case, one who is unable to determine the distinction even by observing the effect has no qualification at all for the practice of inference. Thus it has been said:

A well-analyzed effect does not deviate from its cause [PVin II 37,15 ~ PVSV 23,26]; therefore, one must apply effort toward the ascertainment of that [cause]. For this very reason, such statements as "for color and so forth [are preceded] by color and so forth" are merely criticisms of what is unintended, because some degree of similarity between cause and effect has been demonstrated, and because that [similarity] is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the present context.

As for the claim that, because consciousness is absent in states such as sleep and fainting, it is impossible for subsequent cognition to be preceded by it—that is incorrect; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend the absence of consciousness in those states. To explain: first of all, one who is asleep does not perceive the absence of consciousness during that state, since consciousness is not admitted to exist at that time. Furthermore, if such an absence were perceived, that very perception would itself be a form of consciousness, and thus there would be no absence of consciousness in that state.

Nor does another person standing nearby perceive the absence of that [object], because in this case the means of cognition—namely, the non-perception of the cause, the pervader, or the essential nature, or the perception of the contradictory—are not operative; for it is impossible for anyone else to have the manifestation of that absence.

Nor is there a non-apprehension of its existence in that state, as there is of a non-existent thing; for, due to the presence of signs such as the specific characteristics of inhalation, exhalation, bodily warmth, and so forth—which are determined to be invariably concomitant with self-cognized consciousness within one's own self—there arises the cognition of inference in that state. Furthermore, even in the waking state, the mental activity belonging to another continuum is not apprehended by persons such as ourselves without the inference produced from the observation of the aforementioned signs.

Regarding the objection that was stated—namely, that since one remembers later on, "Nothing whatsoever was thought by me," there must have been either a non-perception of the object or a non-perception of its own nature during that state—that too is without substance.

This is because it is the same even in cases that are the objects of inference arising from the force of the mark (*liṅga*) of recollection—such as the perception of a cow at a later time during the conceptualization of a horse, which occurs simultaneously with the self-cognized knowledge of the touch of grass while walking in the waking state, where one subsequently thinks, "I did not perceive anything. Nor is it correct to say that the same fault applies here to the proponent of the doctrine of self-cognized consciousness (*svasaṃvedita-vijñānavādin*), for he accepts that there is a certain measure of self-cognized knowledge corresponding to whatever [object] exists.

Furthermore, as for the argument that it has been demonstrated that multiple properties—such as being immediately preceding (*samanantara*) or being a cooperating cause (*sahakārin*)—would be simultaneously attributed to a single moment of cognition, this is not a valid objection because we accept such a possibility. Therefore, since there would be no basis for the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) between two cognitions within one's own continuum (even though they belong to the same person), there could be no unifying cognition (*anusandhānapratyaya*), just as there is none between different continua. Yet, such a unifying cognition is observed. Consequently, the self is established by the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the unifying cognition itself, which is excluded from plurality.

Now, it might be argued that the probative power of a reason (*hetu*) is preceded by the apprehension of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with its own probandum (*sādhya*), and that such apprehension occurs in another locus (*dharmin*). However, in this case, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) in a locus other than the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) by virtue of being produced by a single agent, such that a single agent could be inferred from that synthesis. If you say, "Just as the reason called 'existence' (*sattā*), which proves momentariness, possesses probative power even without the apprehension of pervasion in another locus, so too is this [synthesis] the case," this is not tenable.

For, since its momentariness has been previously ascertained by perception and the pervasion [of that momentariness] with the object of ascertainment has been observed, the very fact that [momentariness], having been excluded from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) by a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*), remains in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), is itself the grasping of the pervasion with its own probandum. For this very reason, they maintain that the ascertainment of the pervasion for this reason occurs only in the subject of the thesis.

Surely, a necessary sequence between the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*) must be admitted, because the ascertainment of pervasion is a constituent factor for the cognition of the probandum; however, if one admits the ascertainment of pervasion here upon the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), then a time other than that of the cognition of the probandum would have to be admitted, yet such another [time] is not experienced. This is true even for the reason consisting of an effect (*kāryahetu*).

However, for this [reason], having been excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) by the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa), its very apprehension within the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) as being pervaded by its own probandum is itself the apprehension of the probandum. Nor does it possess these two forms [separately], because the exclusion from the dissimilar instances itself implies the positive concomitance (anvaya).

However, there is this distinction: for some [reasoning], a specific property-possessor (*dharmiviśeṣa*) is presented in order to demonstrate the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*); but in this case, even without presenting a specific property-possessor, the demonstration of pervasion occurs by implication of the mere property-possessor through the principle that "whatever exists is momentary. Furthermore, that existence (*sattva*), being perceived as established in some particular locus, serves as a factor for the realization of momentariness; thus, the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is also present here, whereas it is not so in the other case.

Regarding this as well, some maintain that this very same logic applies. How so? For in that case, the exclusion of the probans from the counter-example (vipakṣa) occurs through the exclusion of succession and simultaneity—which are its pervaders (vyāpaka); here too, the exclusion of the probans characterized as "recognition" (pratisandhāna) occurs from the counter-example due to the absence of "being restricted to a single cognizer" (pramātṛniyatatā), which is its pervader.

Now, in that case, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) is ascertained by perception—since the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākaraṇa*) through either succession or simultaneity is ascertained by perception—how is it here? Even here, since the pervasion of recognition is ascertained within one's own continuum (*svasantāna*) by virtue of being preceded by the necessity of a cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*), how is it not the same?

Now, one might ask: "What is the meaning of this statement, 'restricted to a single cognizer' (*pramātṛniyatatā*)? If, at best, what is being indicated by way of a different formulation is the proof of having a single agent, then once that is admitted to be ascertained through perception, how can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) be understood through a subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)? This is not so; the apprehension of 'restriction to a single cognizer' is not the same as the apprehension of 'having a single agent'."

For all entities indeed enter the sphere of linguistic convention only when they are determined as being restricted to specific locations and so forth; the determination of the cognizer is likewise observed to be exactly thus: "Now, I am here. Just as there is non-connection with other locations and so on, so too is non-connection with other cognizers ascertained. For instance, just like a jar and the like, which have a manifestation restricted by nature to non-connection with other objects and governed by the constraints of space and time, there is likewise an absence of any ascertainment regarding its unity or plurality.

According to the view of the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣin*), since that [reconnection] is absent from other continua which have multiple agents, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of reconnection—observed in some cases and excluded from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*)—with having a single agent.

Just as when the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is observed through either succession or simultaneity, there is no such certainty—namely, whether that [efficiency] is produced by momentary things through succession and simultaneity, or otherwise—and yet, once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the subverting factor has been determined through perception, the pervasion of the fundamental reason is subsequently established through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*); so too, even when the state of having a single agent is not determined, if the pervasion is ascertained within one's own continuum through the recognition (*pratisandhāna*) that is restricted to a specific cognizer, then at a later time, regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)...

Since there is no absence of the pervading property of being restricted to a single cognizer, the pervasion of recognition by way of having a single agent is established. If this were not accepted, then in the absence of certainty regarding the cognizer—whether it be "I" or "another"—there would be no certainty regarding the object of cognition, and the world would become blind and mute. If that which is metaphorical were the object of manifestation as being restricted to a cognizer, the fault would be that it is not a perception of the self.

In this regard, it might be argued: "This determination regarding the restriction of the cognizer exists; however, is it rightly held to be caused by a single agent within one's own continuum, or rather caused by some other cause? And that [causal relation] characterized as the nature of cause and effect within a single continuum has already been demonstrated previously. True, it has been demonstrated, but not yet proven. For instance, the fact that the restriction of the cognizer is caused by that [specific continuum] and not by another is not an object of perception; nor is it an object of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For in this context, what is being stated would have to be called inference (*anumāna*), and that too is refuted by the refutation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is it reasonable to accept that the determination of momentariness is based on a restriction established by the relation of cause and effect (*hetuphalabhāva*), because that [relation] will be refuted later on.

Nor can it be argued that for this very same reason there is no restriction regarding the fact of having a single author; for it has already been established previously that [the self] is proven by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) and by the inference based upon that. Furthermore, by way of a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*), it was shown that the cause of the synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*) is equal to the reason of "existence" (*sattva*) which establishes momentariness.

However, unlike momentariness, the oneness of the self is not established by perception; therefore, the objection that the fault of mutual dependence would arise if its establishment were admitted on the basis of inference does not apply. Consequently, because [the existence] of one who goes to the next world is established by the means of knowledge consisting of perception and inference, the sūtra stating "due to the absence of one who goes to the next world, there is an absence of the next world" is established as being devoid of substance.

As for what is said—that consciousness residing within one body cannot migrate into another body, since during life such migration into another body is not observed, and that it might occur at the time of death in the next world is difficult to establish—that too is not tenable. For it is observed even in the living that conceptual states such as scholarship and so forth, which reside within the body of a youth, migrate into the body of old age; likewise, specific bodily conditions such as restlessness and various vocal modifications [migrate].

How then is it that there is no transition of the living being into another body? If it is argued that this very same body is merely differentiated by stages such as infancy and childhood, whereas the body of another birth arises from the semen and blood of different parents and thus originates as a distinct body—this too is incorrect, because even the bodies of infancy and childhood are distinct from one another.

Just as the distinction between the restlessness of the bodies of infants and children is observed to persist through the transition into the bodies of youths and so forth, so too will the distinction between restlessness and other qualities arising from one's own previous birth-potential persist through the transition into the bodies of future existences and subsequent births. Therefore, the body at birth and so on does not follow from the semen and blood of the parents, but rather follows from the body of its own continuum, just like the bodies of the elderly and others.

Otherwise, the body would not possess bodily movements distinct from those of the parents' bodies, such as their fickleness and so forth. Now, if it is argued that the unity of the body—which pervades its various states—is established through recognition despite the differences between the stages of infancy, childhood, and so on in this life, and therefore, by the force of that example, it is not logical for consciousness to migrate into a body of another birth which is entirely different, that is incorrect; for precisely because of this, the *kārmaṇa-śarīra* (karmic body), which effects the migration of consciousness between the bodies of prior and subsequent births, is established as being in some sense one.

For instance: first, it has been established here that cognition in this life and so forth originates from the cognition of one's own previous births. Furthermore, since this [cognition] is observed to move through the various states of infancy, childhood, and so on within this life—states which possess a single underlying form as understood through uncontradicted recognition in the form "this is that very same body"—its movement is likewise inferred to exist in the states of prior and subsequent births, which are similarly endowed with a persisting underlying form.

Furthermore, it is not possible for a gross body—which serves as the substrate for form and other qualities perceivable by the senses of those such as ourselves—to persist through the state of a body in another birth, since its destruction is observed at that very time through burning and other such means. Therefore, the existence of the *kārmaṇa* body is established; it is that which pervades the states of two births, is accompanied by properties such as heat, and effects the migration of consciousness.

Since the substratum (*avasthātṛ*) that pervades the states of previous and subsequent births is in some way distinct from those states, when it conforms to the fickleness and other qualities of its own body—which is distinct from the bodies of the mother and father—why would the subsequent state not conform to the properties of the substratum? Therefore, that very thing whose impressions (*saṃskāra*) it necessarily follows is the body; it is logical that the [present] body is a successor to the previous body.

Now, as for the objection that the relationship of cause and effect cannot be established because perception does not operate with respect to the prior and posterior [moments], and that if it were established through inference, there would be the fault of mutual dependence—that too has been refuted; for in that case, universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*) would follow, so by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could there be either a refutation or a proof for anyone? This is because it has already been demonstrated that even this world would result in non-existence.

Now, once it is established that a specific effect is preceded by a specific cause, let the existence of a previous birth be proven according to the manner described. But how can the existence of a future world be proven, given the absence of any means of valid cognition regarding what is yet to come? To this we reply: it is also [proven] precisely from a specific effect. For instance, a specific effect is simply a particular kind of existence (*sattva*), and this is not defined as a relation with "Being" (*sattā*); for that [relation] will be refuted later.

Nor can it be defined by the characteristic of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), because that would entail the non-existence [of the entity] at the moment of the cessation of the continuum. For instance, if the cessation of the continua of sound, cognition, lamps, and so forth is admitted, then the final moment of that continuum would be non-existent since it does not produce a subsequent moment; and if that is non-existent, the preceding moments would also be non-existent because they do not produce causal efficiency, resulting in the total absence of the entire continuum.

Now, it might be argued that this fault does not apply because the final moment of the continuum (*santatyantakṣaṇa*), even though it does not produce another moment of its own kind within the continuum of an omniscient being, still exists by virtue of producing a cognition that apprehends itself. That is incorrect; for if it does not produce a derivative moment belonging to its own continuum, it is impossible for it to produce a cognition apprehending itself that resides in the continuum of another. Indeed, the status of a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇatva*) is never observed in the absence of the status of a material cause (*upādānakāraṇatva*).

Alternatively, if that [taste] were present, there would be no non-erroneous cognition of color and so forth—which depend on the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—even though they do not exist at that time; for it is admitted that even when a moment of color fails to produce its own subsequent effect-moment, it acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) in the continuity of taste by producing a moment of taste, since color and so forth existing at that same time are absent even when that [taste] exists.

Therefore, since there is no possibility of being a cooperative cause in the absence of being a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), if one accepts the annihilation of one's own continuum, existence characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) becomes impossible. Thus, existence must be accepted as being characterized precisely by arising, passing away, and persistence. Consequently, from the reason characterized by a specific effect, in the manner already described, it is established that the self possesses a connection with the future time, just as it does with the past time.

As for what was also said—that if the existence of the self and its connection with specific fruits of action are accepted as established by scripture, then inference is redundant—that too is the behavior of a foolish lord; for it is not proper to reject a thing that has arisen through the power of its own causal complex simply because it is "redundant. Nor is it proper to reject even perception on the grounds that objects are established by scripture.

Furthermore, regarding an object for which perception and inference are not applicable, the validity of scripture is accepted by those who maintain that scripture is a means of valid cognition; as it has been said:
"Since the Veda (āmnāya) has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless" [Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 1.2.1].

That too is incorrect; for just as it has been established that even regarding an object already perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*) may still operate when there is a point of disagreement, so too, why would scripture (*āgama*) not be the domain of acceptance with respect to the nature of the self (*ātman*)—which is established by both perception and inference—or with respect to its specific connection to the fruits of karma?

Nor is it reasonable to claim that scripture lacks authority in this regard, for its authority has been established by virtue of its being composed by the Omniscient One. Furthermore, scripture teaches the relationship between specific actions and their fruits:
"Excessive undertaking of activities and possession of property are the cause of rebirth as a hell-being" (Tattvārthasūtra 9.19).

By such statements as these, the foremost of exponents, desiring to establish that this very [self] is the object of inference, has formulated the aphorism. Furthermore, how the connection between action and its fruit is also determined through inference regarding the self, we shall explain in its proper place right here. The scripture (āgama) which establishes the nature of the self and establishes the specific connection between actions and their fruits is as follows: "The self is one" (Ācārāṅga Sūtra 1.1.1);
"Formerly committed, difficult to overcome, performed actions... [etc.]

This and other such [arguments] are already established for one who is asleep. Thus, since the self—which possesses a nature experienced through the successive states of hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods—is established by the means of valid cognition consisting of perception, inference, and scripture, it is settled that the etymological derivation of the word *bhava* (existence) is not equivalent to the derivation of words like *ḍittha*, because [in the former case] there is no absence of a referent.
[The prima facie view – establishing that the world was created by God:

Here the Naiyāyikas say: "Regarding the acceptance of a Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, its fruition, and latent dispositions, the objection was raised that he must be either eternally existent or non-existent. To that, we reply: there is no harm to us in establishing his eternal existence, because we accept him as endowed with a collection of attributes such as eternal knowledge and so forth, on the basis of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, this might be correct if there were some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing the existence of such a person, but that does not exist. To explain: for people like us, perception does not reveal the existence of such a person.

As for the claim that he is apprehended by yogins who are distinct from us, there too there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever. For when perception does not function to grasp his essential nature, then even the report of the existence of his attributes—such as eternal knowledge and so forth—is impossible.

Inference, too, is not tenable as a means of making known the nature of this [world], because when perception is negated, that which is preceded by it (inference) is also negated. Furthermore, inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) has no application here, because there is no logical mark (*liṅga*) whatsoever that could establish it; for the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and the structural arrangement (*saṃsthāna*) of the earth and so forth are utterly distinct. Moreover, the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasakti*) has been shown by the fact that the word "structure" applies to both, and thus identity cannot be established through mere verbal similarity despite the difference in actual entities—as stated in [PV II 12ab]: "Because of the identity of the word...
and so forth. Therefore, inference is not capable of proving that [world].

Nor is there scripture (*āgama*), because the existence of an eternal [author] is not admitted here; or, even if it were admitted, [scripture] would not function with respect to an established entity that is not a product. Nor does [scripture] preceded by God possess validity, because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Furthermore, even that which is not preceded by God cannot be established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since its defects are suspected.

If that [universe] were preceded by another God, it must be explained from what source His existence is established; for if He is not established, He lacks authority, and there is the fault of the logical consequence of multiple Gods. If you say, "Let it be so, what is the harm? Since we are exceedingly eager to establish even one, how much more so many?", [the answer is] no, except for the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, there is no comprehension of Him even through scripture (*āgama*). Thus, since His essential nature is unestablished, how can He be the cause?

Regarding this, they say: as for what was stated—that perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in that regard—that is indeed so. Furthermore, as for the claim that no form of scripture (*āgama*) has the capacity to reveal its own nature, it is replied: even if scripture lacks such capacity, there exists inference (*anumāna*) that establishes its nature. We shall demonstrate how scripture also functions with respect to an established object by way of the observation of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

If one were to negate inference preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvakānumāna*), it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the operation of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*) is admitted therein. Now, one might object: "This inquiry is appropriately undertaken regarding the status of inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), yet the Cārvākas do not accept its validity. This objection is not worth mentioning, for the validity of inference has already been established.

As for what was said—that because the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) residing in the earth and so forth is not perceived, there is no understanding of God (*īśvara*) from it—in that regard, how could the Buddhists, who themselves accept that the earth and other elements are effects, speak in such a manner? Furthermore, even for those such as the Cārvākas who do not admit that the earth and other elements are effects, how could those things which possess specific configurations (*saṃsthāna*) be non-effects?

Everything possesses configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and is an effect, and that is seen to be preceded by a person (*puruṣa*). As for those who say: "The state of being denotable by the word 'configuration' is merely common to the earth and so forth with jars and the like; in reality, no single common object exists that is shared by both," for them not only is there an absence of a common referent here, but even in the case of smoke and so forth, there is no single common referent shared between preceding and succeeding individual instances.

Now, it was stated there that the absence of conceptualization (*akalpanānimitta*) arises from the perception of the actual object; however, in this case, since such an appearance does not exist, there is no conceptualization of a pervasive entity. For instance, having seen the specific construction of some object such as a jar being made as preceded by an agent, one infers that even another object like a jar or a palace, whose agent is unobserved, must likewise have been preceded by an agent due to its specific mode of construction. But the configuration of the earth and so forth has never at any time been understood to be preceded by an agent.

Nor is such [a configuration] seen in other subjects (dharmin), such as cloth and the like, which possess a visible agent; for that [configuration] is distinct from the configuration found in earth and so forth, and therefore, the understanding of being preceded by an agent does not arise from it. Thus, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), this is not a proof; this is incorrect. For if the unestablished nature of the reason is asserted with respect to those cognizers who have not grasped the relationship [of concomitance], then the same applies to smoke and the like as well.

Now, it might be argued that even though the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has been grasped, because the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is observed in things such as threads, the cognition of their being produced by God and so forth does not arise; however, this is incorrect. For those who have grasped the invariable concomitance of "being an effect" and the like with "having an intelligent cause," they certainly understand from that [reason] that these things are preceded by God and so forth. Therefore, for those who are proficient (*vyutpanna*), there is indeed the comprehension of the presence of the reason—such as the fact of possessing a specific configuration and the property of being an effect—in the subject (*dharmin*); but for those who are unproficient (*avyutpanna*), this is absent even in the case of well-known inferences such as that of smoke.

Furthermore, even if the configuration of the earth and other elements differs from the configurations of palaces and such, the Buddhists and others still maintain that the earth and so forth are effects (*kārya*). And it is observed that an effect is preceded by an agent, instruments, and so on; therefore, because they are effects, one may infer that they are preceded by an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇa*). Now, if it is argued that the property of being an effect preceded by an agent and the property of possessing a specific configuration do not lead to the realization of the probandum (*sādhya*) because they differ from those [palaces], [we reply: [This argument is flawed. For instance, when one infers fire from smoke, although the smoke in a kitchen differs from the smoke rising from a mountain, the nature of being smoke remains the same; thus, the inference of fire proceeds from the general property of being smoke. Similarly, even if the configuration of the earth differs from that of a palace, the property of being an effect remains identical. Therefore, just as the inference of fire is established from the general property of being smoke despite differences in particular instances, so too the inference of an intelligent cause is established from the general property of being an effect, despite the difference in configurations. Thus, the conclusion follows.

For this very reason, since the refutation that "the cognition of an agent is logical for one who does not perceive the agent simply because one perceives a configuration that follows the presence or absence of a presiding agent" applies equally even to the case of being an effect (*kāryatva*), how can [the latter] be a means of valid cognition? If this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference; for if smoke and the like, which likewise follow the presence or absence of the causal complex of fire and so forth, were to exist on a mountain in exactly that same manner, then the cognition of fire and so forth would indeed occur.

Now, if it is argued that smoke and the like are of such a nature as to be excluded from non-smoke, then why is it not accepted that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth, as they exist in earth and other substances, are likewise of such a nature? Or, if it is claimed that those who do not perceive an agent fail to understand [the existence of an agent] because they observe "being an effect" in earth and other things, then let it be granted that those who do not perceive fire and so forth on a mountain peak and the like also fail to understand [the existence of fire] from smoke and the like.

Furthermore, it is not correct to say here that there is no commonality of the term (*śabda-sāmānya*) nor any following of the real entity (*vastvanugama*), for it is possible to assert the commonality of the term even in the case of smoke and the like. Therefore, from the perspective of the Śākyas, "being an effect" and so forth are not unestablished (*asiddha*).

Nor is it according to the view of the Cārvākas or Mīmāṃsakas, for even in their view, like a structure, the earth and other elements—which are necessarily effects—must be produced by the conjunctions of their own parts, just like a jar; and they will necessarily undergo destruction through disjunction. Thus, either from such potential destruction, or from the nature of being a constructed arrangement, there is the inference of being an effect. As was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya:

Even in the case of those entities whose origin is not perceived, since their form is apprehended, by observing that their form is produced through the conjunction of threads, it is inferred that it will perish either through the loosening of that conjunction or through its destruction.

By this, he states that destruction occurs due to the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) because that which possesses configuration (*saṃsthānavat*) is not perceived to arise [independently]. Likewise, since the earth and so forth possess configuration and are seen to be born from the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), there will be the possibility of their destruction; and from the possibility of destruction, there follows the inference of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which leads to the cognition of an agent (*kartṛ*). As it has been said by the knowers of Nyāya:
"The perception of reality occurs either through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or through inference (*anumāna*)."

And because the properties of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and being perishable (*vināśitva*) possess coextensive pervasion (*samavyāptikatva*), the inference of one from the other is accepted; therefore, regarding the statement "where both properties [are present]" [ŚV *Anumāna* 9], for the followers of Jaimini, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) for being an effect and so forth.

Nor is there a lack of proof (*asiddhatva*) according to the Cārvāka view; for since they possess a structured arrangement (*racanāvattva*), the cognition of their being effects is necessarily established even for the earth and so forth, which arise from unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*). Otherwise, because no author is observed for the arrangement of the Veda, it would not be an effect; for in that case too, one could say this much: "The inference of the Vedic arrangement’s being an effect does not follow from its being an arrangement; rather, let only worldly arrangements—which are seen to conform to the presence or absence of an author—be preceded by an author, but not the Vedic one."

Now, since no distinction is perceived between these two, if the Vedic [text]—just like the worldly—is preceded by an agent, then let the structural arrangement of the earth and so forth also possess that same nature, like the structural arrangement of palaces and the like, because no distinction is observed. Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

[Objection: Let it be that the reason is not unestablished; nevertheless, the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*) from this is not tenable, for the comprehension of the probandum does not arise from mere presence-in-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*). [Reply: But is it not the case that the pervasion of "being an effect" and so forth with "being preceded by an agent, object, and instrument" has not been apprehended in the case of pots and the like?

It is true that there is such a recognition of the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) as it exists in a jar; nevertheless, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) here. For pervasion is grasped by including all instances, whereas in this case, at the very time of grasping the pervasion, one observes that some effects are not preceded by an agent—just as, for example, with the trees in a forest. Thus, not every effect is preceded by an agent.

Now, if in that case there is no certainty regarding the absence of an agent, but rather merely a non-perception of the agent—and since such non-perception occurs even when an agent exists—how can there be an observation of the reason (*hetu*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*)? But where, then, is there a non-apprehension of agents who do exist? For example, in the case of jars and the like whose production has not been perceived. It is logical that there is a non-apprehension of the agent in those cases, because the time of their production is not perceived; and at that time, the agent is present there, while at other times, due to the absence of his presence, he is not apprehended.

Furthermore, when stationary objects such as forests are perceived to have come into existence, the presence of an agent must necessarily be cognized, just as it is in the case of a jar or similar things whose birth is being perceived. Therefore, since the absence of an agent—who would meet the conditions for perception—is ascertained in those cases, the pervasion (vyāpti) between the reason, such as "being an effect" (kāryatva), and "having an agent" is not established at the very time the pervasion is grasped, because the reason is observed there despite the absence of an agent.

Furthermore, because it is impossible to postulate both the seen and the unseen [simultaneously]: the abandonment of the status of being a cause for earth and other elements—which is observed—and the postulation of an unseen agent as the cause, is not logical. Now, if it is argued that there is no negation of the causality of earth and so forth even when an agent is postulated—since even in the presence of that [agent], another cause is still postulated—that is incorrect; for whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something is the cause of that thing, and the other is the effect.

However, earth and the other elements follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) [of the plant]. In that regard, forest trees and the like that grow from seeds sown in the ground do not depend on anything else; how, then, could there be an instrument distinct from these? Even if one were to imagine such causality, the fault has already been stated in the passage beginning with "in the healing of Caitra’s wound" (*caitrasya vraṇarohaṇe*). Therefore, even though the reason possesses the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), it is non-informative because of the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

If it is argued that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) [of the reason] because those [counter-examples] are included within the subject (*pakṣa*), that is incorrect. How could actual counter-subjecthood (*vipakṣatva*) be set aside by a subjecthood imagined according to the opponent's whim? Subjecthood (*pakṣatva*) is spoken of only when pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established, provided there is no apprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) or its absence. At the time of apprehension, if there is a suspicion of deviation, and once certainty is reached, if one were to conceive of the capacity to prove by including the object of deviation within the subject, then no reason whatsoever would ever be deviant.
Therefore, there is no non-deviant reason for establishing God (*īśvara*).

On this point, they say: there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or lack of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*) with respect to stationary objects (*sthāvara*) and the like produced by [divine] attraction, because a reason (*hetu*) that exists in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is called deviant. However, the non-perception of an agent in those cases does not constitute a certainty of the absence of having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*). Now, it was argued that since the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*) are met, a certainty of the agent’s absence is appropriate there; but this is not correct, because the conditions for perception are not admitted to apply to an agent in those cases.

As for what was said—that because we observe earth and the other elements follow the positive and negative concomitance [of the effect], it would lead to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to postulate a cause distinct from them—under such a postulation, even merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) would not be causes. Yet they are not without causality, since their status as causes has been established; for there is nothing in the world that is not a means to pleasure or a means to pain for someone.

Nor does the production of its means occur independently of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa). However, this much is the distinction: for the most part, the body and so forth are projected by specific adṛṣṭas, whereas objects of enjoyment for all [beings] are projected by common adṛṣṭas. This cannot be denied because it is accepted by all [schools], beginning with the Sāṃkhyas; and the reasoning has already been demonstrated. This must also be accepted by the Cārvākas, since the proof for this was previously stated in response to them.

But that which is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not unestablished for anyone. Now, if it were the case that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is not a cause simply because it does not conform to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with its effect, then we need not say that God (*īśvara*) is not a cause because he does not conform to positive and negative concomitance with effects such as stationary objects (*sthāvara*), which exist apart from the earth and so forth.

Now, it might be argued that the diversity of the world is not possible without the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as its cause, and therefore it is postulated. Since the earth and other elements are common to all things that arise, the diversity of effects must be produced by diverse causes known as the unseen force. However, even when the unseen force is thus postulated as a cause, it is not logical to reject the causality of God (*īśvara*) as well.

Just as the diversity residing in the cause is postulated because it would otherwise be impossible for diversity to exist in the effect, so too, why is an intelligent agent not accepted, given that the nature of the effect itself would be untenable without him? Nor can he be rejected on the grounds of non-perception in the case of plants and other things born from the earth, for they fall under the category of "unperceivable" (anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta), like the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, not every causal complex falls under the category of being perceivable.
For this very reason, even when causes are being perceived, their status as causes is not directly perceived, since that status is apprehended solely through the effect.

The existence of auxiliary causes constitutes the causality of that which is being perceived. Even though some auxiliary causes are themselves visible, others—such as the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—are understood only through their effects. Thus, it is established that although God is a cause, His essential nature is not grasped by direct perception. Consequently, because the agent has not reached the conditions for perceptibility, there is no lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the case of stationary beings whose birth is observed, since the reason (*hetu*) is seen to function therein. For a reason that is certain to exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is fallacious (*vyabhicārī*).

But surely, just as a reason whose presence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is certain is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*), so too is one whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful. Regarding the aforementioned stationary things, is the non-perception of an agent due to the absence of an agent, or is it rather that, despite its existence, there is no perception because it has not reached the conditions for perceptibility (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāptatva*)? Thus, when the negative concomitance is doubtful, no reason is a prover. Even in the case of smoke and the like, at the time of perceiving the pervasion by including all individual instances, not all instances of fire are visible.

Furthermore, while those instances of smoke are invisible, as long as there is doubt regarding their perceptibility, the suspicion that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is uncertain does not cease. For where fire is not seen and smoke is seen, there is no certainty as to whether the non-perception of fire is due to its absence or rather because it has not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*). Therefore, smoke too, because its negative concomitance is doubtful, is not a means of cognition.

Now, smoke is the effect of fire; since its own nature would be impossible in the absence of that [fire], one postulates the existence of fire even though it is not perceived. But why is this effect, being perceived here, postulated to exist without a cause? Well then, let there be a postulation of a cause whose power is observed, but not of an intelligent agent. How is it that fire and the like have their power observed with respect to smoke and the like? If you say "by means of perception and non-perception," then [the same applies] to the intelligent agent as well by those two means.

In the postulation of causality, there is equality with fire and other such causes. Just as smoke and the like, being produced by a causal complex such as fire, are observed never to occur without that complex—since otherwise their very nature would be lost—in the same way, everything that possesses origination is observed to be preceded by an agent, an object, and an instrument. Because this is observed even once, its nature consists in being produced by those factors. Once its nature is thus determined, how could it arise in the absence of any one of them?

Furthermore, in the case of stationary things (sthāvara) for which no agent is perceived, the non-perception of an agent is due to the absence of a body and so forth, not because of non-existence. Where agency resides in a body, there the potter and others are indeed perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa). But here, since the presiding over the material cause and so forth occurs through mere consciousness (caitanya), how can there be the operation of direct perception? Nor should it be said that, in the absence of a body and so forth, agency is also untenable; for an inconsistency is observed between the effect and the body—as, for example:

Every conscious being effects the activity and cessation of its own body; therefore, there is a deviation [from the rule] in that case. Now, if it is argued that [activity] may occur only in a body because it is observed there and not elsewhere, that is not so; for our point to be proven is simply that an effect is produced by means of a body, whether that body belongs to oneself or belongs to another—this distinction makes no difference here. By this, the following argument is also refuted: "How can an insentient entity follow the will of that [sentient being]? (Vākyapadīya 1.43).

Is it because we observe that insentient things such as the body act in accordance with the will of a self? Nor should it be argued that the capacity to be impelled by effort is an auxiliary function belonging only to that which is insentient and does not follow its own will; for there is no contradiction even in the existence of effort in the case of God. Furthermore, it is not correct to ask how there can be effort in the absence of a body, since we observe that a body is impelled by effort even when another body is absent.

Because there is no body for the agent, there is no apprehension [of the cause] in the case of immobile beings that arise without being ploughed; it is not because of its non-perception therein that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason. Even for those who assert that the causal relation is established through perception and non-apprehension, if that [method] establishes some causal relation—for instance, the status of the sense organs and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) as causes even without those two [perceptions and non-apprehensions]—then the same applies to God (*īśvara*). Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For this very reason, there is no counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*) either; for when one reason established as being concomitant with the probandum (*sādhyānvita*) is present, there is no room for a second such [reason] therein, since it is impossible for a single real entity (*vastu*) to possess two contradictory forms. Nor is there sublation (*bādha*), because the state of having a non-intelligent cause has not been apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The absence of the reason where the probandum is absent is established precisely because the reason is pervaded by its own probandum.

Nor is there the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*dharmyasiddhatā*), because the collection of causes and effects—consisting of the elements such as earth and the group of living beings—is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). How the reason is perceived through those [elements] as its substratum has already been demonstrated previously. Therefore, in the cognition of God, there is no lack of proof for His existence.

Nor is there the fallacy of the reason being contradictory to a specific qualification (*viśeṣaviruddha*). If one were to admit that the reason is contradicted by such a qualification, then no reason whatsoever would remain uncontradicted, because even in well-established inferences, contradictions regarding specific qualifications and the like are easily found. For example, just as this smoke establishes fire, it also establishes the absence of fire limited to this particular location; for there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the aforementioned smoke with a fire limited to this specific location.

In this way, the contradictory nature (*viruddhatā*) of the reason (*hetu*) must be stated by way of delimitation through time and so forth. Now, if it is argued that there is no contradiction because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason exists with fire alone, independent of place, time, and other such factors, then—similarly, although in the example the agent is non-omniscient, not the Supreme Lord (*anīśvara*), possessed of artificial knowledge, embodied, and situated upon the earth and so forth, since the effect in general is pervaded by having an intelligent cause—nevertheless, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the previously mentioned qualifiers which constitute the specific properties of the subject (*dharmin*), there is no contradiction even though [the reason] establishes the opposite of those [qualifiers].

For a reason (*hetu*) is indeed "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it brings about the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhya*). However, these [specific qualities] do not constitute the *sādhya*, because it is intended that from this reason only the fact of being preceded by an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇapūrvakatvamātra*) is to be proven. Furthermore, the fact that reasons contradicting specific qualities (*viśeṣaviruddha*) are not genuine fallacies has been determined in the aphorism: "A contradictory reason is that which, having accepted a tenet (*siddhānta*), contradicts it" (NS 1.2.6).

For this reason, the following is not a valid objection: when a probandum is established by a preceding reason, does the subsequent [reason] establish a further qualification of that very probandum already established by the preceding one, or does it create an obstruction to the establishment of the probandum by the preceding reason? The first alternative is not tenable; for even if another reason were to introduce a qualification there, how could that possibly cause a failure in the establishment of the probandum by the preceding reason? It is just as when the impermanence of sound is established by the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and then another reason is employed.

Even if the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*) were established, there would be no impairment of the former [reason], and it is the same here as well. Alternatively, even if the latter alternative [is accepted], the obstruction to the establishment of one's own probandum is effected by demonstrating the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*); and the absence of pervasion occurs through the absence of any one of the characteristics of a valid reason (*hetu*). Nor is the absence of any such characteristic asserted merely by pointing out a reversal regarding a specific property of the locus (*dharmiviśeṣa*). Furthermore, there is no lack of probative force (*agamakatva*) when the absence of the characteristics of the reason is not established. Therefore, there is no "contradiction with a specific [property]" (*viśeṣaviruddha*).

The specific qualities (*viśeṣas*), however, are established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) at a later time once the substratum (*dharmī*) has been established; they are not accepted on the strength of the previous reason alone. And that other means of valid cognition consists of scripture (*āgama*) and another reason (*hetvantara*). Furthermore, that [other reason] is designated as either "purely negative" (*kevalavyatirekin*) or as being preceded by positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekapūrvaka*).

Just as, through the perception of odor and so forth, when the mere instrument that accomplishes it is established, the establishment of a specific instrument occurs by means of the exclusion of what is possible—this being based on the method of pure negative concomitance (kevalavyatireka)—so too here, since [the world] is an effect, when the mere cause possessing intelligence is established, the establishment of a specific cause occurs by means of the exclusion of what is possible, and this is based on the method of pure negative concomitance.

For instance—some maintain that once the mere existence of an intelligent cause has been established by the fact of being an effect (*kāryatva*), and when properties such as being connected to a body and artificial knowledge—which were previously implicated—are sublated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the establishment of a specific intelligent cause follows from the force of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Others think: "Where a reason possessing both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*) does not establish a specific [qualification], there let the establishment of a specific [qualification] arise from a purely negative reason (*kevala-vyatirekin*) preceded by that [positive-negation], as in the case of the sense organs like the nose; but here, since the specific [qualification] is established by the former reason, there is no need to postulate another reason."

Just as when the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of smoke with fire is established, the cognition "there is fire in this place" arises by virtue of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and not from the positive or negative concomitance alone—for those two [concomitances] cannot possibly involve fire as delimited by this specific location—even though at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), that location is necessarily implied by the inclusion of all [loci], since otherwise pervasion would be impossible here; nevertheless, at the moment of apprehending the pervasion, that implication occurs in a general form and not in a specific one, and thus there is the comprehension of the particular.

It is not caused by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), but rather is produced by the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). For this very reason, they call inference a memory (*smṛti*) produced by a presently existing cause; and the presently existing cause is precisely the property of being a characteristic of the subject. Thus, even though the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" and so forth is established merely with respect to an intelligent cause in general, the cognition of a specific cause arises through the power of the property of being a characteristic of the subject.

When the creator of such things as the earth is necessarily established as being connected with non-artificial knowledge, bodiless, omniscient, and singular—then, since the specific qualities are established by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), there is no room for fallacies such as "contradiction of the specific" (*viśeṣaviruddha*).

Others maintain that the specific [nature of the probandum] is established through the force of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Thus, while there is a pervasion of smoke in general by fire in general, there is likewise a pervasion of a specific smoke by a specific fire. Consequently, upon the cognition of a specific smoke, the recollection of the positive concomitance is not with respect to fire in general, but rather with respect to a specific fire. Similarly, from the observation of such a qualified effect, there is no recollection of the cause in general, but rather a recollection of a specific cause capable of producing such a specific effect.

In that recollection, the specific instrument is understood through the very force of the logical concomitance (*anvaya*); thus, there is no room for the objection of "contradiction by a particular" (*viśeṣaviruddha*).

Whether these positions are correct or incorrect, the learned will investigate them; we have no insistence on this matter. Rather, in every respect, we establish that "contradiction by a particular" is not a valid refutation, based on a critical examination of its defining characteristics.

Nor do we here endeavor to establish the specific particulars of the probandum through the sublation by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor by the force of pure negative concomitance (*kevalavyatirekin*) rooted in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nor by the power of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), nor by the fact that a specific effect is invariably accompanied by a specific cause; in every respect, there is no lack of pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*) regarding the reason under discussion.

It has been stated that there is no room for a contradiction regarding specific [conclusions] because those specific conclusions, having been proposed, are sublated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that regard, which proposed specific [conclusion] is refuted by which *pramāṇa*? First, the connection with a body is [refuted] due to the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), just as the self—though devoid of another body—is seen to possess agency in actions such as maintaining its own body. Now, while it is logical for the self to be the agent in actions such as maintenance, which require a substratum like a body, because the self possesses effort (*prayatna*), this is not the case for God (*Īśvara*), since He lacks that [effort]. And thus, according to your own school, the primary definition of an agent is as follows:

"Agency (*kartṛtā*) is the conjunction of knowledge, the desire to act, and effort. By whom was the negation of effort made in the case of God, since He is devoid of those [other two]? Because effort is produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind, and since that is impossible for God due to the absence of its cause, it is negated. But how then can there be cognition in God? For that too is produced solely by the conjunction with the mind. Let that too not exist; what loss is that to us? [Objection: But its non-existence is itself [the point], and not some other thing.

Let that [the specific property] also exist; in its absence, of what would the "specificity" characterized by the conjunction with the body and so forth be proven? For this very reason, others have said: "The negation of a supersensible object should not be undertaken through the proof or the refutation of any particular [property], because in the absence of such an object, the proof of the specific property or the cause for its refutation would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). Rather, one who accepts a supersensible object must be asked for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it. If he demonstrates a logical reason (*hetu*) that functions to establish it, then, having accepted it as 'so be it,' he should be understood [as correct]."

Now, if [the Lord] does not manifest himself, it is simply because of the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that he does not exist, and not because of the absence of specific qualities. Therefore, there is a inherence (*samavāya*) of knowledge, volition, and effort in the Lord; however, those [qualities], such as knowledge and so forth, are distinct from the knowledge and so forth of people like us. And this distinction arises from their connection with attributes such as eternity. Thus, the body of the Lord—the specific agent—is not established, because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Nor can "non-omniscience" be established as a specific quality observed in potters and the like [which would then be attributed to the Creator]; even if that were established, it would merely result in a contradiction with the specific [intended] property, as there is no pervasion [between non-omniscience and agency]. For no effect whatsoever is produced by a potter or similar agent who is not all-knowing. [Objection: But surely, if the potter and others were omniscient, then anyone who is currently not omniscient [would have to be so too]; for it is exactly thus: whoever performs an action knows the collection of its causes, such as the material cause, and its purpose; otherwise, the performance of that action would be impossible.

Furthermore, omniscience depends upon the effect to be produced and its causes. Therefore, just as a potter and others, as the makers of their own effects, know everything regarding the material cause and so forth, so too the Lord, being the maker of all, knows the purpose of the instruments and the material cause and so forth of everything that is the subject of dispute, precisely because He is the creator. Thus, how could He not be all-knowing?

Others, however, say: the apprehension of restricted objects by the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) occurs when they are presided over by the Omniscient One. Just as in a living body, the sense organs—which apprehend restricted objects such as sound and so forth—are presided over by the Omniscient One who possesses unrestricted objects; likewise, some say that death is characterized by the cessation of the activity of the senses when they are no longer presided over by consciousness.

Furthermore, since there is a grasping of specific objects by the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), that [grasping] must also be presided over by an omniscient being whose objects are not restricted. That presiding agent of the knowers of the field, whose objects are unrestricted, is the omniscient Lord (*īśvara*). But if this is so, since He alone is the presiding agent of all the knowers of the field, what is the use of the knowers of the field, who are like useless internal tumors? [We reply: Nothing at all, except for the fact that their existence is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

But surely, in this way there would be an infinite regress: just as the *kṣetrajña* is the presider over the sense organs and the Lord (*īśvara*) is the presider over him, so too there must be another presider over that [Lord]. Let there be an infinite regress if there is some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it; however, we do not perceive any means of valid cognition that establishes such an infinite regress, since [the existence of the Lord] is established by inference alone. Furthermore, there is scripture (*āgama*) regarding this matter—thus says the venerable Vyāsa:
"There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable."
All beings are the perishable; the immutable is called the imperishable.
"But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Supreme Self (paramātman), the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them" (BhG 15.16f.).
Likewise, a Vedic scripture is found that establishes this very point:
"He who has eyes on all sides and faces on all sides, arms on all sides and feet on all sides—
he, the one God, producing heaven and earth, hems them in with his arms and wings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.3), and so forth.

Nor is there a lack of validity for those [words] that convey the essential nature [of things], because they possess the quality of being generators of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, the validity of a means of knowledge consists in its being a generator of valid cognition, not in its being a generator of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*); and this [quality] certainly exists here [in the case of words denoting essence]. As for engagement and withdrawal, these occur for a person due to their desire, once they have determined that something is a means to pleasure or pain. If it is argued that the validity of these [words] lies in their being subsidiary to an injunction (*vidhi*) and not in their having the essential nature as their object, that is incorrect.

Because they convey their own specific meaning, they are auxiliary to injunction; for it is thus: praise functions as an incentive by conveying its own meaning, whereas censure functions as a deterrent. Otherwise, if their meaning were not understood, there would be either engagement in or withdrawal from prescribed and prohibited acts without distinction.

Likewise, it is observed that even an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*) possesses the power to impel a person only by means of communicating its own meaning; this should likewise apply to sentences whose primary purpose is to describe the nature of things (*svarūpa-para*), because there is no difference in their status as sentences and because there is no specific reason [to the contrary]. Similarly, if sentences concerning the nature of things were devoid of authority, then in cases such as "water is pure," "darbha grass is purifying," and "the impure is unclean"—where the nature of these things is not understood—there would result an indiscriminate tendency toward both engagement and avoidance, even when these statements serve as auxiliary elements to an injunction (*vidhyaṅgatā*). Yet, this is not the case.

Because it is observed that [a person] engages only with pure things and desists from impure ones; thus, when there is an understanding of the nature of things from sentences whose meaning consists of their own form (*svarūpa*), and because engagement is seen toward what is desired and desistance from what is undesired, it is known that—by virtue of producing valid cognition regarding the nature of things—such sentences possess the capacity to cooperate with injunctions (*vidhi*) for either engagement or desistance. Otherwise, due to a lack of such knowledge, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in regard to engagement.

Now, if the validity of words were based solely on their having two forms [literal and figurative], then even such statements as "the stones float" would have to be considered true according to their literal meaning. This is not so; for figurative interpretation (*upacāra*) occurs only where there is a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the primary sense, whereas in its absence, the statement possesses validity. Since there is no subverting proof whatsoever regarding the demonstrations of the existence of God, one must accept that they possess validity in their own form. Thus, He is understood through scripture (*āgama*), which has established validity.

And the Lord’s role as the supervisor of the individual souls (kṣetrajñas), who are engaged in perceiving their respective objects by His mere existence, is like the light of the sun for crystals and other substances engaged in reflecting the forms of objects placed near them. Just as those substances lack the capacity to grasp the forms of the objects placed near them without the solar light, so too the knowers of the field (kṣetravids) lack the capacity to perceive their own objects without the Lord; thus, the Blessed Lord exists as the omniscient one.

For this reason as well, he is omniscient: the very nature of cognition is to manifest a real object that is present; any deviation from this occurs due to the presence of some defect. This, at least, is the case for cognitions based on the eyes and other sense organs.

Furthermore, as for that eye which is not dependent [on external conditions] and is not obscured by the impurities of passion (*rāga*) and so forth—given that its very nature is the illumination of objects—why should there be an obstruction to its capacity to illuminate objects, as in the case of a lamp and the like situated within a chamber? [Objection: But how is it known that the obscuration of passion and so forth is absent therein? For there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that. [Reply: In the absence of a means of valid cognition, let there be doubt regarding passion and the rest, but not their non-existence.

Attachment and the other afflictions have perversion as their cause; in the absence of such a cause, how could they exist therein? Furthermore, perversion has unwholesome factors (*adharma*) as its object, yet there is no unwholesomeness in the Blessed One. Or, even if it were present, how could there be the arising of such an effect from it—an effect that is impossible for those like us even to conceive—given the consequence of having to postulate numerous unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*)? Moreover, attachment and the rest are observed to arise toward objects that accomplish what is desired or undesired; yet for the Blessed One, there is nothing whatsoever that accomplishes the desired or undesired, because he has attained all his goals.

As for that activity which consists in the creation of the body and so forth, some have stated that it is for the sake of play (*krīḍā*); however, such activity occurs only for those who have already attained their purpose, and not for others. Therefore, what was stated by the author of the *Vārttika*—namely, "For play belongs to those who have not found delight, and the Blessed One does not seek delight because he is free from suffering" [NV 462]—is refuted. For it is not the case that those who are suffering engage in plays; therefore, activity is not for the sake of play.

Others think: "The Blessed One's activity proceeds from compassion. [Objection: "In that case, let the creation of living beings be exclusively of the nature of happiness. [Reply: Not so; this fault applies if he were an independent creator, but if he is dependent [on other factors], how could the creation be of a single form? Dependent on those [factors], he creates bodies and so forth of such a kind as are the means for the experience of such fruits—whether meritorious or non-meritorious—as correspond to the respective latent dispositions (*karmāśaya*) of each being.

Some hold that there is no contradiction of His lordship (*īśvaratva*) even when He is dependent on other factors, just as the light of the sun is dependent on crystal and the like, or just as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who presides over the instruments, remains the Lord despite such dependence; so too here, there is no subversion of His lordship.

Others think: "Just as a master bestows different fruits in accordance with the differences in service, but is not thereby a non-master, so too the Lord produces fruit in dependence on the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*); therefore, it is not proper to say He is a non-Lord."

The author of the Bhāṣya states the activity of one impelled by compassion; even though that activity is motivated by such [compassion], the objection raised by the author of the Vārttika does not apply.

"He would create only the auspicious, impelled by compassion" (ŚV Sambandhākṣepaparihāra 52), and so forth; for the Blessed One, perceiving that the latencies of action (*karmāśaya*)—whether of the nature of wholesome or unwholesome—do not perish without the experience of their fruit, brings about the creation of living beings for the sake of that experience. The experience of the fruit of action is brought about by means of the body and other such factors; however, for certain unwholesome actions, there is exhaustion through expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).

Even in that case, karma that yields long-term suffering is exhausted by the experience of a small amount of suffering; however, there is no exhaustion of karma without its fruit being given. Even for those who hold the view that when error ceases through right knowledge, the afflictions produced by it are destroyed so that—even though the latent impressions of karma (karmāśaya) still exist—they do not project a body and so forth due to the absence of auxiliary causes, even in their case, wholesome karma does not give rise to the knowledge of reality without meditative absorption (samādhi).

However, for one engaged in the accumulation of merit through the practice of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), there arises manifold suffering; therefore, how could the creation of living beings consist solely of happiness? Even the creation of hell-beings, animals, and so forth, serves as a cause for future prosperity (*abhyudaya*) when those who have not performed expiation experience extreme suffering therein and subsequently attain a distinguished state. Thus, it is established that even in the creation of suffering beings, the Creator acts out of compassion. Consequently, "not being omniscient" is not a distinguishing fault [of the opponent's position].

Nor can it possess a connection with artificial knowledge, because such knowledge lacks the restriction to specific objects (pratyarthaniyama). Whatever knowledge is impermanent depends upon the body and so forth, and is thus restricted to specific objects; but in the absence of a body and so forth, how could that [eternal] knowledge have such restriction? Let that knowledge have restricted objects—its having restricted objects does not undermine our position.

How is there no contradiction? If he were of such a nature, it would follow that immobile beings could not arise simultaneously; and if they do not so arise, his status as a creator is not established. If that is not established, for whom is there the specific quality of being connected with artificial knowledge? Now, if one were to postulate multiple cognitions in God—each restricted to its respective object—in order to avoid the impossibility of simultaneous effects, would those cognitions exist in a continuous stream (*santāna*) or all at once? In the first alternative, the same problem arises again.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that effects do not arise simultaneously. Or, if cognitions were to arise simultaneously, one would have to admit a connection with a body and so forth for [the agent], and that has already been refuted. Alternatively, on account of the multiplicity and magnitude of the effects, let there be many intelligent agents, but not a single omniscient being endowed with all powers.

[Objection: But even in this view, does it not follow that there would be a plurality of Īśvaras? [Response: Let it be so; what is the fault? [Fault: There would be no activity toward a single object by those who are independent and whose desires are mutually contradictory. [Objection: Suppose, then, that among them some are dependent on one [of the others]; in that case, he alone is the Īśvara, while the others, being subordinate to him, are non-Īśvaras. [Objection: Or suppose it is like the unanimity found among architects and others when constructing a great temple or similar work; it is the same here as well. [Response: This is not so; in that case, there is unanimity because they have been constrained by the intention of someone [else].

But here, there is no single regulator of many [causes]. Or, if such a being exists, he is indeed Īśvara. Thus, whatever specific feature is stated as a means of proof or for refutation, its refutation must be carried out by the logic previously explained. Therefore, the probans for establishing Īśvara does not suffer from the fallacy of contradicting a specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*).

There is also the non-arising of both the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*), because the *prasaṅga* lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*), and since the contrapositive is rooted in it [the *prasaṅga*], it likewise fails; furthermore, it would result in the abandonment of what is accepted [by the opponent]. Moreover, that which is asserted by the Śākyas—that there is no agency due to eternity—is also refuted in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaṅga*. As for the claim that there can be no agency without activity (*vyāpāra*), that too is rejected because activity characterized by knowledge, desire to act, and effort has already been explained. To establish this, the author of the *Vārttika* presents two further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
