The manifest world, consisting of the great elements and so forth, is presided over by a conscious being and serves as the cause of pleasure and pain for living beings, because it possesses form and other qualities, like a chariot and such. Likewise, the great elements, earth and the rest, proceed toward their respective functions, such as supporting, only when presided over by an intelligent cause, because they are impermanent, like an axe and such instruments. (Regarding the following passage, cf. TSP 52,16ff) However, Aviddhakarṇa stated these two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to establish that [intelligent cause]: [The text continues: "The great elements and so forth are presided over by a conscious being, because they possess form and other qualities, like a chariot and such. Similarly, the great elements, earth and the rest, proceed toward their own functions, such as supporting, because they are impermanent, like an axe and such. That which is perceptible by two sense organs and that which is not perceptible by them—both having entered into the state of being the subject of dispute—is preceded by an intelligent cause, because it is characterized by a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts, like a jar; by way of contrast, atoms are [not so]. In this context, "perceptible by two sense organs" refers to the three kinds of substances known as earth, water, and fire, which are perceptible by both the visual and tactile organs, and which possess magnitude, consist of multiple substances, and are endowed with the causes for the perception of color and other qualities.

Air and the like are ungraspable, because magnitude (*mahattva*), the state of possessing multiple constituent substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and inherence of color (*rūpasamavāya*) are held to be the causes of perception; and these do not exist in air and the like. As it has been said:
"Perception occurs in that which is large due to its possession of multiple substances and due to color" (VS 4.1.6);
"There is no perception of air due to the absence of the manifestation of color" (VS 4.1.7).

The formation of matter (*rūpa-saṃskāra*) is the aggregation of matter; however, the non-perception of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth is due to their lack of magnitude (*amahattva*). Others, however, maintain that even air (*vāyu*) is perceptible by the sense organ of touch (*sparśana-indriya-pratyakṣa-grāhya*).

However, with regard to being perceivable by two sense-faculties, it was stated that there is non-perception because of the absence of inherence in form (*rūpa*). In that context, if one were to prove in a general sense that whatever is both perceivable and imperceptible by two sense-faculties is preceded by an intelligent cause, there would be the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), since this is admitted by both parties in the case of jars and the like, and thus no dispute exists. Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with what is accepted (*abhyupetabādhā*), because atoms, space, and so forth are not accepted as such, and because they are eternal, their [alleged] status would be contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge. Therefore, for that purpose, the term "that which has entered into the state of being the subject of dispute" (*vimatyadhikaraṇabhāvāpanna*) is included.

"Vividhā matiḥ" means various opinions, disagreements, or conflicting views; the sense is that which has become the locus (*adhikaraṇabhāvāpanna*) of such [conflict], that is, that which has become the subject of dispute. This being the case, only the body, the senses, the worlds, and so forth, are here made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*), so there is no contingency of including atoms and the like. Furthermore, even if the probandum were merely "having a cause," there would be the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); therefore, the term "intelligent cause" (*buddhimatkāraṇa*) is employed.

With respect to the Sāṅkhya, there is no proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the Sāṅkhyas assert that the intellect (*buddhi*) is non-different from primordial matter (*pradhāna*); and a thing cannot possess its own self by means of itself. [The term "from its own constituent parts" (*svārambhaka*)] refers to a specific configuration—the conjunction consisting of accumulation—of those parts; it is distinguished and delimited by that, and the state of being so is what is meant. The qualification "distinguished by the configuration of its own constituent parts" is included because the property of being distinguished by a configuration is over-extended (*vyabhicārin*) to things such as "cowness" (*gotva*). Therefore, the mention of "its own" (*sva*) is made.

However, [qualities such as] cowness (*gotva*) and so forth are distinguished by the arrangement of the parts that originate the substance (*dravya*), and not by the arrangement of their own originating parts. Therefore, that which possesses such intelligence is God (*īśvara*); this is the first [point]. The second [point], however, we maintain: the material causes (*upādāna*) of the body, the world, and the instruments—whether sentient or insentient—begin their respective effects only when presided over by a conscious being, because they possess color and other qualities (*rūpādimattvāt*). Whatever possesses color and other qualities begins its own effect only when presided over by a conscious being.
"That which is this conscious being, the presiding director of the material cause and so forth of the body, the world, and the instruments—that is the Blessed Lord Īśvara.

Uddyotakara, however, provides the proof: "The causes of the world—namely *pradhāna*, atoms, and unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)—require a presiding director possessing superior intelligence for the production of their own effects; because they proceed after having remained inactive, like threads, a shuttle, and so forth" [NV 457].
Praśastamati, however, says:

At the beginning of creation, the linguistic usage of persons must have been preceded by the instruction of another, because for those who have subsequently awakened to it, such usage is restricted to specific objects; just as the linguistic usage of children—who are unacquainted with verbal conventions—is restricted to specific objects such as cows and so forth, and is preceded by the instruction of their mothers and others. The phrase "because for those who have awakened it is restricted to specific objects" means that for those who have become awakened to it, it is fixed according to each respective object.

It is established that He who is the source of the worldly convention at the beginning of creation, preceded by instruction, is the Lord, whose excellence of knowledge remains unimpaired even during the period of dissolution (*pralaya*).
Furthermore, Uddyotakara has set forth other proofs for his establishment:

"The manifest world, consisting of the great elements and so forth, is presided over by an intelligent cause and serves as the occasion for pleasure and pain, because it is insentient, because it is an effect, because it is perishable, and because it possesses form and other qualities, like an axe and similar tools. [NV 459]

Now, let it be that from this collection of reasons the proof of God’s being the cause of the entire world is established; but how is His omniscience established, by virtue of which He might become an object of devotion for those who desire the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*)? We reply: it follows from the proof of His being the creator of the world. And thus Praśastamati and others have said:

Because of the agent’s thorough knowledge of the material cause, the instruments, the purpose, and the recipient of the action. For in this world, whoever is the agent of something knows its material cause and so forth; just as a potter, who is the agent of jars and the like, knows their material cause—the lump of clay; the instruments—the wheel and so forth; the purpose—such as fetching water; and the recipient—the householder. This is established.

Likewise, Īśvara is the creator of all worlds; he knows their material causes, characterized by atoms and so forth; their instruments, such as merit (*dharma*), space (*dik*), and time (*kāla*); the instruments of linguistic convention, characterized by universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*); the purpose, which is experience; and the persons designated as recipients. Therefore, his omniscience is established.

For this very reason, the following objection should not be urged here: "If it is to be proven that the earth and so forth are preceded by an omniscient being, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), and the logical reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because we observe that effects such as jars are pervaded (*vyāpti*) by having a non-omniscient agent; if it is to be proven that they are preceded by a partially omniscient being, there is a contradiction with what is accepted (*abhyupetabādha*); and if it is to be proven that they are preceded merely by a cause, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of karma. This is because [we are proving] in general that [the earth, etc. are preceded by an agent who is cognizant of their own effects, as well as their material causes (*upādāna*), instruments (*upakaraṇa*), and recipients (*sampradāna*).

And in that regard, the example of clothing and so forth certainly exists as proof. For its being preceded by an agent who is cognizant of the material causes, instruments, and so on, is well-established for all the world; how could this be otherwise made out, or how could it be denied?

(102) Nor, however, is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) by means of *karman* (action), because action is ignorant of the material causes and so forth of the effect characterized as the entire universe; or, if it were cognizant of those, it would merely be another name given to that very Blessed One himself. The rest has indeed already been considered here.

Thus, since it is established that [the Buddha] is endowed with qualities such as superior knowledge through the aforementioned collection of reasons which are free from all defects, and since his authorship of the teaching belongs to him alone and not to other yogins, it remains the case that the statement "this is the teaching of the Conquerors" is incorrect; this is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

[The Counter-Argument – Refutation of the World’s Being Created by God] Here it is replied: as for what was stated—that because the operation of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference is admitted therein, the refutation of inference preceded by perception results in proving what is already established—that is irrelevant; for even *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* inference does not function as a means of establishing that [the world’s being created by God].

For instance: "The body, the world, the sense organs, and so forth, are preceded by an intelligent cause, because they are effects, like a jar. In this case, since the locus (dharmin) is unestablished, the reason characterized as "being an effect" is first of all unestablished in its substratum (āśrayāsiddha).

For instance: first of all, it is not logical that the form of a whole (*avayavin*), such as a body and so forth, appears as a single gross entity; for a single gross thing consisting of a body and so forth, which occupies different locations and so on, is impossible. Indeed, it is not logical for one thing to occupy multiple locations and so forth, because the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is the defining characteristic of difference, and because occupying different locations and so forth constitutes the nature of contradictory properties. Furthermore, if there were no difference despite this, then even in the case of jars, cloths, and the like—which are everywhere admitted to be distinct—the consequence would follow that their difference would cease to exist.

For we do not perceive any other basis for difference in that case once it has been accepted as being distinct. If it is argued that the difference there exists due to a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*), we say no; because a difference in appearance itself cannot be established without a superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) acting as the differentiator.

Now, as for the argument that "the whole is not one, because it is characterized by contradictory properties," is this an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*) or a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*)? First of all, an independent proof is not tenable, because since the whole is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the reason suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Alternatively, if it were established by a means of valid cognition, then because it is employed immediately after stating a thesis that is sublated by the very means of valid cognition that establishes it, it would be vitiated by the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

Nor is it correct to say that there is no fault of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) because the whole (*avayavin*) is established for the opponent; for is this [whole] established for the opponent by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or without a valid cognition? If it is by means of a valid cognition, then why is it not established for you as well? For that which is established by a valid cognition is the same for everyone. And thus, that very reason (*hetu*) is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). If, on the other hand, it is without a valid cognition, then it is not established even for the opponent, and so once again there is the fault of the unestablished locus.

Therefore, the first position is not tenable, nor is the second; for a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) is that demonstration wherein the acceptance of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is shown to be necessarily concomitant with the acceptance of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Now, the relationship of pervader and pervaded between "difference" and "the superimposition of contradictory properties" is not established for the opponent. This is because difference is accepted even in the case of color and taste, despite the absence of the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by spatial distinction (*deśa*) and so forth. Furthermore, it should not be argued that even when such [contradictory properties] are present, non-difference is established by valid cognition in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.

Since the first position has already been refuted simply by its non-acceptance, as for the objection raised against the *prasaṅga* argument—that there is a difference between color and taste even in the absence of the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by spatial distinction—that indicates a lack of understanding regarding the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), but does not negate the existence of that relationship; for if, despite a difference in location, some non-difference were established, then [only] in the absence of the pervader...

Because the superimposition of contradictory properties exists [in the case of a single entity], there would be no pervasion of that [entity] by such [superimposition]; however, when there is a difference between color and taste despite the non-difference of location, then the difference of location would not be a pervader of difference. But it does not follow from this that difference would not be a pervader of the superimposition of contradictory properties. For if, even when difference is excluded, the difference of location and so forth were not excluded, then—since the pervaded would not be excluded even when the pervader is excluded—the superimposition of contradictory properties upon location and so forth would be pervaded by difference.

Nor is this established anywhere. As for the claim that, because non-difference is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, there is no cessation of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*)—characterized by distinctions such as defects—even when difference is excluded, that is incorrect; for a universal and the like are not established by means of valid cognition as having a non-different nature. And it has been said:

If the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) were not the differentiator of entities, then, in the absence of any other differentiator, the entire universe would be one; for even the difference in appearance (*pratibhāsabheda*) lacks a basis for establishing differentiation without that [superimposition]. Since the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is thus established, how could there be no scope here for a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) argument?

Now, it might be argued that because of the appearance of unity, there is oneness of the body and so forth despite differences in location and other factors; this is not so. For the parts situated in different locations are distinct due to the difference in their appearances. Indeed, the constituent parts do not appear as having a single form, for if they did, the whole would result in being no larger than a single atom. Furthermore, there is no perception of any other substance, such as a "body-whole" (*avayavin*) distinct from those parts, even though it would meet the conditions for perceptibility. Nor is it the case that its meeting the conditions for perceptibility is not admitted by others, for it is stated:
"Perception occurs because of largeness, because of possessing multiple substances, and because of color" [VS 4.1.6].

Because of this statement, it is established that "non-perception" is qualified by the phrase "of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility. Furthermore, the non-perception [of the whole] is also established, since a substance such as a body—which possesses a form graspable externally and distinct from its middle, upper, and other parts—does not appear in visual perception. Nor can it be argued that the whole is not perceived separately from its parts because they occupy the same location; for the claim that they "occupy the same location" is untenable when subjected to logical analysis.

For instance: Is the co-location of the part and the whole merely technical or worldly? If it is technical, that need not be proclaimed here, as technical conventions are not under discussion. Nor is that established there according to your own intention.

For instance: you define the directions that initiate the whole (avayavin), such as the body, as being entirely distinct from the hands and other [parts] that constitute it; yet the locations that initiate those parts, such as the hands, must be distinct as well, since the doctrine of the initiator and the initiated (ārabhyārambhaka-vāda) has been refuted. Therefore, "occupying the same location" (samānadeśatva) is not a technical convention. Nor is it common-sense (laukika), because for us, the fact that space—which is well-known in the world—occupies the same location [as anything else] is unestablished.

Furthermore, although the location characterized by light and so forth is established as being the same [in both cases], wind, sunlight, and other such factors are perceived as distinct from one another. For instance, even when entities such as wind and sunlight occupy the same location, they manifest separately due to their distinctness; yet the manifestation of a composite whole (*avayavin*) does not occur in this way. Therefore, there exists no distinct composite whole, such as a body and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that even in the very dim light, the appearance of the whole (*avayavin*) is perceived despite the non-appearance of its parts, how then can its non-existence be established on the basis of the absence of such an appearance? This is incorrect; for a vague appearance of that kind is not logically capable of establishing the true nature of the whole, because that vague appearance contradicts its own nature as it is manifested in a clear cognition. Alternatively, one might claim that the whole possesses two natures: a clear one and a vague one.

In this context, the "indistinct" is the object of cognition through dim light, whereas the "distinct" is the domain of cognition through bright light. Now, by what means is this twofold nature of the whole (*avayavin*) apprehended? It cannot be by the cognition through dim light, because in that case the distinct form, which is the object of cognition through bright light, does not appear; for that [cognition] is experienced as manifesting an indistinct nature of it. Nor can it be by the cognition through bright light, which manifests its distinct nature, because in that case the nature manifested by the cognition through dim light does not appear.

For at the time of a clear manifestation, the object that appears as a whole (*avayavin*) does not appear with an indistinct form; so how can this [indistinct form] be the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the whole? If it is argued that the essential nature of the whole perceived in dim light is now seen clearly, and thus the two are one;

Now, is the clear form apprehended by means of an unclear form, or is the unclear form apprehended by means of a clear one? If the first alternative is held, then it follows that the whole must possess an unclear form, because the clear form appears as having entered into the state of an unclear form.

Now, if the second alternative is accepted, then there would necessarily be a connection with two distinct natures, because that which is indistinct appears as having entered into a clear nature. Thus, there is no apprehension of two natures belonging to the whole (*avayavin*). As for the appearance of unity between the distinct and indistinct forms, it is a mere conceit devoid of actual appearance; otherwise, just like a cognition of bright light, even a cognition of dim light would have to be a perfectly clear appearance.

Now, it may be argued that the distinction between clear and unclear appearances there is caused by the presence or absence of light. But surely, even by light, only the nature of the whole (the object) itself should be manifested. If that [nature] appears in its entirety even in dim light, why is there not a clear manifestation produced by its manifestation in that case? Otherwise, if a difference in the appearance of cognition were possible even without a difference in the manifestation of the object, then the distinction between form and taste would no longer be established as a basis for their differentiation.

Now, if it were argued that the nature of the whole (*avayavin*) is perceived as one and the same in both cases, while the manifest and unmanifest forms are merely the two aspects of the cognition itself—that too is incorrect; for if those two were aspects of the cognition, how could they appear in the form of a whole? Since they do appear in that form, they must be admitted to be the two aspects of the whole. Indeed, apart from the manifest form and the unmanifest form, no other intrinsic nature of the whole appears. Therefore, because it does not appear, the whole simply does not exist.

Furthermore, for a whole (*avayavin*) whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, there must be a distinction corresponding to its manifest and unmanifest aspects. Indeed, unity cannot exist when there is a difference in appearance, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, it is not reasonable to claim that the form of the whole appears indistinctly in the dark even when its parts do not appear; for that would entail the aforementioned logical fault.

Furthermore, do you admit that the whole (avayavin) appears when only a few parts appear, or rather when all the parts appear? If it is the first position, it is not tenable; for even when only a few upper parts of a large pillar submerged in water appear, the whole—the pillar as an entity pervading all its parts—does not appear. If it is the second position, that too is not tenable.

Because it would follow that the whole (*avayavin*) could not be perceived due to the impossibility of perceiving all its constituent parts situated in the middle and the far parts. Now, if you maintain the position that the whole is perceived when many parts are grasped, that too is not tenable; for since perception apprehending the parts located in the near part does not grasp the parts located in the far part, it is impossible for that [perception] to grasp the pervasion of the whole by those [parts]; because if the pervaded is not grasped, it is impossible to grasp its being the pervader by means of that [non-grasping].

Alternatively, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of apprehension. For it is thus: whatever appears in a certain form is the object of conventional usage as being existent in that very form—just as blue, appearing in the form of blueness, has that very form as its object. And the whole (*avayavin*) appears as being connected with the parts located on the near side; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Nor can it be said that the whole appears as unobstructed even when the parts situated on the far side and separated by an interval do not appear, because when that [whole] appears, it does not appear as residing within those [distant parts].

And when one thing appears while another form does not appear, the latter is distinct from the former—just as the nature of a cloth, which does not appear, is distinct from a jar that is appearing. Furthermore, when the nature of the whole connected with the parts situated on the near side appears, the nature of the whole connected with the parts situated on the far side does not appear; how then is this [far-side whole] not distinct from it? Moreover, the undesirable consequence (atiprasaṅga) of [assuming] non-distinction even in such a case has already been demonstrated.

Nor is the fact that the whole is connected to its parts located on the near side apprehended by a perception that apprehends the parts and the whole as existing on the far side. For in that case, since those [far-side] parts appear [in the cognition], it would be the very nature of the whole as connected to them that appears, and not its connection with the parts on the near side; because those [near-side] parts do not appear there. And when they do not appear, the form connected to them also does not appear, because when the pervaded is not cognized, its pervader is also not cognized.

Nor can memory grasp the actual nature of the whole as connected with its parts situated in the prior and posterior portions, because memory functions in accordance with perception, and perception has already been denied as a grasper of that [whole]. Furthermore, the self is not capable of grasping the pervasiveness of the parts in the prior and posterior portions of the whole, because it is illogical for the self to be a grasper of that merely by virtue of its existence.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving it even in states such as sleep, intoxication, or fainting; rather, [the cognition] is assisted by perception. And it has already been demonstrated that no perception or other means of knowledge is possible that could grasp the pervasion of the parts by the whole.

Now, it might be argued that when the near side has been seen and subsequently the far side is seen, the perceptual cognition of recognition—“this is that very same [object]”—produced by the sense faculty with the assistance of the immediately preceding memory, grasps the pervasion of the prior and posterior parts of the whole (*avayavin*); but this is incorrect, because it is impossible for such a cognition of recognition, having that as its object, to be perceptual (*pratyakṣa*).

For perception follows the senses, and the operation of the senses is not possible regarding the apprehension of parts situated on the near or far sides [of an object], because their operation is impossible with respect to what is obstructed; if it were possible, then their operation would also extend to what is extremely remote, such as the summit of Mount Meru. Therefore, the operation of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—which is of the nature of perception and follows upon that [sensory data]—does not apply there.

Furthermore, it is not possible for a sense faculty, even when assisted by memory, to operate upon that which is not its object. Whatever is not the object of a certain faculty does not function [toward it] even when assisted by memory—just as the eye, even when assisted by the memory of fragrance, does not operate toward odor and the like. And since the nature of a whole (*avayavin*), characterized by its connection with parts situated on the far side and thus spatially remote, is not an object of the senses, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) born of the senses cannot have the essential form of the whole as its apprehended object.

Nor is there a single cognition in the form "this is that very same [thing]"; for "that" is the nature of memory, while "this" is the essential character of perception. Thus, because they possess the forms of being indirect and direct respectively, these two cognitions do not have a single nature. If it is argued that "this is that very same [thing]" constitutes a single act of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) because they appear as having a single substratum, we say no; for when there is a difference in form, unity is untenable even if there is a determination of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just as in the case of perception and memory.

Even elsewhere, difference consists only in a difference of form (*ākāra*), and since that exists here as well, how can there be oneness? Furthermore, [the cognition] would result in being "that" alone and not "this" as well; so how could there be a single recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? Even if the two forms "that very one" and "this" appear without merging with each other, they would still be two distinct cognitions with distinct forms and distinct objects. How then could there be a single recognition whose object is one, given that a difference in appearance establishes a difference in the object? No.

Furthermore, even if there were a difference in appearance, there would still be no difference in the object; for to establish the non-difference of an object apart from the non-difference of its appearance would be to accept a cognizable object (*prameya*) without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that case, everything would be established for everyone. Therefore, the apprehension of the unity of the whole (*avayavin*) does not arise even from recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). As for inference (*anumāna*) which grasps the nature of the whole, since perception has been refuted, its refutation is already accomplished as being preceded by perception. Furthermore, the refutation of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) will be set forth in the context of the refutation of the whole; so let this suffice for now.

Now, if there is a cognition of a substance such as "this is one jar" which is distinct from its parts, how can there be a non-existence of the whole? No; for even when there is the determination of a jar, what is determined are its parts and the mention of its name, not a substance that is a whole, because no one ever experiences a form of it that is devoid of color, shape, and the form of syllables. And yet, the essential nature of the whole is admitted to be devoid of color, shape, and the form of syllables.

Furthermore, that [object] does not appear in conceptual cognition (kalpanājñāna) with that same form, nor does an appearance of one form establish the true nature (vastusvarūpa) of an object that has another form; otherwise, the appearance of blue would establish yellow, and thus there would be no determination of the real object.

Therefore, even though its form is delineated by conceptual construction, the external object does not exist; there is merely this beginningless, single conventional usage which has a false referent. Nor is a single external entity established by mere convention alone, because even in the case of "the nature of blue and so forth," unity would result for the nature itself due to the non-difference of the convention.

Now, if in that case the unity [of the object] is sublated due to the difference in perceptions—such as its being of a nature that is intensely blue and so forth—then here too, let the unity of the body and other things be shattered due to the difference in the appearances of the external form as upper, lower, middle, and so on. Therefore, there exists no external object consisting of parts.

Now, in the absence of a whole (*avayavin*), there must be a distinction among its parts, such as the hands and so forth, due to the imposition of contradictory properties like spatial differentiation; and since those parts, such as the fingers and so forth, are likewise distinct for that very reason, this distinction continues down to the atoms (*paramāṇu*). Furthermore, it is impossible for these [atoms] to be the objects of a gross appearance (*sthūla-pratibhāsa*); yet, a gross and subtle external appearance in the form of blue and so forth clearly manifests.

Furthermore, a gross form cannot exist in individual atoms, for if it did, they would forfeit their status as atoms. Nor can a gross form exist in atoms when aggregated, because even in the state of aggregation, atoms remain subtle by their very nature. Furthermore, there is no aggregate distinct from those [atoms], for if there were, it would entail the doctrine of substance (*dravyavāda*), and the fault in that has already been stated. Therefore, grossness is not possible in atoms in any way whatsoever.

Furthermore, an appearance of one kind cannot reveal an object of a different kind, for otherwise it would follow that the perception of blue could establish the existence of yellow; and if that were so, the determination of fixed objects would be destroyed. Moreover, even the atom cannot logically possess unity because of its simultaneous connection with multiple directions. As it has been said: "Because of its simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms], the atom has six parts."

Furthermore, since those parts themselves would have to possess parts due to their connection with various directions, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, even atoms do not exist; thus, if the whole (*avayavin*) were not perceived, it would follow that nothing at all could be perceived. Since this leads to the non-appearance of any manifestation, there is no room for a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*). This [objection] is incorrect.

Even in the absence of a composite whole (*avayavin*), since atoms arise in uninterrupted succession in the form of jars and the like, and since the atoms of cognition that apprehend them likewise arise in that manner as the apprehenders of those [objects], there is neither an absence of external objects nor an absence of their appearance. Thus, how could there be no room for the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding the absence of a gross, unitary composite whole? Furthermore, if the composite whole were absent, it would follow that even atoms do not exist; therefore, [the objection] based on the absence of appearance [is invalid].

If it were established that there is no room for a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga-sādhana), then all the more so would the fault of the "unestablished locus" (āśrayāsiddhatā) apply to the reason characterized as "being an effect" and so forth, with respect to an object consisting of atoms or consisting of cognition, both of which are non-existent.

Furthermore, it is our intention to demonstrate that God is not established by the reason characterized as "being an effect" (kāryatva), because of the fallacy of the unestablished substratum (āśrayāsiddhatā) when external objects are denied. If, however, you also adopt a position consistent with the doctrines of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda) or emptiness (śūnyavāda), then since all the factors constitutive of inference—such as the property to be proven (sādhya), the example (dṛṣṭānta), the subject (dharmin), and the property that serves as the means of proof (sādhanadharma)—would be unestablished, how could God be established through such a formulated syllogism?

Thus, because the composite whole (avayavin) which serves as the substratum for reasons such as "being an effect" in the case of bodies and so forth is unestablished, the reason is unestablished in its substratum (āśrayāsiddha).

Likewise, in the formulation of the thesis as "an intelligent cause," the use of the possessive suffix in "intelligent" (*buddhimat*)—which qualifies the property to be proven—is untenable. This is because if that cognition were distinct from [the cause] and were not its effect, the relationship expressed by "its" (*tasya*) would be impossible. If it is argued that [the cause is called intelligent] because that [cognition] is its quality (*guṇa*), we say no; for if [the cognition] is neither its effect nor non-distinct from it, one is unable to establish the restriction that "this is its quality" and not that of space or other things.

If it is argued that inherence (*samavāya*) establishes this distinction, no; for if that inherence is also a separate entity from those two, the same fault remains: since inherence would persist everywhere even if it were distinct, the distinction could not be established by it either. If it is argued that because it is an effect of the nature of the Lord, that knowledge is a quality of the Lord’s self, how is this known? If you say it is because [the knowledge] exists when He exists, then why should it not also be an effect of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, since it exists when they exist as well? If you say it is an effect of Him because it does not exist in His absence, that is not so; [for the same logic would apply to other causes].

Because it [the Self] is eternal and all-pervading, that [inherence] is impossible for it. If you argue that its status as an effect of that [Self] is due to its being manifested within that Self, then what is this "manifestation" (utkalitatva) of it therein? If you say it is its inherence (samavetatva) in that, we ask: what indeed is this so-called inherence? If you say it is existing there by way of inherence (samavāya), then does it exist there pervasively through inherence, or non-pervasively? If it is pervasively, then it would differ from the cognition of people like us.

Just as that [agency] is postulated for that knowledge even though it is unperceived, so too, in the case of forest trees and the like which grow spontaneously, although their status as effects—accomplished through an agent, an instrument, and an action—is observed in objects such as pots, they may nonetheless be devoid of an intelligent creator. Thus, the reason characterized by "being an effect" (kāryatva), when intended to prove that something is preceded by an intelligent cause, becomes inconclusive with respect to stationary things; in seeking gain, one has incurred the destruction of the root.

Now, if it is argued that it exists there even without pervading it, then just as it has an operation with respect to bodies and the like that arise in different locations despite its non-proximity to them, so too the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) will have an operation directed toward upward flaming and so forth, even though it is not present in the locations of the fire and other elements.
[Thus: "The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of wind, and the initial motion of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen force" (VS 5.2.13).

By this sūtra, the indication of a reason intended to prove an all-pervading self (*sarvagatātman*) would be inconsistent; for even an unseen quality (*adṛṣṭaguṇa*), though not present there, can possess causal efficacy in effects such as the upward flaming of fire and so forth, just like other qualities characterized by specific attributes such as cognition (*jñāna*). Furthermore, no distinction characterized by being a general quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*) or a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is possible between a quality and its possessor if they are distinct entities.

Furthermore, since inherence (*samavāya*) is without distinction everywhere, from what source does this division arise—that it subsists in that [substance] alone by means of it, and not elsewhere? If you say that being inherent (*samavetatva*) consists in being contained therein (*ādheyatva*), then, given that space (*ākāśa*) and so forth are all-pervading just like the self (*ātman*), it would be impossible to maintain this division that being contained in them occurs only in their own self and not elsewhere. Consequently, if that cognition were distinct from its own self, the relation "that very [self] has that cognition" would be untenable.

Now, it might be argued that even if those cognitions are distinct, this fault does not arise because their relation exists in the form of inherence (*samavāya*); however, this is incorrect, because inherence is untenable. To demonstrate this, we shall refute inherence through a reductio ad absurdum: Is inherence a relation between things that exist, or between things that do not exist? If the position is that it belongs to non-existent things, that is not logical, for it would follow that even a hare’s horn, a sky-lotus, and the like would possess inherence.

Now, if it is argued that there is no such consequence because those [qualities] are absolutely non-existent, we ask: from what does the absence of absolute non-existence in the self and its cognition arise? If you say "from their inherence" (*samavāya*), then there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the absence of absolute non-existence in those two would be established once their inherence is established, and their inherence would be established through the absence of that [non-existence]. Thus, it is a case of mutual dependence. Furthermore, if inherence is what constitutes existence, then prior to their inherence, from where would their existence come? If it were from another inherence, that is untenable.

Because its oneness is admitted. Even if they were manifold, if their existence prior to inherence in another [substratum] were due to that [inherence], then their existence prior to inherence in that [inherence] would also have to be admitted as being due to another inherence; thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, their existence prior to inherence is held to be intrinsic (*svata eva*), then there is no infinite regress; however, if existence is admitted even apart from inherence, the postulation of inherence is useless. Thus, the claim that "the existence of categories arises from their connection with existence" does not inspire confidence.

Now, it is claimed that prior to inherence (*samavāya*), things possess neither existence nor non-existence, and that existence consists in the inherence of *sattā* (the universal of being). This is incorrect; for if, prior to that inherence, those things do not even produce the cognition of a yogin, how can they not be non-existent? And if they do produce that cognition, how can they not be existent? Furthermore, since existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive, the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other; thus, when non-existence is negated, why is existence not affirmed?

Furthermore, if that were the case, how could there not be a negation of non-existence? Thus, what was stated by Uddyotakara is incorrect: "Prior to its connection with cowness, it is neither a cow nor a non-cow; through its conjunction with cowness, it becomes a cow" [NV 318, 21]. Moreover, if the existence of categories arises from inherence (*samavāya*), it must be explained where the existence of inherence itself comes from. If it were from another inherence, there would be an infinite regress.

Now, if the existence of inherence (*samavāya*) is intrinsic, then let that same [intrinsic] existence belong to the categories (*padārtha*) themselves; thus, the further postulation of the inherence of existence (*sattā-samavāya*) is again useless. Furthermore, if it is claimed that inherence has existence by its own nature, how can it be reasonable for a sensible person to say that other categories have that very same nature? For when salt possesses salinity by its own nature, it does not follow that soup and other such things possess it apart from that [salt]; this [objection] is untenable.

For it would be appropriate to state that [inherence] exists once the nature of a thing has been established through direct perception; however, it is not established by direct perception that inherence and the like possess existence by way of their own intrinsic nature, while other categories possess existence because of the presence of that [inherence].

Furthermore, there are two alternatives regarding this inherence (*samavāya*): is it postulated as belonging to two things that are inherent (*samavāyin*), or to two things that are not inherent? In that regard, if the position is that it belongs to two things that are not inherent, that is not tenable; for it would follow that such inherence would apply even to a jar and a cloth, which are absolutely distinct. Nor can the state of being inherent be established for two non-inherent things through a distinct inherence by making them non-distinct [from it]; for by the imposition of contradictory properties, it follows that the inherence itself would be distinct from those two.

Nor is it distinct [from the two relata]; for if it were to bring about inherence in something distinct from them, those two would again lack the state of being inherent. If, however, it were to effect mutual assistance between them, there would be an infinite regress. But if the two are inherently inherent, what is the use of postulating an inherence as their cause? Or, if the conventional usage of "inherence" is established for those two by means of inherence—well then, if the nature of the two inherent things is within the scope of valid means of cognition such as perception, then since that very [perception] establishes the conventional usage as well, its postulation for that purpose is indeed useless.

Now, it may be argued that such a conceptualization of inherence (*samavāya*) is improper because it is established by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for if it were indeed established by that [perception], then this [objection] would be valid. However, its own nature does not appear within the means of direct perception. For the triad consisting of the self, the cognition, and its inherence is not within the range of sensory direct perception. Nor is it an object of the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), since you do not admit that. Nor is it an object of the direct perception of the internal mind (*manas*) immediately following [the cognition] inhering in the same object, because that has already been refuted.

Furthermore, even in the case of external objects such as a jar and its color-form, this triad—the jar, these color-forms and so forth inherent in it, and this distinct inherence existing between them—does not appear with distinct natures in perceptual cognition.

Alternatively, if that were the case, since substance, quality, and inherence would be established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there would be no dispute regarding their distinct natures—whether in the relationship of quality and qualified or in inherence—and nor would there be the delusion of oneness regarding a jar, its color, and so forth; consequently, the composition of a treatise for the purpose of refuting those [errors] would be pointless.

[Objection: "But surely, just as the Jainas [assert] that even when non-one-sidedness (*anekānta*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), or the Buddhists [assert] that even when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is perceived, the world has the delusion of not perceiving it due to the force of impressions (*vāsanā*) instilled by their own false scriptures (*durāgama*), and thus the composition of treatises (*śāstra*) is for the purpose of dispelling that [delusion]; so too would it be here. [Response: If that were so, then for those devoid of such treatises—such as women and children—there would be no delusion regarding the perceptibility of inherence (*samavāya*); consequently, they would have no cognition such as "this cloth is white," but rather [only] "this is a cloth."

The cognition would be: "These are qualities such as white, and this is another thing, inherence (*samavāya*), which exists in the interval between them. In this case, because inherence is subtle, even though it is perceptible, it is not specifically discerned; therefore, by metaphorically attributing the qualities of color and so forth to that [inherence] as residing therein, there would be the apprehension "the cloth is white. But this is not so; for if it were thus, there would also be the apprehension "the man is a staff" with respect to a staff. Furthermore, if this apprehension arose through metaphorical attribution, it would be of a faltering nature, like the cognition of "cow" applied to a *vāhīka* (a barbarian).

Nor is it reasonable to claim that when there is the cognition "this object is inherent here," inherence appears as a qualifying attribute; for apart from color and other forms appearing externally, nothing else—inhering internally, devoid of vocalization, and lacking the forms of color, shape, or syllables—is perceived as bearing the character of a perceptible object while existing externally as the very nature of inherence. Furthermore, the nature of inherence is accepted by others [the Naiyāyikas] as being devoid of the forms of color and so forth.

Nor does that [inherence] appear even in the conceptualizing cognition; nor can an appearance of one kind establish an object of a different kind, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, inherence is not within the scope of the means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

But as for the one who says: "Since inherence (*samavāya*) is eternally inferable, its being an object of inference is established; therefore, this fault does not apply," and his inference—namely, "The cognition 'the cloth is here in these threads' is preceded by a relation distinct from the threads and the cloth, because it is a cognition of the form 'here,' like the cognition of water in a bronze bowl"—he too speaks incorrectly.

Because it will be demonstrated later that no other category (*padārtha*), such as inherence (*samavāya*), which is eternal and uniform in nature, can possibly function as a cause; furthermore, there is no common worldly cognition in the form "the cloth is in the threads," "the cow is in the horn," or "the tree is in the branch. Rather, cognition arises and is experienced in the form "the threads are in the cloth," "the horn is in the cow," or "the branch is in the tree. If this cognition were based on inherence, it would follow that the threads and so forth are actually produced by the cloth and so forth.

Furthermore, if inherence (samavāya) were not related to its inherent relata (samavāyin), it would be illogical for it to produce the cognition of a relation in them, nor could it be their very relation; for the conjunction between a staff and a person, being unrelated to the Sahya and Vindhya mountains, is neither the cause of a cognition of relation regarding them, nor is it their relation.

Or, if that [inherence] were connected to them by itself, why would substances, qualities, and actions not be connected by themselves to their own substrata, such that the postulation of inherence would become useless? Furthermore, how would the cognition "inherence exists in these inherent things" not prove the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason under discussion, if one accepts that this connection exists by itself?

If its connection to that [substratum] were through another inherence (*samavāya*), an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) stretching to the very limits of space would result. If its connection to that were by virtue of a relationship characterized as the qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) relation, then its connection to those [relata] would likewise depend on the power of another relationship characterized as the qualifier-qualified relation; if so, that same infinite regress occurs. If its connection to them were by virtue of the power of inherence, there is clearly the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
If those [qualities] were related to it by their own nature, then cognition and the rest would also be related to their own substrata by their very nature; let that be for now.
Thus, since a relation is not established when cognition is distinct from that self, the possessive suffix (*matup*) is untenable.

Now, even if that cognition were non-different from that Self, its [creation of the world] would still be untenable; for that very thing cannot be possessed of itself by itself. Furthermore, if there is no difference between that Self and that cognition, and if the cognition were to enter into that Self, then, due to the absence of cognition, that Self—being devoid of cognition and thus insentient in nature like space and so forth—how could it be the creator of the world? Moreover, in the absence of the collection of specific qualities such as cognition and the rest, that Self, being an "Self" just like our own selves and others, [would be indistinguishable].

Due to the deficiency of those [qualities], there would be no state of being a transmigrator for the self, as if it were liberated; for you accept that liberation belongs to a self endowed with the absolute destruction of the nine specific qualities, and according to your own admission, this [destruction] is equally present even in the selves of people such as ourselves.

Now, if it is admitted that although there is no difference in their being selves (*ātman*), that Self is distinct from the selves of us and others, then why is it not likewise admitted that although there is no difference in their being effects (*kārya*), the effects such as mountains and trees are distinct from effects such as jars by virtue of having no agent? And in that case, the reason characterized by "being an effect" and so forth would not be non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) with respect to mountains and the like, whose agents are not perceived.

If, on the other hand, that [intellect] enters into that [pot] as its very self, then it must be admitted that only the intellect appears, devoid of any substratum. And thus, since even the intellect of people like us would likewise lack a substratum, the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*) would be impossible; consequently, because the status of having an intelligent cause is unestablished even in the case of a pot and so forth, the example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

Now, if it is admitted that even though the nature of being a cognition is common to the cognitions of ourselves and others, there exists a specific distinction in that [divine] cognition characterized by its lack of dependence, then one must likewise admit that even though the nature of being an effect is common to the effects of earth and so forth and the effects such as pots, there exists a specific distinction in the latter characterized by not being preceded by an agent; thus, once again, the reason characterized by "being an effect" remains inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*) for them.

Furthermore, it must be stated whether that cognition is momentary or non-momentary. If the position is that it is momentary, then how could it arise in the second moment without its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), namely the self; its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), namely the contact between the self and the mind; and its instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa), namely that body and so forth? And if it does not arise [in the second moment], how can insentient atoms and the like—being unguided by consciousness—engage in the production of effects such as mountains and the like, just as an axe or similar tools, being insentient, cannot act without being directed by a conscious agent?

Because we do not accept that activity can occur without being presided over by volition (*cetanā*). Consequently, since trees and such would not arise, the world would become devoid of effects. If, on the other hand, it is accepted that their production occurs even without inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) and so forth—on the grounds that their cognition differs from the cognition of beings like us—is it not then the very same objection: why is the difference between the effect of a mountain and the like, and the effect of a jar and the like, not likewise accepted?

Furthermore, if the cognition of the Lord arises independently of any inherent cause (samavāyi-kāraṇa) or other such causes, then even for liberated beings, bliss and so forth would arise even in the absence of instrumental causes such as a body; consequently, liberation would not consist of an insentient nature of the self devoid of cognition, pleasure, and the like.

Now, if that cognition [of yours] is non-momentary, then why is the cognition of people like us not likewise accepted as non-momentary? If you say that the cognition of people like us is not non-momentary because it contradicts means of valid cognition such as perception, then for that very same reason of contradiction, one should not accept that the state of being an effect in stationary things—whose production is unobserved—is preceded by an intelligent cause.

Now, the inference that establishes the momentariness of our own intellect—which serves to subvert the acceptance of its non-momentariness—does not, however, apply to immobile beings whose production is unobserved. What, then, is that inference? It is this: "Intellect is momentary, because, while being perceptible to persons such as ourselves, it is a specific quality of an all-pervading substance, like sound."

Now, one might object: "Just as the possibility of this inference—which subverts the acceptance of the non-momentariness of cognitions by people like us—is evident, so too will we demonstrate the possibility of that same [inference] which subverts the acceptance of being preceded by an agent in the case of stationary things (*sthāvara*) whose production is unobserved; therefore, you should not maintain such zeal regarding this matter.

Furthermore, let it rest for now that just as the inference of the momentariness of cognition is vitiated by many defects, so too will it be demonstrated during the investigation into whether sound consists of atoms (*paudgalika*).

Or, just as there is this distinction characterized by non-momentariness and momentariness between the intellects of God and those of people like us, despite the lack of difference in their being intellects, why is a similar distinction—characterized by having an agent versus not having an agent—not accepted for effects such as trees and pots? Thus, once again, that same refutation characterized by the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason "being an effect" and so forth applies to the present probandum.

Thus, it is established that when the probandum (*sādhya*) is defined as "having an intelligent cause," the suffix *-mat* (possessive) is impossible; furthermore, since there is no possibility of subverting the body and so forth by means of various types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), a reason such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), which is employed immediately after stating a thesis that is subverted by inference—just as Devadatta’s possession of the quality of scholarship (inferred from signs such as his exposition of scriptures) cannot prove the probandum of "foolishness"—is either "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) and thus non-probative, or the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is subverted by inference, just like the case of "being his son."

Likewise, the reason "because it is an effect" (*kāryatvāt*) is also unestablished (*asiddha*). To explain: what is this "being an effect" of the body and so forth? If you say it is either the inherence (*samavāya*) in its own causes of that which previously did not exist, or the inherence of existence (*sattā*), then from what [does it arise] "previously"? If you say it is from inherence in the cause, then at the time of that inherence, since there is an absence of essential existence (*svarūpasattva*) just as before, the qualification "previously" is meaningless; for a qualification is purposeful only when it is possible [for the property to apply] and when there is a possibility of deviation [from the rule].

In this case, however, there is indeed a deviation [from the definition], not a possibility. To explain: if the body and so forth exist in their own nature at the time of inherence in the cause, then, since they would exist prior [to production] just as they do at that time, they would lack the status of being an effect; thus, the qualification "previously non-existent" (*prāgasataḥ*) is employed. But when, as before, there is an absence of existence in its own nature even at the moment of inherence in the cause, then the qualification "prior" (*prāk*) does not serve any purpose; let it simply be "non-existent" (*asataḥ*).

Nor is it logical for that which is non-existent to have a inherence in its cause, because that would entail the same for things such as a rabbit’s horn. If you argue that this consequence does not apply to the rabbit’s horn because it lacks a cause, from what [source] do you derive this? If you say "from its non-existence," then regarding the body, organs, and so forth—which are likewise non-existent—what accounts for this distinction: that a cause exists for this [body, etc. but not for a rabbit’s horn and the like? Nor is it a valid answer to say that a cause for the body and so forth is perceived while one for the other is not; for this [distinction] could only occur if both cause and effect were perceived, such that one could say, "this is the cause of this" and "this is the effect of this. (109)

Furthermore, that perception does not occur through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by another person; for the Naiyāyikas hold the view that "the cause of apprehension is the object of apprehension"—as explained in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *arthavat pramāṇam* (NBh 1.2): "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is 'possessed of an object' (*arthavat*) when, in producing a cognition that is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinative nature, there exists an object as its auxiliary factor, distinct from the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)."

Furthermore, that which does not produce [an effect] cannot be a "cooperative cause" (*sahakārin*), based on the etymological derivation of *sahakārin* as "that which acts together. Nor can that which is non-existent—like the horn of a hare—be the cause of cognition or anything else, because of the contradiction involved. Moreover, perceptual cognition arises from the contact of the sense organ with its object; this contact of the sense organ is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) consisting of cause and effect. It must therefore be considered: how can even that [conjunction] be produced by that which is non-existent?

Furthermore, in the absence of conjunction, there could be no "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) for the sense organ with respect to color and so forth, nor could there be "inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*) with respect to the universal "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so on; thus, everything becomes untenable. By this, its connection with universals such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is also refuted. Therefore, perception does not have the body and so forth as its object. For this very reason, inference either does not exist or is likewise impossible. Thus, just like a donkey's horn and the like, because cause and effect are not perceived, it is not logical to claim that the body and so forth have a cause while the horn of a hare does not.

If, however, the view is that it is "existent" because it possesses a body, organs, and so forth—thus avoiding the status of the son of a barren woman and the like—then from what source does it possess those? From inherence in a cause (*kāraṇasamavāya*). And from what does that [inherence] arise? From existence (*sattva*). This is a circular argument (*anyonyasaṃśraya*): existence follows from its inherence in that [cause], and that inherence follows from existence. If it is argued that it is "existent" precisely because of the inherence of existence (*sattāsamavāya*) in what was previously non-existent, then from what was it prior? It was prior to the inherence of existence.

Surely, one must state everything [as follows]: at the time of inherence (*samavāya*), if there is an absence of existence by way of its own nature (*svarūpasattva*) just as before, then the qualification "as before" (*prāk*) is meaningless; and furthermore, if that which is non-existent were to possess inherence (*sattāsamavāya*), it would follow that even things such as a donkey's horn could do so, since there is no distinction [between them].

The qualifier "prior" was stated by the opponent for the purpose of excluding things such as a rabbit's horn. But if the body and so forth lack their own essential existence (*svarūpasattva*) at the time of their connection with Being (*sattā*), what distinction is there from that [non-existent thing]? This is the distinction: things like a tortoise’s hair are absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsatt*), whereas this other [the body] is neither itself existent nor non-existent; therefore, precisely because of its connection with Being, it alone is said to be "existent. Who else but you, whose nature is dull-witted, would speak in such a manner?

For instance: by the statement "it is not existent" (*na sat*), its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is expressed, because this [negation] is characterized by the negation of existence (*satpratiṣedha*). Nor is it an entity (*bhāva*) by virtue of being designated "non-existent" (*asat*), because an entity consists in the negation of non-existence and lacks any other form. This is precisely the logic of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*): "Two negations convey the original meaning. Otherwise, how could the negation of selflessness (*nairātmyaniṣedha*) be established as "possessing a self" (*sātmaka*) in the following argument: "This living body is not without a self, because it possesses breath and so forth"?

On this point, some say: "The formal argument (*prayoga*) is not stated in this way; rather, it is: 'The living body possesses a self (*sātmaka*), because it possesses breath and so forth (*prāṇādimattvāt*). Even by those who formulate the argument in this manner, they must necessarily accept that the absence of having a self (*sātmakatvābhāva*) is pervaded by the absence of possessing breath and so forth (*prāṇādimattvābhāva*). Otherwise, the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would not be eliminated. And if that [pervasion] is accepted, then this must necessarily be stated: the possession of breath and so forth, as perceived in the living body, excludes its own absence; for..."

And when [the absence of life-breaths] ceases, it ceases by taking along with it its own pervaded [concomitant], the absence of being endowed with a self; otherwise, the latter would not be pervaded by the former. That which does not cease when another ceases is not pervaded by that other, just as cloth and the like, which do not cease even when a lamp ceases, are not pervaded by it; and the absence of being endowed with a self does not cease when the absence of possessing life-breaths ceases.

If it is argued that [the reason] is excluded, even if that exclusion occurs, if "possessing a self" (*sātmakatva*) is not established, then its absence is not excluded either; for even in the absence of the absence of "possessing a self," the absence [of the reason] remains as it was. If it is argued that it *is* established, then this principle follows: "two negations convey the original meaning. And thus, this too is correct: "This living body is not devoid of a self, because it possesses breath and so forth."

Others, however, think as follows: because of the statement that "a property observed elsewhere is either affirmed or denied in some subject," it is simply the case that selflessness (*nairātmya*) has been observed in jars and the like to be pervaded by the absence of breath and so forth (*aprāṇādimattva*); that very same [selflessness] is denied in the living body by means of the absence of breath and so forth, but a possession of self (*sātmakatva*) is not affirmed [therein], since that has not been observed elsewhere.

It may be well said that the non-selfhood (*nairātmya*) established in those [cases], such as a jar, is being negated; nevertheless, if by the force of that negation there were no possession of self (*sātmakatva*) in the living body, then its negation could not apply to it. For when "non-selfhood" is itself another negation, a further negation of that would have to be sought; and if that were so, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and thus no negation of non-selfhood would be possible. Furthermore, even if non-selfhood is indeed perceived in things like jars, why is it negated elsewhere?

Otherwise, the scholarship perceived in Devadatta would have to be denied in Yajñadatta and others. If you argue that this is because we observe the possession of breath and so forth in them, this would be correct only if the possession of breath were incompatible with selflessness (*nairātmya*), just as fire is incompatible with coldness; but it is not so. Otherwise, everything would be compatible with suffering (*aśauca*). [If it were so,] the inherent nature of possessing breath would be incompatible with and thus exclude selflessness.

Therefore, due to the absence of the state of possessing vital breaths and so forth, the absence of that [self] is excluded, just as cold is excluded by the presence of fire; and that [absence], while being excluded, excludes its own pervaded [concomitant], namely selflessness (*nairātmya*), just as the absence of smoke excludes the absence of fire. To this, the answer has already been given: if the absence of selflessness were not possessed of a self, then selflessness would remain in its original state.

Let it be then that the negation of selflessness possesses a self; if that were so, since it is stated that "prior to its connection with existence, the body and so forth were not non-existent," its existence at that time is asserted, while its non-existence follows from the designation "not existent"—thus there is a contradiction. Therefore, one must admit that it was indeed non-existent, and thus there would be no distinction between the son of a barren woman and the like on one hand, and the body, organs, and so forth on the other. If it is argued: "Let it be so; nevertheless, existence belongs only to the body and so forth due to their connection with existence, but not to the horn of a donkey and the like, because such is observed [in the former]," it has already been stated in response to this that there is an absence of any means for such observation.

[The incidental refutation of the category of existence (*sattā*): Moreover, if existence itself were non-existent, how could there be the existence of anything else, just as in the case of the son of a barren woman? If it is existent, and if that existence is due to another existence, there would be an infinite regress. If it is self-existent, then things themselves would also possess existence by their own nature; thus, the postulation of that [separate category] would be useless. Furthermore, if existence is accepted as being self-existent, then a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated [to prove it].

Now, if existence (*sattā*) exists inherently—on the grounds that otherwise the existence of the body and so forth could not be accounted for through its connection with that [existence]—then there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): if the existence of the body and so forth is established through its connection with existence, then the existence of existence itself is established; and from that, the existence of the body and so forth is established through its connection with it. Thus, a clear case of circular reasoning (*itaretarāśrayatva*) arises. Furthermore, if it is argued that existence exists inherently because it is the object of the designation and cognition "existent," like subordinate universals (*avāntarasāmānya*) and the like—that is not so.

There is no deviation [of the definition] with respect to substance and the like—for substance and so forth are also the objects of the designation and cognition "existent," as in "existent substance," "existent quality," and "existent action. Nor is it accepted by the opponent that these are existent in themselves, for that would entail the absurdity of the conceptualization of "existence" (sattā) being useless. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that the status of being the object of that [designation and cognition] depends on something else in the case of substance and the like, but not in the case of existence itself; for even in the case of existence, such dependence is possible.

Now, if its existence there depends on that [other factor], it must be stated what that other factor is. But surely this is the same for substance (*dravya*) and so forth as well. If you say that it is "existence" (*sattā*) in that case, then here too it is the same: "substance and so forth. For just as substance and so forth are existent through their connection with existence and not by themselves, so too existence is existent through its connection with the intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattva*) of substance and so forth, and not by itself. If you argue that substance and so forth lack intrinsic existence and therefore this fault does not apply, then you must state what the fault would be if that [intrinsic existence] did exist.

Is it not the case that if it [the universal] exists by its own nature (*svataḥ*), the fault would be the consequence of the absence of intermediate universals (*avāntarasāmānya*)? And if it does not exist by its own nature, then, like a donkey’s horn and so forth, the fault of its total non-existence follows all the more clearly. Furthermore, how could one who does not accept a connection with "existence" (*sattā*) there accept a connection with an intermediate universal? Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that substance and the other categories, being non-existent by their own nature, do not possess intermediate universals.

Now, as for this [argument]: "Substance and the rest do not exist in themselves, because they possess intermediate universals (*avāntara-sāmānya*); whatever exists in itself does not possess an intermediate universal, like universals, particulars, and inherence"—this is a negative (*vyatireka*) reason. This is not so; for if substance and the rest, as subjects (*dharmin*), were established by some means as existing within the range of cognition, then how could one maintain their connection with intermediate universals? Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here to prove that "substance and the rest do not exist in themselves" or that "they do not possess intermediate universals."

Now, this [is the argument]: substances and so forth do not exist inherently (*svataḥ*) because they possess intermediate universals (*avāntarasāmānya*); for whatever exists inherently does not possess intermediate universals, just as the cognition of a universal establishes existence as being inherent. If that [cognition], while establishing existence, does not subvert the proposition that they exist inherently, then how is it that when those [entities] become existent through that [cognition], the cognition of them—establishing existence as inherent—does not subvert the proposition that "they do not exist inherently," which has their non-existence as its object?

If you do not accept this answer—that those [entities] which do not exist in themselves are objects of cognition only through their connection with existence, for it has been stated that those which do not exist in themselves cannot become objects of cognition through such a connection—then [we ask]: furthermore, how could those intermediate universals belong to a substance (*dravya*) and so forth, which are absolutely distinct from them, such that the reason "because of possessing intermediate universals" would be established? If you say, "Nevertheless, they belong to it," we say no.

The illustration by way of dissimilarity—“they might also exist in relation to one another because of the inherence of universals (*sāmānya-samavāya*), like [the case of] ‘remainder’ (*pariśeṣavat*) or ‘particularity of the inherence of universals’ (*sāmānya-samavāya-viśeṣavat*)”—is incorrect. If it is thought: “Those [qualities] inhere in substances and so forth; therefore, they belong to that [substance] and not to universals and the rest, because the opposite is the case,” that is not correct. If the meaning of “inhering therein” is that they are connected by means of inherence (*samavāya*), that is not tenable; for inherence has already been refuted and will be refuted further on.

Or, let there be inherence (*samavāya*); even so, the doubt does not cease: "In whatever substance, quality, or action there exist the intermediate universals (*avāntarasāmānya*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*), in those very same things there also exist [particular] universals such as earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), color-ness (*rūpatva*), and motion-ness (*gamanatva*). Since inherence, like those [universals], possesses universality and is omnipresent, it too—like substances and the rest—is co-existent with its own existence; thus, the intrinsic existence of substances and the like is not negated. What [is the answer]?

Is existence (sattā) existent because of its relation to substance and so forth, or is substance and so forth existent because of that [existence]? That is not so; for substance and the like do not possess existence by virtue of existence, since existence itself is unestablished.
