Since existence (*sattā*) is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no room for a *prasaṅga* argument (a reductio ad absurdum) to be advanced in this manner, because its subject matter is sublated by direct perception. Furthermore, it cannot be asserted that at the time of the manifestation of a substance, existence does not appear with a distinct form through a differentiation from the individual (*vyakti*) within the perceptual cognition; for one experiences a perceptual awareness that possesses both a recurring form and a differentiated form.

Furthermore, a cognition possessing two forms is not possible apart from an object that is both inclusive and exclusive. For a cognition does not arise independently of its object; otherwise, it would follow that even the cognition of the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa) such as blue would likewise exist [without an object].

Now, if it is argued that just as for one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), the cognition of a mass of hair-threads and the like arises even in the absence of an external object, so too will a cognition with a recurring form arise among distinct things even without an underlying common nature, and therefore no establishment of existence [for that nature] follows from it—this is incorrect. For in the case of the ophthalmic cognition, the unreality of the mass of hair-threads and so forth appearing therein is established through the recognition of the defect in the causal conditions which sublates it.

However, in the case of the perception of existence (*sattā*), there arises neither a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) nor a full awareness of defects in the cause; thus, the cognition grasping it is not false. For instance, even with respect to distinct objects such as jars and cloths, a cognition arises that delineates non-difference in the form "existent, existent"; and this is never observed to undergo subversion at another time, since for everyone at all times, the expression "existent, existent" applies to jars, cloths, and so forth.

Furthermore, even opponents accept that cognition which functions within conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As they have stated: "Validity [is established] by way of conventional practice" (*prāmāṇyaṃ vyavahāreṇa*). Thus, it stands as follows: a cognition with a recurring form (*anugatākārā*), which delineates a common nature (*sādhāraṇarūpa*) not apprehended through the cognition of excluded forms (*vyāvṛttarūpapratīti*), is a valid means of knowledge because its well-ascertained nature is beyond sublation. And since it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the sense faculties, it is perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For instance—when one with wide-open eyes perceives objects such as jars and cloths, there arises the cognition "existent, existent," which delineates an existence inherent in their form; and since this cognition does not occur in the absence of that [existence], how can it not be a perception (*pratyakṣa*), given that it conforms to its presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? Therefore, among many distinct things, a cognition of a uniform form determines a single identity. And that specific, recurring nature which persists through these diverse jars and so forth is precisely what constitutes a universal (*jāti*).

Now, if it is maintained that the universal (*jāti*) is distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), and yet at the time of perceiving the individual, no other form appearing as a commonality (*anugati*)—distinct from the object of contact with that [individual's] own nature—is manifested, then how can that be a universal? This is not so; because even for a living being who has not grasped a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), the thing first appears; subsequently, the cognition follows its identical form in only certain cases, and not everywhere.

Furthermore, a difference in cognition (*pratipattyanyatā*) is the basis for the conventional usage of difference in all cases, even in the case of color, taste, and so forth, which occupy the same place and time; since this difference in cognition exists even with respect to a universal (*jāti*), how could it not be admitted that the universal is distinct? For instance, when distinguished from the form of the individual (*vyakti*), the universal appears clearly as having a nature of inclusion (*anugati*), and when distinguished from that [individual], it appears as having a nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); thus, how can a universal that appears as distinct from the very nature of the individual not be accepted as being distinct?

Now, [the opponent might argue that] because they are apprehended by a single sense organ, the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are one, whereas in the case of color, taste, and so forth, there is a distinction because they are grasped by different sense organs; but that too is inconsistent. For even wind, sunlight, and the like—which are apprehended by a single sense organ and occupy the same location—are perceived as distinct and are therefore admitted to have distinct natures. Likewise, the pair consisting of the universal and the individual, though objects of specific sense organs, are distinct precisely because they appear as distinct.

For instance—even when a cloth is perceived in the absence of a jar, the cognition of existence (*sattā*) previously established as "existent" is observed. If, however, only the individual (*vyakti*) were existent and not the genus (*jāti*), and even if that [genus] were non-different from it, then, like the form of the individual, the non-inclusion [of the genus] would always occur. Therefore, the genus is of a single uniform nature, because it appears exactly in that way in perception.

Since the apprehension of the relationship [of denotation] for both word and inferential mark occurs in that very [existence], existence is also cognized through them. Thus, because existence is ascertainable by means of valid cognitions such as perception and so forth, there is no application of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*) inference to refute it.
This [position] is incorrect.

For at the time of perceiving an individual, a universal does not appear as something manifesting externally in its own form as an object of apprehension; indeed, at the moment when two objects such as a jar and a cloth appear, a universal—whether established as distinct or non-distinct from them—does not appear at that very time, because no other form corresponding to it appears there as an external object of apprehension. And it is the appearance of an external object of apprehension, not an internal appearance, that establishes the existence of an external thing.

If, however, that [cognition] were also the establisher of that [external object], then, since pleasure and the like—which possess forms revolving within the heart—are also manifested, their establishment would have to occur externally; and in that case, it would follow that sound and other objects are of the nature of pleasure, which would be nothing other than the Sāṅkhya view.

Now, if it is argued that pleasure and so forth do not appear as external forms and therefore they are not external, then one must likewise not admit that the universal (*jāti*) is external, since it too does not appear as having an external form; for even the conceptualizing mind, when delineating the form of a jar or the like—which was actually seen in perception—projects it externally, yet that [delimited] word appears only internally.

But it does not illuminate a universal (*jāti*) that possesses a body distinct from that [object]. Therefore, there exists no external universal to be apprehended by it. For even though things such as circles of hair appear externally in the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), they are not accepted as being real in that way, because they are objects of sublated cognition. A universal, however, never appears in any cognition as having an external form; so how could it be an object for the acceptance of its existence? It is only the intellect (*buddhi*) itself that, while pots, cloths, and so forth are appearing, shines forth with a common form as "existent, existent."

If, then, there is no external universal (*jāti*), how is it that cognition (*buddhi*) appears in a uniform form? For it is not logical that it should possess such a form without an external cause. But who says that the cognition of a universal is independent of an external cause? Rather, we say that an external universal is not the cause; instead, certain external individuals themselves are the cause of the cognition of a universal.

Now, if the recurring form based on individuals were external, then just as the cognition "cow, cow" arises upon seeing individuals such as Khaṇḍa and Muṇḍa, so too would there arise upon seeing a mountain peak and the like a cognition of the same form, "cow, cow," since there is no difference in the distinctness of the individuals; but that is incorrect.

Even though there is no difference in their being distinct individuals, since the cognition "this is a cow, this is a cow" is observed to arise with respect to individuals such as those with broken horns or those with dewlaps, it is concluded that these [individuals] alone are capable of producing that [cognition]; however, because the cognition "this is a bull, this is a bull" is not seen with respect to mountains, peaks, and so forth, they are not the basis for it.

And just as when emblic myrobalan fruits and the like are used according to the prescribed method, the result characterized by the cessation of disease is obtained, it is concluded that those [fruits] alone are capable of that [result], and not things such as cucumbers or curd, even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities.

Now, if it is argued that even when entities are distinct, there exists the cognition "existent, existent," and that the very oneness found among these distinct entities is the universal (*jāti*), to this it is replied: Is that oneness in pots, cloths, and so forth something other [than the individuals], or is it non-other? It cannot first be other, because it does not appear as such, as has already been stated. Nor can it be non-other, because a single form does not appear.

For it is not the case that the cognition of a jar and the cognition of a cloth have an identical form of appearance, nor is the word "existent" observed [to apply to both] in such a way that a continuity based on that [cognition] alone would be logical rather than a continuity based on a universal (*jāti*), since the latter is not observed. Furthermore, even the nature of one cognition does not follow into the nature of another cognition; thus, that too is not a universal. Therefore, the doctrine of a persisting universal is a false doctrine.

Furthermore, those who advocate for it accept that a universal (*sāmānya*) pervades multiple individuals. Yet, its state of such pervasion cannot be established by any cognition. To explain: at the time when a proximate individual appears, the genus (*jāti*) clearly manifests as being in contact with that specific individual, but not as being connected to other individuals, because it is impossible for it to appear [as such] due to their lack of proximity.

And since that [other individual] does not appear [in the cognition], its being mixed with it is also not apprehended; how then could the universal manifest with a body connected to other individuals that are not present? For only that form which appears in a clear perception is appropriate for it, because a nature that does not touch upon perception is impossible; or, if such were possible, it would follow that it is distinct from the perceptible nature [of the object]. If there were identity between them, then because all distinctions would be sublated everywhere, the world would not be manifold.

Furthermore, the nature of the universal (*jāti*), which is beyond the range of perception and connected to other individuals, would be non-existent because it does not appear; or, if it were to appear, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that those other intervening individuals connected to it would also appear, whereby the entire world would appear. Now, if it is thought that at the time of perceiving a proximate individual, the universal connected to other individuals does not appear;

But when another individual is perceived, at the time of that perception, the universal appears as residing in it; thus, the determination of its common nature occurs subsequently. Consequently, when the connection with other objects is later observed, why would its pervasion by those [other individuals] not be grasped? This is incorrect; for even at the time of perceiving another individual, the nature of the universal manifests as excluding that [new] individual alone, and not as being in contact with the previously perceived individual.

Since that [universal] transcends the range of direct perception, its related form also transcends it; how then can there be a cognition of a universal that is connected to both manifest individuals, whether proximate or remote?

Now, if it is argued that the universal (*jāti*) is cognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as being related to multiple individuals, then what indeed is this recognition? If it is perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can the universal—which is to be determined by it and which pervades one or many individuals—be perceptible? Or, if recognition, arising immediately after the operation of the eyes, is not perception, why [should it be]? Since even non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception follows the positive and negative concomitance of the sense organs, its status as perception is equal in this case as well; yet this is incorrect.

If recognition were produced by the senses, then at the very time of perceiving the first individual, there should be a determination of the form of the universal connected to all individuals. If it is argued that at that time there is no realization of the true nature [of the universal] due to the absence of the assistance of memory, whereas upon seeing the second individual, the sense organ—conjoined with the memory arising from the awakening of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) deposited by the previous perception—produces the vision of the true nature, that too is incorrect.

For the eye, even when assisted by memory, is capable of producing a cognition only of an individual and its resident universal that are present before it, and not of a previous individual, because of the latter's absence. Therefore, perception does not connect the universal residing in that [previous] individual with another individual currently being perceived.

Now, [an opponent might argue]: "The activity of the sense organ does not inhere in memory because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*); therefore, it cannot effect the synthesis (*sandhāna*). The self (*puruṣa*), however, by virtue of being the agent (*kartṛ*), is that in which memory inheres; thus, when an object has been apprehended by the eye, it will synthesize the universal (*jāti*) residing in the previously perceived individual instance shown by that [eye]. This is incorrect; for even that [self] is not an independent grasper of objects, but rather possesses perception as its auxiliary. 113

If, on the other hand, the self were an independent grasper of objects, then even during sleep, intoxication, fainting, and so forth, there would be the cognition of the universal (jāti) that pervades all individuals. Therefore, the self too is a knower of objects only when accompanied by perception (*darśana*). And perception follows the specific form of an individual present before one; it does not [grasp] the universal and so forth belonging to an individual previously seen, which is merely within the range of memory. Thus, the self, even when accompanied by perception, is not capable of connecting with that [past object].

Now, it might be argued that the self will connect the form of the universal brought forth by memory with that [object]; but even here, memory is observed to follow after an object previously perceived, its scope being the perception of a particular that has already been set aside as present before one's eyes.

How, then, can [the senses], which do not operate toward that which stands before them, be capable of synthesizing their own objects—such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth—with it? Furthermore, how could the Self (*ātman*) itself be capable of performing that synthesis if it were unremembered? For instance: when there is seeing, and the nature of the seer has arisen, the form of the rememberer—which is produced by memory—is not manifest, being submerged within that [seeing]. But if it were to manifest, then in that case he would be merely the seer, not the rememberer.

Now, if the nature of the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) appears as having entered into the form of the rememberer (*smartṛ*), even so, he is merely a rememberer and not a seer. Or, if they appear as distinct from the natures of the seer and the rememberer, then there is a difference between the two, and thus no unity. For instance—the nature of the seer appears as the manifestation of the objects of vision, while the nature of the rememberer appears as having descended into the object of memory for the person; how, then, can there be a synthesis of these two prior and subsequent forms?
Furthermore, as for the claim that a cognition arising from the recollection of a previously perceived object is "perception" when it is connected with the eye—this too is incorrect;

The sensory cognition does not grasp the prior form that is the object of memory; how then could it appropriate that synthesis? For the appearance of that synthesis is the appearance of what was previously seen; and since the sensory cognition, in its connection with that appearance, grasps an object beyond the senses, its appearance would be non-distinct and its apprehension of the object would be of something not present. How, then, can there be identity between those two? Furthermore, if the sensory cognition does not itself touch upon the grasping of the imperceptible, then in that case—

How can a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces that [recollection] be accepted if the cognition of the sense-faculties is [actually] devoid of it? Furthermore, if an object perceived as having the nature of a memory-object were apprehended by perceptual cognitions, then every perception would be a "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*), since the prior nature, which is the domain of memory, would appear as being present.

Now, if cognition apprehends an object that was not present there at that time, then it would be a case of *viparītakhyāti* (misapprehension). But how could perceptual experience—which, even when arising from a prior mental impression (*saṃskāra*), grasps an object as being actually present before one—be a case of misapprehension? [Objection: Surely, because it is infused with the form of the previous [object], its grasping of an existing object is impossible.

For a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣabuddhi*) that apprehends a form brought forth by memory as being present is incapable of establishing the existence of a body currently appearing, because memory can arise even when the form has vanished. And the sensory cognition following it, by pursuing that very [memory], does not have existence as its locus.

Therefore, the sensory cognition, avoiding the grasping of a prior form, operates with complete clarity regarding the present; thus, it is capable of manifesting only the universal (*jāti*) residing therein at that very moment. Consequently, there exists no universal residing in both the preceding and succeeding individuals. For only that form which resides in the second individual and appears is real; however, the form residing in the previous individual does not appear, and therefore it is not real.

Consequently, since a universal (*jāti*) that pervades multiple individuals is not established, neither the inferential mark (*liṅga*) nor the word (*śabda*) can operate with respect to it; thus, there is no cognition of it through those two either. Furthermore, just as a universal that is distinct from and permeates individuals is impossible, this will be demonstrated in its proper place; let it suffice for now. Thus, since existence (*sattā*) and inherence (*samavāya*), as postulated by others, are unestablished, the "effect-ness" (*kāryatva*)—defined as either inherence in a cause or inherence of existence in what was previously non-existent—is itself unestablished. Therefore, the reason characterized by effect-ness is also unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).

Now, it might be argued that this fault would apply if "being an effect" were presented as the reason with the definition stated above; however, since "being an effect" is presented as the reason with the definition of "coming into being after not having existed," there is no such fault.

But even so, how is such "effectness" established for the earth, mountains, and so forth? If there is disagreement regarding this point, then their effectness is proven through inference; and that inference is: "The earth, mountains, and so forth are effects, because they possess an arrangement [of parts], like a jar. How then is the reason characterized by effectness not established in their case? This is incorrect; because in this formulation as well, since the whole (the earth, mountains, etc. is unestablished, the reason "because they possess an arrangement" suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). And that lack of establishment has already been demonstrated previously.

Furthermore, if "arrangement" (*racanā*) means the configuration of parts (*avayava-sanniveśa*), and "possessing that" (*tadvattva*) means being produced from it—as in the case of earth and so forth—then the reason "because of possessing arrangement" (*racanāvattvāt*) has an unestablished qualifier (*asiddha-viśeṣaṇa*), since this "configuration of parts," which is synonymous with conjunction (*saṃyoga*), is itself unestablished. Likewise, because the substantive (*viśeṣya*)—namely, being produced by conjunction—is unestablished in earth and the other elements, the reason under discussion is also unestablished in its substantive. How is conjunction unestablished, such that the reason under discussion would be vitiated by the aforementioned defect? It is said: because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend it, and because there exists a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). To explain: [The passage continues with the argument against the existence of conjunction.]
[An incidental refutation of conjunction:

Number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, and action—these are perceptible by the senses because they are inherent in substances possessing color. (VS 4.1.11)

From this statement, it is accepted by the opponent that conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which inheres in the two perceptible objects, is graspable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, at the time when the two objects produced from their own causes appear in a perceptual cognition, no other conjunction appears as an external object of apprehension distinct from them; nor does any other nature of conjunction—devoid of color, shape, or syllables—appear in a conceptualizing mind (*kalpanābuddhi*) apart from the two aforementioned objects and the internal verbal expression.
It appears. Thus, because conjunction, which has reached the conditions for perception, is not perceived, its non-existence follows, like the horn of a hare.
Therefore, as Uddyotakara said:

If conjunction were not a distinct entity, then the field, seed, water, and so forth—being indistinguishable [from one another]—would always produce their effects, such as sprouts; yet this is not the case. Therefore, because they do not initiate their effects at all times, the field and other factors depend upon another instrumental cause for the production of the sprout, just as the collection of materials such as a lump of clay depends upon the potter and others for the making of a jar. That which is required by the field and the rest is established as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Furthermore, this conjunction, because it is perceived as qualifying two substances, is established by direct perception as being a distinct entity from them. For instance, when someone is told, "Bring those two substances that are conjoined," he brings only those two specific substances in which he perceives the conjunction, and not merely any substance whatsoever.

Furthermore, for a person standing at a great distance, the cognition of a forest—which actually possesses intervals—arises as if it were devoid of intervals; this is a false cognition (*mithyābuddhi*). Such a false cognition never arises without the experience of a false object. For one who has not experienced the sight of a cow, the delusion that "this is a cow" does not occur with respect to a *gavaya*. Therefore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) must necessarily be accepted as primary.

Likewise, by the negative statement "Caitra is not wearing earrings," neither the earring nor Caitra is negated, because both exist elsewhere, such as in another location. Therefore, what is negated is the conjunction of Caitra with the earring. Similarly, by the affirmative statement "Caitra is wearing earrings," neither Caitra nor the earring is enjoined, because both are already established. By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), what is enjoined is the conjunction.

Therefore, the claim that "conjunction (saṃyoga) certainly exists" [NV 219] must be regarded as refuted; for it has been demonstrated that conjunction does not appear in either non-conceptual or conceptual perception apart from the manifestation of the essential natures of the two conjoined substances.

Nor is the postulation of conjunction justified on the grounds that the cognition of "conjoined" would otherwise be inexplicable, because the cognition of "conjoined" arises precisely from two entities existing in a state of immediate proximity.

And as long as those two [objects] are accepted as being the objects of the cognition of "conjoined" by virtue of producing conjunction in that state, why are they not accepted as the causes of the cognition of "conjoined"—and thus its objects—indirectly even in the absence of actual conjunction? Furthermore, the cognition in which a forest with intervals appears as if without intervals is not preceded by the experience of primary (non-figurative) entities, because it is non-figurative due to the fact that the cognition is unerring.

In such cases as "Caitra is not wearing earrings," it is neither the earring related to Caitra that is negated nor affirmed, but rather the conjunction [itself]. Nor can it be argued that the relation between Caitra and the earring is impossible without a [further] relation, for is that relation one between two things already related, or between two unrelated things? It cannot be between two unrelated things, because a relation is impossible between unrelated things, just as it is between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains.

Furthermore, it is impossible to establish a non-different relation between two unrelated things through a different relation, because they would remain distinct due to the imposition of contradictory attributes. Nor can the relation be different [from the relata], for even if that difference exists, it would follow that the two things are unrelated in their own nature; since it is illogical for one thing to be related to another without some benefit conferred by the latter, and if one were to postulate a further benefit, it would lead to an infinite regress. On the other hand, it is useless to postulate a relation for the relata themselves, because even without a relation, they possess the very nature of being relata by their own essence.

As for what was stated—that soil, seed, water, and so forth do not possess the capacity to produce a sprout apart from a specific state, and that this specific state is their power (śakti) consisting of conjunction—that is insubstantial; because just as soil and the others, when endowed with that specific state, produce conjunction, so too, being endowed with that same state, they will bring about the effect such as the sprout. Thus, the postulation of a power of conjunction existing in the interval between them is redundant.

Now, if you maintain the position that the collection of causes does not function to produce an effect apart from the power of conjunction (*saṃyoga-śakti*), then, in order to produce that power of conjunction, that same collection must likewise function apart from another power of conjunction; thus, yet another power of conjunction must be postulated, and for that too another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If, on the other hand, they produce that [conjunction] even without that power, then the effect, such as the sprout and so forth, would likewise be brought about even without it; thus, the postulation of a power of conjunction existing in the interval between them is useless. Furthermore, earth and the other elements are not capable of producing even the power of conjunction apart from a specific state [of their own]; for if that were admitted, there would be the consequence of its production at all times, which would entail the consequence of the incessant production of sprouts and the like.

Nor is it the case that earth and other elements produce conjunction while depending on the action of one of the two [conjoining things] and so forth; thus, this fault does not apply, because all the objections stated regarding the position of conjunction apply equally even to the production of action. Therefore, there is no conjunction other than a distinct entity produced by a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*); for conjunction is the object of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) and lacks any establishing evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*).

As for the designation "these two substances are conjoined" or "this is the conjunction between these two," that is based solely on two entities produced in such a state, depending on whether other distinctions are excluded or not excluded; therefore, no separate conjunction is established. Furthermore, if those two were non-momentary, that relation would not be tenable, because their relation—namely, inherence (*samavāya*)—has already been refuted and will be refuted hereafter.

Nor is this [effect] related to that [cause] simply because it is produced by it, for it will be demonstrated later that there is a contradiction in the capacity to produce if [the cause] were non-momentary. Even if [the cause] were momentary, the two would merely arise in immediate succession depending on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and not through any other "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). Thus, in the argument [stated as] "because of having a configuration" (*racanāvattvāt*), the qualification of the reason—the specific conjunction characterized as a configuration—is unestablished; and since that is so, the qualified subject possessing it is also unestablished. Therefore, the reason is unestablished in both its aspects.

Now, it might be argued that the Buddhists indeed accept the fact that the earth and so forth are effects; therefore, the opponent cannot charge this reason (*hetu*) with being unestablished (*asiddha*). But even here, one must consider: what kind of "effectness" has been observed in temples and the like—through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—to be pervaded by having an intelligent agent as its antecedent? It is that kind of effectness which, when perceived in ruined temples and the like even by ordinary people and investigators who have not witnessed the actual act of making, produces the cognition of something "made. Is such [effectness] present in the case of the earth and so forth?

The reason characterized as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because such an effect is not perceived. Or, if it were perceived, then even one who has never observed its production would have the cognition that it was produced in cases such as ruined temples and the like. For an effect that has been well-discriminated through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) does not deviate from its cause, since that would entail the consequence of its being causeless.

Therefore, since the notion of "having been made" (kṛtabuddhi) is untenable for one who does not perceive an agent when observing the state of being an effect in earth and so forth, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*); for that "state of being an effect" which has been ascertained in temples and the like as being pervaded by an intelligent cause is absent there. Only the mere state of being an effect (*kāryatvamātra*) is established in those cases.

Furthermore, even if a property (*dharma*) is established by its very nature as being distinct from another, it is not sufficient for establishing the intended probandum when it is taken as a reason (*hetu*) on the basis of a mere verbal identity, because there is no contradiction in its presence even in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*). This is just as when "being merely a modification of clay" is taken as a reason to prove that an anthill was made by a potter, while taking the anthill itself as the subject (*dharmin*).

Since the state of being an effect—which is pervaded by having an intelligent cause in cases such as temples and the like—is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [in those cases], yet unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of the earth and so forth, and since it is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the earth and so forth, the desired probandum (*sādhya*) is not established from that [reason].

Is this not indeed the futile rejoinder (jātyuttara) known as "balancing the effect" (kāryasama)? To explain: when it is stated that "sound is impermanent because it is produced," the proponent of the futile rejoinder challenges this as follows: "Is this 'producedness' adduced as the reason that which resides in jars and the like, or that which resides in sound, or that which resides in both? In the first case, the reason is unestablished (asiddha), for a property belonging to one thing cannot reside in another. In the second case, the example is devoid of the probans (sādhanavikala). In the third case as well, these same two defects apply."

And this has been established as the futile rejoinder (*jāti*) called "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*); as it has been stated: "That demonstration of the non-establishment of the probandum by means of a slight difference in the nature of being an effect is *kāryasama*" [PS VI.8]. When the general property of being an effect (*kāryatva-sāmānya*) is accepted as being presented as a proof for impermanence, just as there is a conceptual differentiation based on the difference of the substratum (*dharmin*), so too, when the fact that the earth and other things have an intelligent cause is desired to be proven merely by their being effects, there is a conceptual differentiation of "being an effect" and so forth based on the difference of the substrata; therefore, this [rejoinder] is invalid.

Since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the general properties of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*) is established by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding their contrapositives, the general property of being an effect, when perceived in a subject (*dharmin*) such as sound, proves its impermanence. Therefore, if one were to introduce a distinction of properties (*dharmavikalpana*) when adducing mere "being an effect" as the reason (*hetu*) in that context, it would result in the fallacy of "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*), which leads to the total destruction of all inference.

However, when it is sought to prove that the earth and so forth have an intelligent cause, the general property of being an effect (*kāryatvasāmānya*) cannot serve as a valid reason (*hetu*). This is because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary case; thus, due to its exclusion from the opposite side being doubtful, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the property of being an effect—which is perceived in temples and the like as being pervaded by having an intelligent cause, and which produces the cognition of "having been made" even in those who have not witnessed the act of making, such as in ruined palaces—is unestablished (*asiddha*) in that specific context [of the earth].

Furthermore, if here a pervasive, eternal, and singular intelligent cause is intended as the cause of the earth and so forth on account of the reason characterized as "being an effect," then, in that case, the example would be devoid of the probandum because the state of being an effect is not ascertained as being preceded by such [a cause] in the subject of the example, such as a pot; moreover, the reason would be contradictory, since in a pot and the like, the state of being an effect is ascertained as being pervaded by having multiple agents who are non-eternal and whose intellects are non-pervasive.

Now, if what is intended to be proven is merely the state of having an intelligent cause regarding the earth and so forth, then the Lord is not established, because the specific qualification—namely, being preceded by a single creator who is the substratum of eternal intellect and who pervades [the effect]—is unproven in the case of the earth and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that only the general property of having an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇatva-sāmānya*) is proven in relation to the earth and so forth, and that this [general property] is established as residing in a specific [cause] by the force of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), because a general property cannot exist without a particular instance; [we reply: this is not so, because the specific instance of having an intelligent cause—which is observed in jars and the like and which resides in a conscious being possessing a body and lacking the capacity to construct the earth and so forth—is impossible in that case.

But surely, in this way, since the specific nature (*vyaktisvarūpa*) of a jar and so forth, which is understood as the locus of a universal, is impossible in the case of the earth and other such things, and because no other specific nature is established as being the locus of the intended universal, and because a universal cannot exist without a substrate, the universal of "having an intelligent cause" itself would not be established in the case of the earth and so forth.

For nowhere does the universal "cowness" attain establishment through any means when it is supported by a specific individual such as a spotted cow, given that such a specific individual is impossible, while cowness supported by another form of individual such as a buffalo is [impossible].

Now, since the property of being an effect would otherwise entail non-existence in the case of the earth and so forth if they lacked an intelligent cause, that universal [of "being an effect"] is indeed established there, even though it resides in individuals distinct [from those previously known]; just as the universal of fire is established from smoke, even when its locus is a mountain peak, which is distinct from a kitchen hearth.

It might be argued as follows: if the mere smoke, excluded from non-smoke, were pervaded by fire, excluded from non-fire, in a manner established through the means of valid cognition characterized by perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), then here too—through some means of valid cognition—the pervasion of the mere effect, excluded from the form [of being produced] by a non-intelligent cause, with the mere state of having an intelligent cause, excluded from non-intelligent causes, would be ascertained by a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*). However, that very [pervasion] is not established.

Now, just as smoke is the effect of fire because it follows the properties of an effect, and if it were to exist even in the absence of that [fire], it would transcend its state of having a cause—thus there is no existence of smoke apart from fire—and so the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*); likewise here too, since mountains and such follow the properties of an effect, they are the effects of an intelligent cause. If they were to exist in the absence of that [cause], they would be causeless; thus, the pervasion is established by a universal induction.

Now, it might be argued that a specific effect characterized by a jar or the like—which is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with an intelligent agent—induces the notion of having been produced even in those similar objects where no such activity is observed; therefore, because that [specific effect] is an effect of an intelligent cause, its occurrence in their absence would render it causeless. However, this cannot be said of "merely being an effect" (*kāryatvamātra*), which has as its cause merely "being a cause" (*kāraṇamātra*). For if that [mere effect-ness] were to occur in the absence of an intelligent cause, it would be rendered causeless. Indeed, that...

If it were to exist in the absence of even the mere cause, it would be uncaused (*ahetuka*). Furthermore, since no specific effect is ever observed without an agent, it is not proper for one who knows the principles of logic to say that the mere state of being an effect (*kāryatva-mātra*) is an inferential mark for a specific agent; otherwise, because a specific smoke is observed in a kitchen and such places to be invariably concomitant with fire at that time, the mere presence of smoke in an incense burner and the like would also have to be an inferential mark for fire at that same time.

Now, if it is argued that there is no contradiction with perception in the case of inferring fire at that time and place, then that same [lack of contradiction] applies equally when inferring an agent in the case of a tree growing without being cultivated, on the basis of the reason characterized as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*). If it is argued that there is no contradiction with perception because the agent of that [tree] is admitted to be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), then what fault is there in admitting that fire is also beyond the senses in the case of incense burners and the like, such that a contradiction with perception would be raised? If it is argued that this is because such [fire] is indeed observed in kitchens and similar places;

Now, we observe that this is the same even in the case of trees and the like: if there were a creator for them, he too would necessarily be perceived as possessing a body, since in the case of jars and such, the creator is always observed to be of such a nature. Alternatively, if it is accepted that an invisible being such as a *piśāca* is the agent of effects such as the breaking of tree branches, or just as Devadatta and others are movers of their own limbs even without another body, or just as [the self] is the mover [of the body], then what fault would there be if the agent of effects such as trees were likewise invisible and devoid of a body? There is no fault whatsoever, other than a contradiction of what is observed.

For instance, even in the case of Devadatta and others, the capacity to impel the parts of one's own body is not observed to exist apart from a specific connection with that body; thus, this much alone is the basis for his agency therein, and not the connection with another body, which is of no use there. Therefore, it is logical that even the agent of trees and such must function in producing effects only while connected to a body, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, if that connection [of the Lord] with the body is admitted to be produced by him, then since he would lack a connection with a body at the time of not yet producing it, he would lack the capacity to produce it; thus, a connection with another body must be admitted. Otherwise, how could one who lacks a connection with a body bring about the effect under discussion? Likewise, if that is admitted, the Lord’s activity would be exhausted in the production of successive bodies, and he would have no capacity to bring about effects such as trees and the like.

Now, regarding that body which was not brought into existence by him, it must be stated here as well: is it an effect or is it eternal? If the first alternative is taken, then even though it is an effect, it does not have a creator as its antecedent; therefore, the reason characterized as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is fallacious (*vyabhicārī*) with respect to that very instance.

If, on the other hand, it is eternal, then just as in that case the transgression of its own nature—characterized by eternity—is admitted despite its being a body, so too in the case of trees and the like, their lack of a creator must be admitted despite their being effects; thus, once again, the reason put forward by them is shown to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*).

However, for a *piśāca* or similar being who lacks connection with a body, agency—just like that of a liberated soul—is untenable. If it is argued that such a being indeed possesses a connection with a body, yet is accepted as an invisible agent because of its connection with an invisible body; [we reply: surely even for a potter and others, visibility consists precisely in the connection with a visible body and nothing else, since the self is invisible by its own nature and not otherwise. If it is further argued that its visibility results from a connection with a visible body;
[Objection: But even though the body of a *piśāca* or similar being possesses the nature of a body, how is it invisible? [Reply:

If you say it is because it is not perceived by the visual operation of people like us, then: just as a body characterized as a *piśāca*—though possessing the nature of a body—is accepted as being distinct from the bodies of people like us precisely because it is unperceivable, why is it not likewise accepted that things such as trees, though being effects distinct from jars and the like, are without an agent? And if this is accepted, then once again the reason under discussion (*prakṛto hetuḥ*) becomes inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*).

Thus, because the faults of being unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and contradictory (*viruddha*) have been pointed out, the probandum under discussion cannot be established by this reason. Therefore, what was stated—that since the "effectness" (*kāryatva*) residing in earth and so forth is not apprehended, God (*īśvara*) cannot be known from it—is indeed rightly stated.

As for the objection raised—that the Buddhists, having accepted that the earth and so forth are effects, how could they speak in such a manner (denying a creator)—that is without substance; for it has been demonstrated that the quality of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which is the basis for establishing the probandum under discussion, is unestablished (*asiddha*) in their case. Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the Cārvākas who do not accept that these [elements] are effects—that for them, how can there be the status of being an effect for things possessed of specific configurations (*saṃsthāna*)—that too is incorrect.

This is because it has been demonstrated that the property of being endowed with a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is vitiated by defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, the claim that the mere fact of being denotable by the word "configuration" is the commonality between jars and the like on one hand and earth and the like on the other, but that there exists no underlying, uniform object common to both—this is exactly so [i.e., true]. However, what was stated—that even in the case of smoke and the like, there is no uniform, underlying object common to preceding and succeeding individual instances, and so forth—is inconsistent;
for it has been demonstrated that the reason is unestablished due to the distinctness of the configuration of earth and the like from the configurations of jars and the like.

As for what was also said—that while those who are proficient indeed possess the cognition of the property of being a subject (dharmidharmatā) regarding reasons such as having the configuration of earth and so forth or being an effect, this does not exist even in the case of smoke and the like for those who are unproficient in well-known inference—that too is incorrect.

For, if those who are "learned" are defined as such by relying on a proficiency characterized by the reason's presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), which are the causes of inference, then no one at all would possess such proficiency regarding the fact that the configuration found in the earth and so forth is an effect—despite its difference from the configuration of a jar—when this is intended to prove the specific probandum under discussion; because the configuration and other such properties pervaded by the aforementioned probandum are absent in the earth and so forth.

Alternatively, if there were an existent creator—possessing a body and so forth, perceptible by the senses of those such as ourselves, endowed with a collection of attributes such as impermanent cognition, and established as pervading the reason of "configuration" (saṃsthāna) in things like jars—then there would be a cognition of such a creator in relation to the earth and other elements. For it is the practice of those who know inference that the cognition of another probandum-property (sādhyadharma)—which lacks the pervasion [of the reason] and is instead overcome by contradictory properties—arises in the subject of the inference (sādhyadharmin) through the power of a reason characterized by the aforementioned definition, and not by abandoning that which pervades the reason.

If, however, one understands [the subject] merely as a cause, then there is no disagreement regarding that, and thus the argument would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). If, on the other hand, you say "of those who are proficient" by relying on a proficiency distinct from the understanding of the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*), then for those whose mental impressions (*vāsanā*) have been instilled by base and false tradition (*durāgama*)—such as the claim that the world was created by some Creator—the cognition of the presence of the reason (e.g., having the configuration of the earth and so forth) as a property of the subject (*dharmidharmatā*) certainly exists.

Furthermore, the establishment of the probandum does not follow merely from the cognition of the property of the subject (*dharmidharmatā*) and so forth as they actually exist; for instance, although the Mīmāṃsaka cognizes the property of the subject in the Veda—such as its having no remembered author—the fact that it is of human origin remains as it was. It is indeed correct that for those who are untrained in logic, there is no [inference] even in the case of smoke and the like when inference is prohibited; for we ourselves also accept this.

As for the argument that, despite the difference in configuration between things like palaces and the configuration of the earth and so forth, the earth and other elements are accepted as being effects—since an effect is observed to be preceded by an agent, instrument, and object—that too is inconsistent; for just because a specific effect such as a jar is observed to be preceded by an agent, it is not thereby logical to assert that even an unspecific effect such as a tree and the like must be preceded by an agent.

Otherwise, since the effect characterized as earth is observed to possess the qualities of color, taste, smell, and touch while being an element (*bhūta*), one would have to admit that air (*vāyu*) also possesses those qualities simply because it is an element. Furthermore, if it is argued that there is sublation by perception and other means of knowledge in this case, that is equally applicable to effects such as trees and the like, as was established previously. As for what was said—that from [the reason] "being an effect" and so forth, which is preceded by an agent, the probandum cannot be understood because of its dissimilarity [to the subject], and so on—that is indeed true.

Because that dissimilarity has been established, it follows that no probans—such as "being an effect" and so forth—which are adduced to prove the existence of God, can be a true proof for Him. This is because the refutation set forth in the passage beginning with "the configuration [of parts] and so forth, which follows the presence or absence of a presiding agent," applies equally to every such reason used to establish God.

If this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the abolition of inference; however, the objection raised in the preceding section—that "if smoke and the like, which follow the presence or absence of the causal complex of fire and so forth in a specific manner, were to exist on the mountain in that same manner, then there would be the cognition of fire and so forth"—has already been answered.

Just as smoke, which is excluded from non-smoke and pervaded by fire—which is excluded from non-fire—is determined through the force of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) in the case of the contrary, and when perceived on a mountain peak or similar location, it causes one to infer the presence of fire in general in that place, which is based upon specific instances of fire such as those fueled by grass or wood that are not restricted [to any particular kind];

It is not the case that mere "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is ascertained as being pervaded by the generality of "having an intelligent cause" (*buddhimatkāraṇatva*) through the force of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) in the contrary case; rather, it is ascertained as being pervaded by "merely being a cause" (*kāraṇatvamātra*). And that [pervasion], when perceived in the earth and so forth, leads to the inference of a cause in general. Just as smoke perceived on a mountain peak and the like leads to the inference of fire in general—connected to it but residing in an unspecified individual—so too, from the observation of "being an effect" residing in the earth and so forth, one infers for those who do not perceive the agent [the existence of] a cause in general.

Who else, other than you who know the nature of inference, would be capable of saying that for those who do not perceive fire and so forth on a mountain peak and the like, there should be cognition of it even from smoke, just as there is for those who do not grasp it?

For if, upon perceiving a specific effect characterized by smoke, a person who has grasped its invariable concomitance attains the cognition of a specific cause characterized by fire on a mountain peak or similar location, then what follows from that regarding the cognition of a specific intelligent cause from the mere observation of a general effect in [the case of] the earth and so forth? From that, there certainly occurs the cognition of a cause in general; for a well-discriminated effect does not deviate from its cause. (PVin II 37,15–16 ≈ PVSV 23,26)

This is because of the principle stated [in II 37,15 ~ PVSV 23,26]: "Therefore, when one thing that is related is understood from another, an effort must be made to comprehend the causal relationship and so forth; otherwise, the means of valid cognition arising therefrom would be a pseudo-means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). As for the claim that it is not reasonable to say that there is no commonality of words (*śabdasāmānya*) or following of the real entity (*vastvanugama*) here, because it can likewise be said that there is a commonality of words even in the case of smoke and the like—that too is incoherent.

Because, unlike smoke and such, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) in earth and other substances does not entail having an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇatva*), since the general property of being an effect has already been established [as non-probative].

Furthermore, as for the argument that earth and the like—being composed of the conjunctions of their own parts like a jar—will necessarily undergo destruction through the disjunction of those parts, that too is inconsistent; for the disjunction of parts, characterized as separation (*vibhāga*), which is proposed as a cause for destruction just like conjunction, is unestablished (*asiddha*). And its lack of establishment should be explained in the same manner as that of conjunction.

In this way, all such arguments—whether the inference of being an effect is based on [the presence of] destruction or on the possibility thereof, or on the nature of being a structured composition (*racanā-svabhāvatva*), and so forth—are to be regarded as refuted. As for what was stated against the Cārvāka to prove "being an effect"—namely, that just as worldly and Vedic compositions are preceded by an author because there is no difference between them, so too the structures of palaces and the earth must likewise possess that same character because there is no difference—that too is incorrect, since the distinction between them has already been established.

It is indeed true that the comprehension of the probandum does not arise from a mere property of the subject (pakṣadharma) devoid of pervasion (vyāpti), because it is impossible for the establishment of the probandum to occur from a reason lacking pervasion. Furthermore, as for the argument that although "being an effect" is understood in the case of jars and the like to be preceded by an agent, yet since some effects are seen to be without an agent—such as trees and so forth in the forests—not everything is preceded by an agent; this too is indeed true. Therefore, up to this point, there is no non-deviant (avyabhicārin) reason for the proof of God.

As for what was also said—that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of immobile things such as plants, since a reason is called "deviant" only when it exists in the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), and that in the case of these [plants], the non-perception of an agent does not constitute a certainty of the absence of an agent—that too is without substance. For if, despite being within the scope of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no certainty of the absence of an agent in the case of plants and the like, then in that case, let there likewise be no certainty of the absence of color and so forth in the case of space and the like.

Now, if it is argued that the non-existence of those [elements] is certain there because of the existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the presence of form and so forth, that is the same here as well. And we shall demonstrate that very means of valid cognition immediately thereafter.

As for what was said—that because we observe the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with earth and so forth, there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in postulating those [elements] as the cause of the effect beyond them, and that under such a postulation even merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) would not be causes, and so on—that is incorrect; for the causality of merit, demerit, and the like is established by the fact that the diversity of the world cannot otherwise be accounted for.

For instance: for all things that possess an origin, the diversity of effects is produced by diverse causes known as *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), since the earth and so forth are common to all. Furthermore, there is no grounds whatsoever for postulating God as the cause, because apart from that [theory of *adṛṣṭa*], no purposeful object is observed that would otherwise remain unaccounted for. Nor can it be asserted that the nature of an effect is impossible without a conscious agent.

For the sons of the Sugata accept that consciousness itself, as it is directly perceived, is the agent of the world's diversity; thus, there is no basis for postulating another Lord distinct from that [consciousness].

Nor is it reasonable to argue that because an unseen [agent] cannot possibly possess knowledge of the materials, instruments, recipients, and so forth for the entire world—even among sentient beings—therefore another Great Lord distinct from them must be postulated as the knower of those things; for his possession of such knowledge is likewise unestablished. Furthermore, there is no proof of his being the creator of the entire world, and if that were established, then his knowledge of those things would be established; thus, it is clear that this involves the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Now, whatever is an effect is observed to be preceded by a creator who possesses knowledge of its material cause and so forth, as in the case of a jar and the like. Since the earth and other elements are also effects, it is logical that they too must be preceded by a creator possessing such knowledge; thus, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). One might object: "But even if the potter or other creators of effects such as jars were established to possess complete knowledge of the material causes and so forth of those jars, only then would it be appropriate to say this."

Furthermore, even that [potter] does not possess the direct knowledge of the various properties of the material cause, instruments, and so forth of the jar—such as its dimensions, constituent parts, number, and so on; thus, his status as a knower of reality remains unestablished. However, a mere awareness of consciousness exists even for an unseen being who serves as the substratum of that [consciousness], namely, the sentient entity who experiences the fruits produced by those unseen forces and presides over a specific body. Therefore, the postulation of a Great Lord (*maheśa*) who possesses knowledge of other distinct things is redundant.

Nor is this an absolute rule—that every effect must be produced by a creator who possesses knowledge of its material cause and so forth; for it is observed that during states such as sleep or intoxication, the movement of the limbs of the body and other parts, though performed even in the absence of knowledge of their material causes, is nonetheless brought about by [the self].

As for what was said—that there is no refutation [of the argument] by non-perception in the case of immobile beings and the like produced without being drawn [to a womb], because they have not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), like that which is unseen—that too is incorrect. For if it is accepted that this [soul] possesses agency while devoid of connection to a body, that is not logically consistent. The example is dissimilar: the liberated soul (*muktātman*) lacks agency because it is devoid of that [connection], but [the claim] is not that [agency is absent] merely due to the absence of a connection with a body; therefore, that [argument] is untenable.

Because the inherence of knowledge and other qualities—which is accepted as the basis for [the Self's] being an agent—is also refuted in that regard. Therefore, its status as the creator of the world must be accepted as arising solely from its connection with a body, just as a potter’s status as the maker of a jar arises from his body. If such a connection is admitted, why does it not follow that he possesses the conditions for perceptibility? Even in the case of potters and others, it is precisely due to their connection with a body that they possess the conditions for perceptibility; the Self, however, is not visible when devoid of such a connection.

And since that connection with a body must also be admitted for Īśvara on account of his being an agent, the non-existence of such an agent in stationary objects and the like is established by the non-perception of one who meets the conditions for perceptibility; how then is the reason characterized as "being an effect" not rendered inconclusive by them?

Now, there is no fault in this: because that body is invisible, it is not perceived even though it exists there. [Objection: Even so, let it be granted that the cognition "when this [body] exists, this [effect], such as a stationary object, is produced," does not occur. Nevertheless, just as the cognition of color and other qualities does not arise in the absence of a sense organ—even when that organ is beyond the reach of the senses—so too, even when the totality of causes such as earth and the rest is present, the effect consisting of those stationary objects might at times fail to arise due to the absence of that body. Why, therefore, would there not be a cognition based on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?

[Objection: Suppose it is argued that this fault does not apply because that body is necessarily present wherever [the effect occurs]. To this we reply: what then is the status of those entities existing simultaneously across the three worlds? For even the body of Maheśvara, being a single material entity with parts, cannot possibly possess simultaneous pervasion of everything. If it were non-material, it would follow that it is partless, and thus its body would be nothing other than space; yet its being a "body" remains unestablished even to this day.

Now, if as many bodies of that kind are postulated as there are successive effects such as sprouts and so forth, then the entire world would be filled by those bodies; consequently, no effects such as sprouts could arise, because there would be no space for their production, nor could the followers of Maheśvara proceed anywhere or desist from anything, out of fear of trampling the feet and other limbs of those bodies. Furthermore, those [bodies] themselves are effects, because they possess parts, just like a jar.

Consequently, in order to perform that [action], one would have to postulate just as many other bodies for him; and if those too were to require further performance, there would be no escape from infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, it is not reasonable to postulate that he performs effects such as stationary objects even with the assistance of bodily activity, because that would entail numerous logical faults.

Nor is it reasonable to assume that this [God] performs his own effect merely by virtue of existing, for that would entail the absurd consequence of the uselessness of postulating a body. If it is argued: "God is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of all things that have an origin; his status as such a cause is possible only through the complete knowledge of all effects and causes, and such knowledge is impossible for one who is non-eternal without sense organs and a body; therefore, he is postulated for that purpose," we say: no.

For him, knowledge that is directed toward the entirety of causes and effects—which is impermanent and produced by a body endowed with sense organs—is not possible, because there is no simultaneous contact of the sense organs with all objects. And the Naiyāyikas accept that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is produced by the contact of a sense organ with its object, as it has been stated:
"Perception is the knowledge arising from the contact of a sense organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature" [NS 1.1.4].

This is because, even among the three positions regarding the specific nature of the fruit of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), that [cognition] arising from the contact between sense-organ and object is accepted as valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). Likewise, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra "When there is apprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition, the means of valid cognition is purposeful because of the efficacy of the resulting activity" (NS 1.1.1), it is established that the means of valid cognition is an auxiliary factor (*sahakārin*)—just like the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*)—in relation to the knower and the object known, within the definition of the fruit characterized as the act of knowing (*pramiti*); and this status of being an auxiliary belongs to the means of valid cognition in the production of its fruit with respect to the object.

Since that which is active produces the result, it too possesses the status of an auxiliary; for the etymological derivation of "sahakārin" (auxiliary) is "that which acts together" (*saha karoti*). Furthermore, an object that is not present—whether past or future—cannot possess an activity directed toward the production of the result characterized as valid cognition.

Furthermore, an object that does not produce valid cognition cannot be the objective domain of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, if one accepts that Maheśvara possesses perceptual knowledge produced by a body endowed with sense organs, it would be impossible for him to possess knowledge of all effects and their causes. Thus, if his status as the creator of the world is accepted on the basis of his connection with a body, it follows that he is actually a non-creator. Consequently, it is not logical to accept a connection with an invisible body for him.

Furthermore, since effects such as jars are observed to be preceded by persons connected to visible bodies, effects such as sprouts should likewise be so conceived. If, however, one were to conceive them thus, that conception would fail because of defects such as contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) and infinite regress (*anavasthā*); thus, the state of being preceded by an agent (*kartṛpūrvakatā*) of effects like sprouts would collapse, and they should not be conceived in that way.

Now, what fault is there in its destruction? If it is argued that the status of being an effect belongs to the sprout and so forth only when they arise in the absence of multiple instruments—and that if a creator were absent, the consequence would be that such an effect is not an effect at all—this is not the case. Otherwise, in the instance of a cowherd’s water-clock (ghaṭikā) and the like, there would be the consequence that smoke would also be absent when fire is absent at that time; yet, at the time of grasping the pervasion, smoke is not understood as being preceded by fire merely because of the absence of a creator. Therefore, in that case, the inference of fire as its cause proceeds from that [smoke].

Now, if it is argued that in this way, the mere fact of being an effect is pervaded by the mere fact of having a cause, and having been apprehended at the time of grasping the pervasion, this [pervasion]—when observed in things such as sprouts—should lead to the inference of a mere cause, and not specifically to an intelligent cause, because the pervasion of the mere effect has been ascertained; [we reply:]...

Furthermore, it cannot be argued that while a specific type of effect is observed to be preceded by an intelligent cause connected to a visible body—as in the case of sprouts and the like—the very fact of being an effect perceived there leads to an inference of being preceded by such a [visible] agent, which would contradict perception; therefore, it must be inferred that it is preceded by an agent whose body is unconnected to visibility.

If that were accepted, why would smoke not also be an inferential indicator of fire in the case of a potter’s kiln and the like, even though the fire is invisible at that time? Nor can it be said that an invisible fire is impossible, for its existence is admitted to be present in the rays of the eye, which are themselves invisible. If it is argued that such a [subtle] fire is postulated because its perception as an immediately adjacent form would otherwise be inexplicable;

Surely, in this way, why is there not the postulation of such a [cause] there, on the grounds that the existence of smoke would otherwise be inexplicable? Furthermore, just as—despite fire possessing a connection with a luminous form—it is postulated that it is visible or invisible depending on whether that form is manifest or unmanifest, why is it not likewise postulated for palaces, sprouts, and so forth, given their status as effects? For the logic is the same. Therefore, it is not tenable that its production of effects such as sprouts occurs through a connection with an invisible body.

Since there is no perception of a creator when there is a connection with a visible body, how can its non-existence not be established? As for what was said—that "not all causal complexes possess the conditions for perceptibility," and so forth—that is indeed true; however, this is false: namely, that even if God is the cause, His essential nature cannot be grasped through direct perception, because He is understood only through His effects, like *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen force).

This is because it has already been demonstrated that, just as in the case of understanding *adṛṣṭa*, there is no possibility of a faultless reason such as "being an effect" for establishing the existence of God.

As for what was said—that in the case of stationary objects (sthāvara), there is no apprehension of an agent either because of the absence of an agent, or else because, even though one exists, there is no apprehension due to its being of an unperceivable nature—thus, when the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful, no reason (hetu) is probative. For even in the case of smoke and the like, at the time of perceiving the pervasion (vyāpti) by including all individual instances, not all instances of fire are visible; and so on, up to the point that everything possessing origination is seen to be preceded by an agent and instruments, because such [origination] has been observed even once to be so.

"Its nature is being produced by that [cause]; since its nature is thus ascertained, how could it have that nature even in the absence of any one of those [causes]?"—this too is inconsistent. For, because a product such as a jar is observed to be preceded by [certain causes] in whatever manner it was previously perceived, and because it has been seen once in that way, its nature as being produced by them is established. Thus, if it were to exist even in the absence of any one of those [causes], it would not be possible for it to exist even once; and it is logical to say this, but not regarding something that is dissimilar to it.

Trees and the like have never been observed to be preceded by an agent and an instrument; rather, they are preceded by causes alone. Therefore, it has been stated more than once that since their existence would result in being causeless in the absence of such [agents and instruments], it is precisely this [fact of having causes] that leads to the inference of [an intelligent creator].

Furthermore, the argument that the non-perception of an agent in immobile things—where no agent is perceived—is due to the absence of a body and so forth, rather than due to their non-existence, has also been refuted; for an answer to this has already been stated. As for what was also said—that since the presiding over material causes and so forth occurs through mere consciousness alone, how can there be the operation of perception?—that is inconsistent.

Likewise, since no instance is observed anywhere of [an agent] presiding over material causes and so forth, why do you not postulate that even material causes such as trees and the like could be their own agents—even without being presided over by an intellect—given that there is no difference in the fact of their being unobserved?

Furthermore, as for what was asserted—that the concomitance of an effect with a body is seen to be fallible because one’s own body parts perform activity and cessation even without another body, acting solely by themselves—that too is incorrect.

Since a conscious being is never observed to accomplish an action in its own bodily parts or elsewhere apart from a connection with a body, it is merely established that one should not postulate such [agency] even where it does not exist; however, the postulation of a connection with another body is not useful in this context.

If the activity of that [Self] in producing effects such as trees is postulated even though it is devoid of a body, then why is the status of being the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of knowledge not likewise postulated for the liberated [Self] as well? If that were accepted, liberation would not be possible as the abiding in the nature of the Self devoid of qualities such as knowledge and pleasure; consequently, the worship of God for that purpose would be rendered inconsistent.

As for the claim that our thesis—that an effect is produced without a body—is not affected by the fact that such an effect resides in one's own body and not in another’s, that too is worthless; for we never observe the production of an effect apart from a body.

Even regarding an effect consisting in the activity of one's own body, it is only that which is connected to that body that performs the operation. Therefore, the refutation remains firmly established: "How can an insentient entity follow the will of that [sentient being]? For we do not observe an insentient thing, such as a body, following a mere will that is unconnected to its own body.

Since even desire cannot exist for that which is unconnected [to a body], how could there be a persistence of that [desire] on the part of an insentient effect, as in the case of a liberated soul? Now, if it is argued that even an unseen desire (*adṛṣṭā icchā*) is postulated for a bodiless pillar, why is it not postulated that effects such as trees are created devoid of an agent? By this, the claim that "there is no harm in the existence of effort (*prayatna*) even for God" is refuted, because in the absence of a body, effort is impossible, just as it is for a liberated soul.

Furthermore, even the existence of an effort to move the parts of one's own body while being devoid of another body does not indicate the presence of effort in the absence of a body, because such a being entirely devoid of a body is never observed anywhere; and conceptual constructions follow what has been observed. Therefore, since there is no body in stationary things, the non-perception of their agent is due to the *absence* of an agent, and not due to the absence of a body. Thus, how is it that these [reasons], such as "being an effect," do not suffer from the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)?

Furthermore, just as the causality of a perceived sense organ is not established merely through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—despite the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which determine the relationship between cause and effect—the same cannot be established for Maheśvara on that basis alone.
