This is because, given the admission of his eternality and omnipresence, negative concomitance is impossible. Therefore, there is no establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) for reasons such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) which have been adduced as proofs for him.

For this very reason, there is no counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*) either; it is true that when one reason endowed with the probandum (*sādhyānvita*) is established, there is no room for a second such [reason] therein. However, it has been demonstrated that it is impossible for the "product-ness" (*kāryatva*) and other such reasons that establish the [existence of a] post (*sthāṇu*) to be actually endowed with the probandum. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that there is no sublation (*bādhā*) because the state of being preceded by a non-intelligent cause is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that is incorrect.

This is because there exists, in the case of sprouts and other things that grow without being ploughed, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the absence of a prior intelligent cause. Now, if it is argued that the absence of such a cause is not established through perception because the maker of the sprout and so forth is beyond the senses, we say no; for even if its absence is not established by perception, there exists an inference that apprehends its absence in that case.

For instance: whatever does not conform to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of something is not its cause, just as cloth and the like are not caused by a potter; and since sprouts and the like do not conform to the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent cause, this is a non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi). Furthermore, whatever is the cause of something conforms to its positive and negative concomitance, just as pots and the like are caused by a potter.

Furthermore, when the cause possessing the capacity for apprehension is present, there is the apprehension of sprouts and the like that were previously unapprehended; and in its absence, even when all other causes are complete, there is their non-apprehension. Thus, effects such as sprouts conform to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Now, since the agent of the sprout and so forth does not meet the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), its existence or non-existence cannot be cognized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, it is not logical to perceive the sprout’s conformity to the presence and absence of that [agent]. But surely, even if there is no perception of its conformity to presence and absence, the perception of its conformity to absence (*vyatirekānuvidhāna*) is indeed logical.

Just as, even when form, light, and attention are all present, the non-arising of the effect—consciousness—at certain times allows one to determine that another cause also possesses efficacy therein; and since that other cause is the power of the sense faculty (*indriya-śakti*), the absence of which prevents the cognition of form from arising, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of a cause whose nature is unperceivable is nevertheless observed through its effect.

The absence of a conscious cause is not observed to be concomitant with the effect, such as a sprout, because we observe that even when the totality of causal conditions—earth and so forth—is present, the sprout and other effects do not necessarily arise. While it is logical to observe a concomitance with the absence of the sense organs' power, since that power is non-eternal and non-pervasive (and thus its absence is possible), it is not logical to observe a concomitance with the absence of a conscious cause.

If it is argued that this is because [the Lord], being eternal and all-pervasive, lacks a negative concomitance (vyatireka), let it be so; nevertheless, the Lord's operation in producing effects such as sprouts consists in the inherence of His knowledge, effort, and volition. Since these are absent at all times and in all places, there would indeed be a negative concomitance with respect to them.

Now, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because the inherence (*samavāya*) [of God] exists everywhere and at all times, we say no; for even though that [inherence] is eternal and all-pervading, since its qualifiers—namely God’s knowledge, effort, desire to act, and so forth—are non-eternal and non-pervasive, one would observe a correspondence with their absence (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because that knowledge and so forth are also eternal, then the production of effects such as sprouts would occur at all times.

If it is argued that [the effect] does not arise at all times because its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are not present, then why do those auxiliaries themselves not always be present, since their own arising is dependent upon that very cognition [of the cause]? Or, if they do not have an arising dependent on that [cognition], then the reason—being an effect and so forth—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by virtue of those [auxiliaries]. If it is further argued that even those auxiliaries do not always arise because their own causes, together with their effects, are not always present, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, because its capacity would be exhausted solely by waiting for successive auxiliary causes (*sahakārī*), that cognition and so forth could never perform the intended action. Therefore, even if one goes as far as possible, one who desires some state [of permanence] must admit either the eternality of the auxiliaries or their independence from [the primary cause] in their production. For if the production of an effect were dependent on them, one must admit that it could arise even in the absence of that cognition and so forth; thus, the postulation of such [dependence] is futile.

Alternatively, if [the cause] were eternal, then because its auxiliaries and its cognitions (tajjñāna) and so forth would also be eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence of the effect being produced at all times. Thus, since those cognitions and so forth would be eternal, there would either always be the production of the effect or never; therefore, those cognitions and so forth must be admitted to be non-eternal. And this being the case, even when the completeness of the other causal conditions is present, there might at some time be no production of the sprout and so forth.

Immediately after the presence of the entire collection of other causal conditions, that cognition and so forth would arise. However, those auxiliary causes, producing that cognition and so forth while being themselves unimpelled by that cognition, likewise produce the sprout and so forth; what is the point of postulating an internal, redundant cognition? If one accepts that [the causes] produce that cognition and so forth only when conjoined with that very cognition, then another cognition produced by those auxiliary causes would itself be unproduced (since it lacks a cause), and consequently, the effect that does not arise immediately following it would also be unproduced.

If that [entity] does not produce the cognition of itself and so forth immediately thereafter, then it follows that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the effect, such as a sprout, would never arise even when all other causes are complete. Furthermore, if those cognitions and so forth were produced from the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), the same undesirable consequence would apply, and there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). In that case, just as in the production of successive cognitions, the auxiliaries would always be engaged in producing further cognitions, and thus they would never be employed toward the primary effect at any time.

If it is argued that that cognition and so forth necessarily arise together with their auxiliary causes, then one must admit that the auxiliary causes and that cognition depend upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*).

Since they do not exist otherwise than together, does that cause characterized by a single causal complex produce that [cognition]—whether it has been produced by other factors such as the cognition itself or not? It cannot be "not produced," because that would result in the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāritva*) for reasons such as its being an effect. Therefore, one must admit that the cognition and so forth have been produced. And since that which is necessarily arising along with what is produced by it depends upon that same single causal complex, it follows that it is dependent on that very complex.

Furthermore, regarding the two alternatives—that this causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is produced by another cognition of that [object]—the two previously mentioned faults would follow. If one accepts the rule that it arises immediately after [the object], then, because it depends on a single causal complex through its auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-hetu*), one must also accept that in that case as well, that single causal complex produces [the effect] when impelled by another cognition of that [object] and so forth.

Otherwise, like an axe or other tools, that which is insentient or not presided over by a sentient being could not possess the capacity for production. Furthermore, since a subsequent cognition necessarily arises immediately after a preceding one from a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it must depend on those same causes through a single causal complex; otherwise, its necessary production immediately following the prior moment would not occur.

Furthermore, regarding the two alternatives—whether another causal complex produces [the effect] when impelled or when unimpelled—the consequence of a pair of faults arises. Therefore, one who wishes to avoid this fault must not accept that the production of that cognition and so forth occurs either immediately after, simultaneously with, or prior to [the cause]; for even in the absence of a rule of production immediately after, simultaneously with, or prior to [the cause], the conformity of the effect, such as a sprout, to the presence or absence of that [cause] would still be observed.

Moreover, it is not perceived; for when the causal complex consisting of earth, water, seed, and so forth is present and there is no obstruction, the effect such as a sprout is seen to occur necessarily.

Therefore, since the concomitance with that [intelligent] cognition—which is pervaded by being its cause—is not perceived, the absence of its causality is inferred regarding the effect such as the sprout. Consequently, there is a sublation of the inference of an intelligent cause by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Why is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) not sublated by the inference of an intelligent cause alone? It is the same as [the case where] the perception grasping its [diamond's] incapacity to be scratched is not sublated by the inference: "Diamond is scratchable by iron, because it is earthy, like wood."

If it is argued that [the inference] does not invalidate that [object] because its object is invalidated by perception (*pratyakṣa*), then how can the inference of an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇatva*) invalidate [its object], given that its object is invalidated by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*)? If it is argued that the non-perception of the pervader does not invalidate [the object of the inference] because its object is invalidated by the very inference of an intelligent cause, we say no.

Could it not also be argued that, because the perception apprehending its being inscribed is sublated in its object by the inference based on its being earthen (*pārthivatva*), that [inference] lacks the power to sublate it? If you reply that this inference is merely a fallacy (*tadābhāsa*) and therefore does not sublate the object of the perception under discussion, this is not so; for it would entail the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

For instance: because the object of that inference is sublated by perception, the inference is a fallacy; and because that inference is a fallacy, perception—having its object unsublated—is not a fallacy, and thus it possesses the power to sublate the object of that [inference]. Thus, a clear circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is evident.

Now, is the non-appearance-like nature of that perception not based on its having an object that is not sublated by inference? Rather, is it based on its non-deviation from what it itself delimits? But if this is so, why is it not also accepted as a point of agreement that for inference as well, its non-appearance-like nature is based on its non-deviation from its own probandum? Or is it that, provided its object is uncontradicted, its very non-deviation from its own probandum is thereby fully established?

But if that is so, since it is impossible to ascertain that the object [of a reason] is uncontradicted, the non-deviation from its own probandum could never be established in inference as the basis for distinguishing it from a pseudo-inference; for the absence of contradiction does not follow merely from the non-perception of contradiction, because such absence exists even in cases where contradictories are present but the cognition of the contradiction has not yet arisen.

Now, it might be argued that where a sublater exists, there must necessarily be an apprehension of that sublater at a later time even if it was not apprehended previously; whereas where there is never an apprehension of a sublater, there is no existence of such a thing. This, however, is incorrect.

For it is not possible for one of limited vision to know, merely by the non-perception of a sublater, that "a sublater will never be perceived here," because the non-perception pertaining to oneself is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the non-perception pertaining to all [beings] is unestablished (*asiddha*). Indeed, one who is not omniscient is incapable of determining that no one at all perceives, or will perceive, a sublater in this case.

Nor can the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) be determined by a means of valid cognition that apprehends non-existence, for such a means has already been refuted and will be refuted further on. Furthermore, an unapprehended absence of a subverting factor cannot be a constituent of an inference, just as the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth [must be known]. Nor can the certainty of the absence of a subverting factor follow simply from the certainty of the non-deviation of the reason from its own probandum; for according to your own view, since the non-deviation from the probandum is not yet fully established, it would be impossible to ascertain it without first ascertaining that very absence of a subverting factor.

Therefore, since the property of being inseparable from its own probandum—characterized by the certainty of the reason's presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—exists even in the inference under discussion, it does not possess the status of a fallacy, just like perception. Now, if it is argued that the inference of "earthiness" is a fallacy because it lacks internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) due to the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary, then by the same logic, the inference of "being an effect" would also be a fallacy due to the absence of pervasion caused by the lack of a subverting proof against the contrary; thus, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) would not function as a subverting proof.

Now, if it is argued that perception is not sublated by inference—such that the inference of "being scratchable by iron" does not have the power to sublate the perception grasping "not being scratchable by iron"—then how is it that the perception apprehending the sun and moon as stable is sublated by an inference produced from the mark (*liṅga*) of their reaching another location? If you reply that its sublation by inference is due to its being a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), then from what source does its status as a pseudo-perception arise? If you say it is because its object is sublated by inference, then surely this is the very same fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Because its object is sublated by inference, that [perception] is a pseudo-perception; and because it is a pseudo-perception, inference—since its object is not sublated by it—is not a pseudo-inference and thus possesses the power to sublate its object. Thus, there is clearly a circularity. Therefore, in all cases, the very non-deviation from what is grasped by itself is the basis for validity.

And since that [reason]—consisting of the nature of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma), positive concomitance (anvaya), and negative concomitance (vyatireka)—is established by valid cognition in the case of the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi), its validity consists solely in its capacity to establish its own probandum; it does not, however, belong to the inference of an intelligent cause, because it has been demonstrated that in that case there is an absence of non-deviation from its own probandum.

Nor is it correct to say that even in the case of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), there is an absence of the determination of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) along with positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), which is characterized by the determination of non-deviation from its own probandum; for it has already been stated that the determination of the non-perception of the pervader as pervading the subject (*pakṣavyāpakatva*) occurs first.

Because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary position, both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) are also understood in that case. For, in the case of jars and other things which are its causes, one observes their following the positive and negative concomitance of that [effect]; the non-observation of that [concomitance] serves as the subverting proof. Alternatively, being its cause is pervaded by the following of its positive and negative concomitance, because in the absence of that [concomitance], the status of being its cause is impossible. If something were to exist even in the absence of that [concomitance] and yet still be its cause, then everything would be the effect and the cause of everything, and there would be no established determination of the causal relation anywhere. (124)

For conformity with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-anuvidhāna*) is the very basis for establishing the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). If one were to postulate a causal relationship even in the absence of that [concomitance], what else could serve as the basis for its establishment? Therefore, one who desires the establishment of the causal relationship only in specific instances—thereby avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*)—must not admit a causal relationship where that [concomitance] is absent. Thus, the causal relationship is pervaded by conformity with positive and negative concomitance; wherever that [pervader] is perceived, [the causal relationship must be present].

In this regard, by means of establishing the conformity with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one sublates its absence; thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established through inference. And because that is established, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is also established. For instance, that very negative concomitance—which consists in the absence of the probans wherever there is an absence of the probandum—is itself the positive concomitance, which consists in the necessary presence of the probandum wherever the probans is present. Thus, the non-deviation from the probandum, characterized by the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), positive concomitance, and negative concomitance, is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

And such an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) is not possible for [reasons] such as "being an effect" (kāryatva), because it has been established that, while pervading the subject (pakṣa), there is an absence of both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) due to the lack of any subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) in the contrary case.

Furthermore, if the body and so forth are to be proven to have an intelligent cause, their opposite—atoms and the like—are non-intelligent causes; nor is it established that there is the operation of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) demonstrating the exclusion from those [non-intelligent causes] of the properties such as "being an effect" which serve as the grounds for excluding them from having an intelligent cause, because [according to you], the pot and so forth are merely atoms that have attained a particular state, once their status as composite wholes (avayavin) has been refuted.

Furthermore, the exclusion of "being an effect" from those [atoms] based on the exclusion of an intelligent cause is not established through perception; for perception—which is designated by the term "perceptual non-apprehension"—operates there as the grasper of "being an effect caused by an intelligent cause. Moreover, since atoms that are not conjoined with other atoms do not appear in a perceptual cognition, the comprehension of the exclusion of the probans (the reason) as being necessitated by the exclusion of the probandum (the property to be proven) cannot arise from that [perception].

Nor can the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instances be established by its total non-observation in causes lacking intelligence, because non-observation of a relation with some [such causes] is inconclusive due to the particular mental states of other minds, and non-observation of a relation with all [such causes] is unestablished; therefore, the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instances cannot be established through pervasion.

Nor can the eternity of atoms and so forth be established through inference, because the property of being an effect—which is contradictory to eternity—is present in them; thus, the reason characterized as "being an effect," while excluding [eternity], is not established as being concomitant with "having an intelligent cause. This is because the contradiction between "being an effect" and "having a non-intelligent cause" is unproven, since that property of being an effect is possible even in things like sprouts, which are produced by non-intelligent causes.

Now, since "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is excluded from eternal things precisely because they are not produced, and since sprouts and other such things that possess the property of arising have been made the subject (*pakṣa*) insofar as they are preceded by an intelligent cause, one should not suspect a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason by means of them. Thus, the reason characterized as "being an effect," while residing in those [subjects], is established as being concomitant with having an intelligent cause. It might be argued: if the absence of an intelligent cause were established in those [subjects] merely by their being made the subject, then, if that were accepted, the employment of the reason would be useless, since the probandum (*sādhya*) would be established by the mere fact of making them the subject.

Now, if the non-existence of that [non-intelligent cause] is established from the statement of the probandum (sādhya) accompanied by that [reason], how can there be the establishment of the absence of a non-intelligent cause for all sprouts and so forth—which are distinct from the eternal—on the basis of their being effects, given that the negative concomitance (vyatireka) has not been ascertained in its entirety? And if that non-existence is not established, there is no ascertainment of negative concomitance in its entirety; thus, how could the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) not occur? Therefore, since negative concomitance is not established through pervasion (*vyāpti*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not established in its entirety; and if that is not established, neither is [the probandum].

Since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established, the reason (*hetu*) such as "being an effect" does not prove the probandum under discussion. Nor is this defect common to all inferences; for in other cases, the establishment of positive and negative concomitance occurs through the force of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary. However, it has been repeatedly stated that such [a subverting proof] does not exist in the case of the present reason.

Therefore, the claim that "the absence of the reason in the absence of the probandum is established precisely because the reason is pervaded by its own probandum" is refuted, since—according to the manner already described—the pervasion of the probandum by the reason under discussion is impossible. Nor is there the fault of the locus being unestablished (*dharmyasiddhatā*); this too is refuted, because the unestablished nature of the locus has already been demonstrated. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "the aggregate of cause and effect" has been shown to be illogical.

For this very reason, there is an absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the cognition of a Lord (*īśvara*), because any proof establishing him would suffer from the same defects, and other [attributes] such as having an insentient material cause have already been refuted. Furthermore, what was stated—that "the reason (*hetu*) is not contradicted by a specific property" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) and so forth—is also inconsistent; for if one were to prove merely a cause from the mere fact of being an effect in the case of bodies and the like, then there would be no room for contradiction since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. However, if one seeks to prove that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent cause, then it has already been demonstrated that the pervasion in that case is unestablished (*asiddha*).

If, however, it is argued that since "being an effect" (kāryatva) is observed in things such as a jar to be concomitant with an intelligent cause, that same property is thereby established for the earth and so forth; then, in that case, since in the example (dṛṣṭānta) "being an effect" is observed to be preceded by an agent who is non-omnipotent, non-omniscient, artificial, and possessed of knowledge and a body, it would therefore establish for the earth and so forth precisely such a [cause], but not a state of being preceded by an intelligent cause endowed with a collection of contradictory attributes such as omnipotence and the like—which are not observed to be concomitant with it.

For it is not logical that smoke in general—which was observed in the kitchen area as concomitant with fire—should, when observed on a mountain peak or similar location, lead to the inference of water which is possessed of properties contrary to fire; for this would result in an over-extension of the principle (*atiprasaṅga*).

As for what was stated—that because the previously mentioned qualifiers, which constitute the specific nature of the subject (*dharmin*), are inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), and so forth—that too is irrelevant; for whatever kind of "effectness" (*kāryatva*) is observed in a jar or similar object as being pervaded by having an intelligent cause endowed with attributes such as non-omnipotence, that same kind of effectness, when observed elsewhere even in a dilapidated palace or the like, produces the cognition of its being preceded by a creator of that same nature, even for one who has not seen such an action.

Furthermore, no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of that [reason] from any property such as non-omniscience (*anīśvaratva*) is ever perceived by anyone there. The very perception of a reason that is pervaded by such a probandum (*sādhya*) constitutes its non-deviation in that case; if that exists, how could it be appropriate for a sensible person to claim that it is not a valid probandum due to deviation from properties such as non-omniscience? Otherwise, even in the cognition of fire from smoke, that kind of fire would not be a valid probandum because of deviation from properties such as connection with a luminous form.

By this, all such [objections] as "Does the latter establish a specific qualification of the very probandum already established by the former reason for the sake of proving its own probandum, or does it create an obstruction to the proof of the probandum by the former reason? are refuted; because if mere "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is adduced as the reason in relation to the earth to prove the probandum, then—since its exclusion from the heterologous class (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful—it fails to prove that [the earth] is preceded by an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇapūrvakatva*).

Now, if it is argued that the "effectness" (*kāryatva*) which is pervaded by having an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇatva*) in the case of jars and the like is adduced as the reason (*hetu*) there, then that [effectness] is unestablished (*asiddha*) in that case; how then could it be an indicator even of the existence of an intelligent cause? Thus, because the non-specific "effectness" lacks pervasion, a contradiction regarding the reason's capacity to prove its own probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed possible even without the operation of another specific proving reason. However, in the case of a specific kind of effectness, the contradiction consists in the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāsiddhi*), precisely because that specific kind is unestablished in that case.

As for the claim that when the impermanence of sound is established by its being produced, there is no impairment of the former [reason] even if its quality-ness (*guṇatva*) is established by another reason—that too is incorrect; for quality-ness is defined as being endowed with properties such as dependence upon a substance (*dravyāśritatva*). If that [quality-ness] is established in sound, then the impermanence previously proven by the first reason is indeed contradicted therein; for since that which has not yet arisen does not exist, neither dependence upon a substance nor inherence as a quality (*guṇatvasamavāya*) is possible for it.

Even for that which has already arisen, [the production of a substratum] is not possible because it perishes immediately after its own arising. Nor is it the case that the arising and so forth of what depends upon that [substratum] constitute that [substratum] itself, for that would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even things like a donkey’s horn would possess that nature. This and other points have been established by those demonstrating the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of the reason (*hetu*) with respect to the substratum and so on; thus, it is not stated again.

In every respect, it is impossible for that which is distinct from the individual cause of its production to possess the nature of a quality (*guṇatva*) while persisting for even a single moment; and we shall demonstrate that if such persistence were possible, its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would be contradicted. Furthermore, regarding the second alternative, your statement that "by pointing out a reversal of the specific properties of the substratum (*dharmī*), the non-existence of any form whatsoever is not being asserted" is also incoherent.

For if the establishment of such a subject (*dharmin*) as earth were to occur from some other reason, then it might indeed be appropriate to say that no form of the reason is absent by way of pointing out a reversal of the specific properties of the subject; however, it has been demonstrated that such a subject is not understood from the proof under discussion. Therefore, neither scripture nor another reason establishes a specific property therein, because a subject characterized as having an intelligent cause is itself unestablished as being the creator of earth and so forth.

Therefore, the argument that this very same [reason], which is preceded by positive and negative concomitance and designated as "purely negative" (*kevalavyatirekin*), is actually a proof of a specific property because it possesses the characteristics of positive and negative concomitance through the grace of "property-of-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*), is cast far aside; for when the locus (*dharmin*) itself is unestablished, the establishment of its specific properties is utterly discarded.

For this very reason, when the specific attributes are established—namely, that the creator of such things as the earth is necessarily possessed of non-artificial knowledge, is bodiless, omniscient, and singular—then there is no room for those [reasons] that contradict these specific attributes; thus it has been established that [the opponent's position] is devoid of substance.

As for what was said—that because there is no pervasion (vyāpti) regarding the connection with a body, the [creator] is refuted therein, yet just as the self (*ātman*), though devoid of another body, possesses activity in the acts of maintaining and impelling a body, so too does the Lord (*Īśvara*) possess activity toward effects such as the earth—that too is incorrect.

Since it has been established that even though the self is devoid of another body, its agency in supporting [the body] and so forth is observed only when it is connected to a body, therefore the Lord’s agency in producing effects must also be accepted as occurring only when he is connected to a body. And if his agency in producing effects such as the earth were possible even in the absence of a connection with a body, then it must be stated: what is it that exists there in that case? If it is argued that "it is simply the inherence of knowledge, volition, and effort, and that has already been stated regarding that [Lord]," we say no.

Because inherence (samavāya) has been refuted, and because no agency other than the connection with a body is observed in cases such as a potter, that very [agency] must be postulated for God as well, since conceptual construction follows what is observed. Furthermore, since the existence of knowledge, desire to act, and effort apart from a body is not observed anywhere, these must not be admitted in God either in the absence of a body.

For instance: in the production of knowledge and the like, the self (*ātman*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the contact between the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥsaṃyoga*) is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the body and so forth are the instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*); and it is not accepted by the opponent that an effect can arise in the absence of these three types of causes. Furthermore, since the existence of the non-inherent cause—the contact between the self and the mind—is not admitted in the case of God (*īśvara*), knowledge and the rest cannot exist there either.

If, even in the absence of non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) and so forth, the production of cognition occurs there [in the self], then why is it not logical for sprouts and the like to arise without the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), namely God? Furthermore, in the absence of cognition and the rest, how could there be the activity of those insentient materials and so forth that are not presided over by Him? For we do not observe the activity of an insentient thing—such as an axe—when it is not presided over by a conscious agent. Moreover, even if such activity were to occur, there would be no restriction regarding place, time, or form for things devoid of intention; this [restriction] belongs only to that which is presided over by Him.

Because its [the potter's] activity is observed to be invariably concomitant with that [the clay]. Now, if this is so, how can there be activity even for a conscious being who is not presided over by another conscious being, like a laborer who is not presided over by a master? Or, if the activity of a conscious being is indeed observed even when not presided over by another, why is such activity not observed in the case of the material cause of a sprout and so forth, which arises from being ploughed and is not presided over by him? Or, is it because the activity of the material cause of a jar and so forth is not observed in the absence of that [conscious agent]?

If it is argued that even the material cause of a sprout and so forth is established as possessing that [activity] only when presided over by that [conscious being], then since activity is not observed in laborers and the like who are not presided over by an owner, let it be established that the owner also possesses it only when presided over by another conscious being. If, however, a Great Lord (Maheśa) is postulated as the conscious presider even of the owner, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because he too would require another.

Furthermore, even if one accepts that a conscious entity also acts when presided over by another conscious entity, the inclusion of the qualifier "unconscious" for the subject (*dharmin*) and the reason "because it is unconscious" in the formal argument—"the unconscious is presided over by a conscious entity"—is not redundant; for if one were to accept that even a conscious entity acts when presided over by a conscious entity, there would be nothing to exclude [from the scope of the argument].

Nor is it untenable for even insentient things—which have attained their arising through the proximity of their own causes—to possess a restriction of place, time, and form, even in the absence of a conscious supervisor; for such restriction is derived from the power of its own causes. Otherwise, even that [restriction] produced by the knowledge of a supervisor would not exist.

If that cognition were the controller of all insentient things and were momentary—wherein its being the object of knowledge is itself its state of being the controller—then those [insentient things] would have to act toward their effects existing at all times at that very same moment. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that all subsequent effects would arise in a single moment. Furthermore, if such a cognition continued to exist in subsequent moments as well, the production of effects in the immediately following time would occur perpetually; thus, this observed sequential existence of effects such as sprouts and so forth would be destroyed.

Furthermore, if [the Lord's] cognition and other faculties were directed toward only a few insentient objects, then those things that are not their objects would not engage in their own effects; thus, the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) would result in being devoid of its effects. For the opponent does not accept any basis for the governance of those things other than being the objects of that [Lord's] cognition and so forth. Now, if that cognition and so forth were eternal;

well then, [one could argue]: "Cognition is momentary, because, while being perceptible to beings such as ourselves, it is a specific quality of an all-pervading substance, like sound"—in this formal argument, there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reason due to the cognition of Maheśvara.

Now, if it is argued that this fault does not apply because of the qualification "provided there is exclusion from that [subject] such as cognition," we say no. A qualification that is incompatible with the counter-example (vipakṣa) serves to exclude the reason from that [counter-example]; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to exclude it. Furthermore, being excluded from that [subject] is not incompatible with non-momentariness, since neither of the two types of incompatibility is established between these two. Nor is the deviation of the reason avoided merely by employing a qualification that is not incompatible with the counter-example.

Otherwise, no reason (*hetu*) would ever be deviant (*vyabhicārin*), because in every case where deviation occurs, it would be possible to apply the qualification "provided it is distinct from this" (*etad-vyatiriktatve sati*). Furthermore, according to the Nyāya school, non-momentary cognition is not possible, because of the statement [in the *Nyāyabhāṣya*]: "Cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) like its object" (*arthavat pramāṇam*). Thus, cognition is accepted as having the object as its effect and as being directed toward that object; yet the object—whether past, future, or occurring sequentially—is not simultaneous with the cognition.

And whatever cognition has for its object a knowable thing that is successive must itself arise successively, just as the cognition of Devadatta and others whose objects are flames and so forth; and the cognition of Īśvara has for its object a knowable thing that is successive—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

This is a *prasanga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum); therefore, one should not suspect that the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). Nor should it be argued that there is no room for a *prasanga-sādhana* here because the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is unestablished due to the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) in the contrary case; for such a proof does exist. To explain: if that cognition of God is produced with its own manifestation by means of an object that possesses succession, then succession is already established.

If, on the other hand, it is not produced [by the object], then, due to the absence of a basis for proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it could not know that [object]; furthermore, your accepted doctrine of validity even in the absence of an object would be lost, because it would entail the consequence of being objectless regarding past and future objects—thus, the existence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position is established.

Furthermore, if that knowledge and so forth were eternal, then since there would be no other cause for the world being presided over by a conscious agent apart from its being the object of that [knowledge], it would follow that the world—having all its causes complete—would arise simultaneously. For instance: whatever has its causes complete necessarily comes into being, just as a sprout, when its causes are complete upon reaching the final stage of the causal complex, comes into being; and the entire world, whose causes such as God’s knowledge and so forth are always complete, would likewise exist all at once.

It might be argued: "The intellect of God and so forth are not the sole causes; rather, they produce their respective effects depending upon auxiliary causes such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), because the intellect of God and so forth function as instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). Therefore, due to the deficiency of these auxiliary causes—merit and so forth—the state of the cause being 'unimpaired' (*avikalakāraṇatva*) is unestablished. This is incorrect.

For if some benefit were conferred upon it by its auxiliaries, then there would be dependence on those auxiliaries; however, since it is eternal and its excellence cannot be imparted by others, there is nothing for it to obtain from its auxiliaries—why, then, should it depend on such things that provide no benefit? Furthermore, why do those auxiliaries themselves not remain constantly present if they are produced by that [cause]? If you answer that it is due to the absence of auxiliaries caused by other factors for their non-proximity, that is no answer.

Since those [auxiliaries] which act in conjunction with it and whose production is dependent upon it must likewise be present at that very time, how can the reason (hetu) be considered unestablished? If you maintain that, while being eternal, it first produces its auxiliary causes such as those cognitions and only afterwards generates the effects such as the sprout, then—because its power would be exhausted solely in the production of one auxiliary after another—it could not produce the effect of the sprout and so forth. If you argue that this fault does not apply because the auxiliaries, such as merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma), are themselves produced by something other than that [eternal cause];

But surely, in that case, the reason "because it has an insentient material cause" would be inconclusive; therefore, since factors such as merit (dharma) and so forth are auxiliary causes whose presence depends upon that [sentient being], the reason known as "the completeness of the causal complex" is not unestablished.

Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because that would entail the loss of its status as having unimpaired causes; for if something were not produced even when its causes are unimpaired, it would follow that it would never be produced at all, since there would be no distinction [between different moments]. By this, the following argument of Uddyotakara is also refuted: "Even though the eternal cause called God is present in its entirety for all entities, there is nevertheless no simultaneous production, because God acts with prior intelligence (*buddhipūrvakāritva*)."

If God were the producer of entities without prior intelligence, merely by his existence alone, then this objection would indeed hold; but when he acts with prior intelligence, there is no fault, because he engages in effects according to his own will. Therefore, the argument that the reason is inconclusive is also refuted.

For the activity and cessation of effects do not depend on the presence or absence of the will of their cause, such that—even though the cause called Īśvara is always present with unimpeded power—they would fail to arise due to the absence of His will; rather, entities conform to the presence or absence of the capacity residing in the cause.

For instance: jars and other such things do not arise from an incompetent potter and the like, even though he possesses the desire [to produce them], because he lacks the capacity for the operations of hands, feet, and so forth; whereas sprouts and the like are observed to arise from seeds and the like, which possess the capacity, even though they lack desire.

In this regard, why do entities depend upon that desire belonging to the cause called Īśvara—which, like at the time of the production of an effect, is always present with unimpeded power—when that desire provides them no assistance? For if they were to arise simultaneously, as they do at the time of production, it would demonstrate that their own causes are complete. Furthermore, since Īśvara cannot be assisted by others, he has no need for anything such that he would have to depend on a desire;
nor is any desire other than a particular state of consciousness possible for him.

If the intellect (*buddhi*) of the Lord is admitted to be eternal, all-pervading, and one, then that very intellect would become the presiding agent over insentient objects; what, then, is the use of postulating a further Lord as its substratum? If it is argued that such knowledge cannot exist without a substratum and therefore the postulation of that Self (the Lord) is necessary—well, even that Self cannot exist without a substratum, and thus by postulating further and further supports, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress of Lords.

Now, if it is argued that its existence as a substance persists even though it is unattached—unlike cognition, which is a quality—this is not a fault. But from what source is its status as a quality established? To say "because it inheres in that [the Self]" is no answer, since that very point remains uncertain. If it is argued that its inherence in that [Self] follows from its being contained therein, then by what is this perceived? Certainly not by God, because He does not perceive either the self or His own cognition; thus, for Him, the perception that "this [cognition] inheres in this [self]" would be impossible.

Nor is it a satisfactory answer to say that the apprehension of that [universal] is simply the inherence of its cognition therein; for this would involve a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): for if the apprehension "this is here" is established, then the inherence therein is established; and if the inherence therein is established, then the apprehension of it is established. Thus, there is mutual dependence.

The Lord does not perceive that knowledge as inherent within himself; and since he does not even know his own knowledge established within himself, who could possibly have faith that he would understand the material and auxiliary causes of the entire world? Nor does that knowledge perceive itself as "I am inherent in the post," because there is no perception of the self nor of its substrate. Furthermore, upon the apprehension of that [knowledge], the cognition "this is my form, situated here" is impossible. Nor does it perceive the self either, because it is admitted to be non-self-cognizing (*asvasaṃvidita*).

Nor is there possible for that Lord even a separate, eternal cognition by which he might comprehend the entire multitude of objects; for that cognition would have to be unchanging—since no other instance has been observed where two homogeneous qualities coexist in the same substance at the same time—and thus such a postulation is impossible even in his case.

Or, if that [external object] were to be postulated, why would the effect, such as a sprout, not also be postulated? Or, even if those two aforementioned cognitions were to exist there, nevertheless, neither of those two cognitions—being devoid of the apprehension of themselves—could apprehend their own substratum, nor a concomitant cognition, nor any other object of experience.

For instance: that which is devoid of self-apprehension does not apprehend another, just like a jar or similar objects; and the cognition under discussion is devoid of self-apprehension. Therefore, since this [cognition] does not apprehend its own concomitant, how could it apprehend that [quality]? If it were to be known by that [concomitant] which is likewise devoid of apprehension, then the same argument would have to be stated; thus, nothing at all would be apprehended. Consequently, the quality-status of the cognition [of color] as being inherent in that [substance] is not established, nor does the substance-status of its substratum attain proof.

Therefore, if sprouts and the like were preceded by an eternal intellect, why would they not arise simultaneously? For, just as Īśvara is eternally present, so too would his intellect be eternally present. Even if one were to argue that Īśvara, though dependent on a non-eternal intellect, is the creator of the world by virtue of being the conscious controller of the insentient, since he is eternal, his intellect would likewise be eternally present; and because the complete causes would be present at all times, it would follow that effects such as sprouts must arise simultaneously.
Consequently, the qualification "because of possessing intellect" is entirely ineffective; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) regarding the logical reason (*hetu*).

Nor is there contradiction [of the reason], because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*). It is not the case that this is so; therefore, the formulation of the contrapositive (*viparyaya-prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not exist at a certain time does not have its causes complete at that time, just like a sprout that is not produced while remaining in the state of a seed stored in a granary. And at the time of the production of a single entity, the entire universe does not exist; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it has been proven that it is impossible for God, or His knowledge and so forth, to be the cause [of the world] if they were deficient in causal factors. Therefore, it is not logical that agency belongs to eternal knowledge, effort, and desire, nor to their eternal inherence (*samavāya*). Consequently, since the connection with a body is perceived as the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of agency—as seen in the case of a potter—the absence of that [body] entails the absence of agency, which is its pervaded (*vyāpya*) property.

And that [agency] is, in some cases, characterized by the employment of instruments through the activity of the hands and so forth—as, for example, a potter’s employment of instruments such as the staff; in another case, it consists in the employment of laborers and the like through the activity of speech—as, for example, a master’s nature of employing servants; and yet another consists in the activity of volitional effort—as, for example, the waking person’s inherent nature of impelling the parts of his own body; and something else [consists in] the impelling of the palate and so forth, or the hands and so forth, through specific states of sleep, intoxication, or negligence; in every instance, however, there is indeed a connection with the body.

Agency is pervaded by [the possession of] a body. If that [agency] were to cease in God, it would necessarily cease along with its own pervader, agency; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that His agency must not be admitted. On the other hand, if His status as the creator of the world is admitted, then the connection with a body must be admitted as the pervader of agency; this is the contrapositive of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*).

Nor is its authorship characterized by the thorough knowledge of the potencies of the causal factors—such that there would be an absence of the [logical] pervasion in the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*)—because, in the case of a potter and others, even when there is thorough knowledge of the potencies of the causal factors such as clay and the staff, the production of effects such as a jar is not observed in the absence of bodily activity; and because, in the case of those who are asleep or intoxicated, even in the absence of thorough knowledge of the causes such as the palate and so forth, the production of the effect of impelling them is observed provided there is effort, which is characterized by exertion.

Even that capacity to perform actions such as the removal of poison through mere utterance is not based on knowledge alone; rather, it is caused solely by a specific effort of the self, which is invariably concomitant with its connection to a body.

Furthermore, God, who is the ordainer of instructions regarding specific *dharma* and *adharma*, is to be worshipped by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) because of His omniscience; otherwise, if He were ignorant, their engagement in following His instructions would not occur due to the suspicion of deception. As it has been said: "Someone possessing knowledge is sought out in order to practice what He has taught."
Those who suspect deception when an instruction is given by one who is ignorant [might think]:

"Even if he were omniscient, because he is bodiless, there is an impossibility of his being a teacher; thus, since the authority of that instruction cannot be established as being produced by him, seekers of liberation would not engage with it. Therefore, if he is to be the author of the instruction, his connection with a body must necessarily be admitted, because the admission of the pervaded (the instruction) is invariably concomitant with the admission of the pervader (the bodily form).

But in the absence of a connection with a body, there would also be an absence of the capacity to impart instruction, which is the pervaded [property]; thus, there are both the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*). Furthermore, the proof establishing the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader has already been demonstrated previously as a proof for the causal relationship—that if instruction were to exist even in the absence of the operation of the palate and other organs, it could not have that [operation] as its cause; therefore, it is not stated again. Thus, this remains established: the Great Lord possesses no agency in the absence of a body.

Therefore, since there is an absence of effort, cognition, and so forth due to the lack of a connection between body and mind, the very existence of God is unestablished. Consequently, in His absence, for whom could a specific quality characterized by the conjunction with a body and so forth be proven? Thus, the statement of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) stands refuted as being devoid of substance, because the demonstration of the pervasion (vyāpti)—which serves as the basis for both the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and its contrapositive (viparyaya)—has been clearly set forth.

As for what was also stated—that there exists in God a conjunction of knowledge, desire to act, and effort, and that these [qualities] are eternal in Him because of His knowledge—that too has been demonstrated to be untenable. Furthermore, as for the claim that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the connection with a body and [being] an agent, that too is incorrect; for it has been established that the connection with a body is indeed pervasive of agency (*kartṛtva*).

As for what was also stated—that "non-omniscience, which is observed among potters and others, is not established [as a probans] therein," and so forth—that too is incorrect. Since a potter and the like must possess knowledge of the specific causes such as karma for the production of effects like jars, it follows that they would be omniscient. Thus, the postulation of another Lord who is omniscient is redundant; for, just as one who knows the supersensible *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) that brings about those effects would necessarily know all things, so too would that [other] Lord necessarily know all objects.

Now, even if there is no perception of the unseen [factors], the potter accomplishes his own effect, such as a jar, simply through his thorough knowledge of the capacities of a few causal factors like the lump of clay and the staff; therefore, it is not established that he possesses omniscience—characterized by the knowledge of all objects beyond the senses and so forth—on the grounds that his status as the creator of all effects would otherwise be inexplicable.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas), being presided over by the Omniscient One, grasp only restricted objects, just as in the case of living bodies where those who perceive restricted objects such as sound and so forth are presided over by an Omniscient One whose object is unrestricted—that too is incoherent.

Since the phrase "of those which grasp objects such as sound" is presented as an illustration, if it refers to the sense organs (*indriya*), then because they are instruments (*karaṇa*), they cannot be the substratum for the action characterized by cognition (*vedanā*); how then could there be the grasping of restricted objects such as sound? Alternatively, if it is not through being the substratum of grasping that they grasp restricted objects such as sound, but rather through being instruments; [then the following applies].

But surely, in this way, even for the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls), there is instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) rather than agency (*kartṛtva*) in the apprehension of objects; thus, it is not established that jars and the like are produced by a non-agent potter through his thorough knowledge of the power of their causes. How, then, from such an example, can the fact that the earth and so forth have an agent as their substrate of cognition be established? If, on the other hand, it is admitted that even though the eyes and other [senses] have restricted objects, they possess agency when presided over by another *kṣetrajña* whose objects are unrestricted—[then what of] conscious beings?

Furthermore, just as there is a conscious supervisor (*adhiṣṭhātā*) who has unrestricted objects for those cognitions that have restricted objects, so too, if one assumes that this [conscious being] also has restricted objects, another supervisor with unrestricted objects must be admitted for him; and for that one yet another, which would result in the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Similarly, when even conscious individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are accepted as having a conscious being as their controller, then the argument—"the unconscious proceeds when controlled by a conscious being, because it is unconscious, like an axe and so forth"—would not require the inclusion of the term "unconscious" as a qualification of either the subject (*dharmin*) or the reason (*hetu*), since there would be nothing to exclude [from the scope of the reason].

As for what was said—that "let there be an infinite regress if there exists some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it, because [the object] is established by inference to that extent"—that too is inconsistent; for if the establishment of one thing is admitted through a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) without a means of valid cognition, why is the establishment of another not likewise admitted from that very same source? Furthermore, even for that much, there is no establishment by means of a valid cognition, because the infinite regress does not entail the invalidity of the means of valid cognition that would establish it.

As for what was also stated—that there is scriptural authority (*āgama*) regarding this matter and so forth—that too is incorrect; for the authority of scripture depends upon its being composed by that [author], and the establishment of that [author] from the authority of that [scripture] results in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Furthermore, the Vaiśeṣikas do not accept the authority of an eternal scripture, because that would entail the uselessness of postulating a Lord (*īśvara*).

Nor can its establishment [of God] be derived from another scripture composed by a different God, because if that scripture's authority were based on its being composed by Him, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate yet another scripture composed by a further God, the same argument would have to be stated for that as well, leading to an infinite regress. Thus, even if scripture possesses authority regarding its own subject matter, God is not established thereby.

As for what was said—that the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) acts as a presiding agent over those [senses] engaged in grasping their respective objects by its mere existence, just as the light of the sun acts [as a presider] over crystals and the like engaged in grasping the forms of adjacent objects—that is incorrect.

Because even the light of the sun cannot be the presiding agent of crystal and the like by its mere existence (*sattāmātra*); and if that were impossible because space and so forth also exist as mere existence, then they too would have to be presiding agents. However, the light of the sun is the presiding agent of those [crystals] by virtue of producing a specific state characterized by them; if, on the other hand, this [presiding agency] is postulated for the Lord (*īśvara*) with respect to the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), then it follows that those souls must be his effects.

And likewise, just as the state of being an effect [is attributed] to individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) despite their being indistinguishable in their nature as selves (*ātman*), so too, because the Lord is indistinguishable in his nature as a self, he would be an effect; thus, another presiding agent over him must be admitted as his creator, and yet another over that one—resulting in an infinite regress.

Now, if it is argued that even while being an effect, he acts toward his own effects without being presided over by another, then the material cause of the world and so forth might also act without being presided over by him; thus, the very reason adduced to prove the existence of a presiding agent is itself inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*).

Furthermore, if its status as a presiding controller were due to its mere existence (*sattāmātra*), then—like space—it would not possess omniscience; thus, the reason that establishes omniscience would be contradictory (*viruddha*), as it would instead establish the opposite. Nor is it reasonable to claim that omniscience belongs to that [Ishvara] alone and not to space and so forth because of the inherence (*samavāya*) of knowledge regarding all objects therein, for inherence has been refuted. Even if it did exist, since it is eternal and all-pervasive, it would follow that it must also exist in space and other such things.

Nor can it be said that there is a distinction between the two inherent relata despite the lack of distinction in inherence itself, because such a distinction is unestablished; and even if it were established, it would follow that the postulation of inherence is redundant, as will be demonstrated later. Furthermore, if inherence were the substratum of those relata by its mere existence, then even mere knowledge [of it] would be sufficient—let alone the complete knowledge of all the causal factors for the entire collection of categories.

As for what was said—that the nature of cognition is indeed to illuminate its own object as a real entity, and that its deviation from this state occurs due to the presence of some defect—that is certainly true.

Furthermore, as for what was stated: since cognition independent of the eyes and other organs is established for the opponent, once that is established, pleasure is also established; therefore, how could the blissful nature (*ānandarūpatā*) of the liberated ones not be consistent? For otherwise, the acceptance that liberation is the self’s essential nature devoid of qualities such as pleasure would not be tenable.

Furthermore, the absence of obscurations such as passion (*rāga*) is not established in Maheśvara, by virtue of which his knowledge might be established as unobscured and having all things as its object; for his very nature is unestablished, and because any non-deviant reason (*hetu*) that would prove the absence of passion and so forth in him has been cast far away through an examination of your own accepted tenets.

As for what was said—that passion and the like have error as their cause, and error has the sign of unwholesomeness (*adharma*) as its cause, yet there is no unwholesomeness in the Blessed One—that too is without substance; for it has been demonstrated that, just as unwholesomeness does not exist there, neither does its cause, nor do wholesome qualities (*dharma*), nor its causes, such as right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

Furthermore, as for the claim that passion and the like are observed to arise toward objects that accomplish what is desired or undesired, and that for the Blessed One there is no object whatsoever that accomplishes the desired or undesired because his desires are fulfilled—that too is without substance.

If there is no object whatsoever for him that is a means to achieve the desired or the undesired, how then does he engage in activity for the sake of adopting the former and abandoning the latter? For intentional activity is pervaded by the desire to avoid what is to be discarded and the desire to acquire what is to be adopted. If activity occurred even in the absence of those two, then God’s activity would not be intentional, like the activity of a madman. Furthermore, the desire to avoid what is to be discarded and the desire to acquire what is to be adopted are themselves pervaded by the state of having unfulfilled desires; [this cannot apply] to one whose desires have been fulfilled.

Because the desire to abandon what is to be rejected (*heyajihāsā*) and the desire to acquire what is to be accepted (*upādeyopāditsā*) would be untenable [in the absence of unfulfilled desires]. Furthermore, the state of having unfulfilled desires (*anāptakāmatva*) is pervaded by a lack of lordship (*anīśvaratva*), since it is impossible for a Lord (*īśvara*) to have unfulfilled desires. Thus, a *prasaṅga* argument is established: wherever intentional activity (*buddhipūrvikā pravṛtti*) is admitted, there the desire to abandon and the desire to acquire must necessarily be accepted; and wherever those exist, there is the state of having unfulfilled desires; and wherever that exists, there is a lack of lordship. Conversely, if there is lordship, there is the fulfillment of all desires (*avāptakāmatva*); and because of the fulfillment of all desires, there can be no concern regarding what is to be rejected or what is to be accepted.

The desire for the abandonment or acquisition of that [object] is such that, in its absence, there is no purposeful activity; this is the contrapositive of the reductio (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*). For this very reason, the objection raised against the independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*) regarding the fallacy of the reason, such as the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), is irrelevant, because here only the establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is required; and that has already been demonstrated.

As for the claim that the activity directed toward the creation of the body and so forth is for the sake of play (*krīḍā*), and that play occurs only for those who have already attained all their desires—that is inconsistent. For play occurs precisely for those who have not yet found delight (*rati*); moreover, it has been established by the author of the *Vārttika* himself that the Blessed Lord does not seek delight, because he is devoid of suffering.

Furthermore, as for the statement that "those who are suffering do not engage in play," that is a remark that disregards the context; for even in the absence of suffering, play is impossible for those possessed of passion and the like unless it is directed toward objects that are desired means for attaining pleasure.

As for the claim that his engagement in that [act] proceeds from compassion and so forth, that too is an unconsidered statement; for it is not logical that those possessed of compassion should produce the suffering of multitudes of living beings by generating bodies of torment. Nor is it appropriate to say that he produces their suffering in such a way while depending on their respective karma, because he would then be merely an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). For if those karmas were independent of God and yet were effects, it would follow that the very reason characterized as "being an effect" is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to him.

Or, if it is admitted that action is produced by Him, then since Maheśvara first ordains action for living beings and subsequently brings about its destruction through the mechanism of experiencing its results, the consequence follows that He acts without foresight; for even prudent people such as cowherds do not destroy an object after having first created it without a purpose. Therefore, it is not logical that one who acts out of compassion—even if dependent upon karma—should cause suffering to living beings.

Furthermore, if he produces suffering for living beings only in dependence upon their own karma, then there is no contradiction to his compassion. In that case, if it is admitted that he produces the bodies of living beings while being dependent on karma, it would be better to admit that the producer is the sentient being who experiences the fruit of that karma and who is himself dependent upon it; in this way, the postulation of an unseen God (adṛṣṭeśvara) is avoided.

It is also incorrect to argue that just as a lord bestows fruits according to the specific nature of service and is not a non-lord, so too Maheśvara bestows fruits in dependence upon karma and is not a non-lord; for just as a king who bestows fruits dependent on service is perceived to possess attachment and the like, cruelty, and dependence on service, all of this must likewise be admitted for the Lord. Otherwise, it would be impossible for one who is otherwise [independent] to bestow happiness and so forth upon only a certain servant while excluding others.

Thus, since he is dependent on karma, he lacks sovereignty; and if his agency were impelled by compassion, he would create only what is auspicious. This establishes the validity of the refutation offered by the author of the *Vārttika*. Furthermore, as for the argument that even the creation of hell-beings, animals, and so forth—being a cause for future prosperity through the attainment of superior states after experiencing the sufferings therein—is established as the Lord’s compassionate engagement even in creating suffering beings, that too has already been refuted.

Since [the Lord], having ordained karma that brings suffering to living beings, effects their welfare by providing the means for the exhaustion of that karma through the experience of its fruits, there arises for Him the consequence of being perceived as having an uneven intellect—like one who, having placed something in an impure place, takes it up and washes it, yet then discards it along with the water used for washing.

Moreover, if it is accepted that the suffering and so forth of those beings—being dependent upon the karma of living beings—produces a penance-like state that serves as the cause for the exhaustion of that [karma], then it follows that this [suffering] must be an effect of that karma. For if there were no benefit produced by that [karma], it would be impossible for it to depend upon it. Furthermore, since a benefit produced by that [karma] cannot be related to it if it is distinct from it, and if it is not distinct, then when that [benefit] is produced, it is simply the production of that very [karma]; how then could it not be its effect?

Now, whenever and wherever it encounters a cooperative cause such as karma, by coming together with that [cause], it produces its respective effect, such as pleasure, at that time and in that place. Since being a cooperative cause consists precisely in the performance of a single effect, there is no fault in its definition as an effect. [Objection: If its nature of producing an effect—which depends upon cooperative causes such as karma—already exists even prior to the presence of those cooperative causes like karma, then even when the cooperative causes are present, this [nature] would produce the effect by its very own essence alone. (131)

If [the cause] were productive by means of another nature, then since everything would be non-productive by its own nature, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of any effect; moreover, because that [cause], being unimpeded and possessing the inherent nature of producing that [effect], exists, the production of all subsequent effects would occur at that very same time.

For instance: whatever is capable of producing something at a given time, necessarily produces it at that time—just as a seed that has reached its final state produces a sprout. Alternatively, if it does not produce it, then at that time it would simply not have the nature of producing it. And since this nature of producing is admitted by you to belong to Maheśvara even when the causal complex of karma and so forth is absent, because he possesses a single, unchanging nature—this is a *svabhāvahetu* (reason based on essential nature).

Now, if in the absence of the totality of conditions such as karma, this [Lord], despite possessing that nature, does not produce the intended effect, then he does not have the nature of being its producer—for whatever does not produce something at a certain time does not possess the nature of being its producer; just as a rice seed does not produce a barley sprout. If it were to possess that nature even while not producing it, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And since the Lord does not produce the intended effect when the totality of conditions such as karma is absent, this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Now, if that intrinsic nature (svabhāva)—characterized by the capacity to produce an effect in dependence upon a causal complex such as karma—is absent when that complex is not present, then how could there not be a difference in that [Lord], given the difference in his intrinsic nature? For there is no other basis for such [diversity]. Thus, since multiple effects such as sprouts, which occur sequentially, cannot be produced by a single non-sequential Lord, his oneness does not achieve proof. Therefore, the possession of attributes such as omniscience, bodilessness, and oneness does not bring about his establishment.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the cognition [of the Lord] cannot be related to artificial objects because such a cognition lacks restriction to each respective object—that too is refuted; for the relation of that cognition to all eternal entities has already been denied therein.

Furthermore, as for the argument that just as architects and others, when engaged in the construction of a great palace and so forth, possess a consensus constrained by a single intention, so too here—if there exists some one director of many [agents] in the production of various effects such as the earth and so on—he alone is God—this too is inconsistent. For there is no such rule that every effect must be accomplished by one person alone, or by many persons directed by a single one; since we observe the production of effects in many different ways.

For instance: in some cases, a single agent is observed as the producer of a single effect, such as a certain weaver [being the maker] of a single cloth; in some cases, a single agent produces many effects, such as a single potter [producing] jars, bowls, and water-pots; in some cases, multiple agents produce multiple effects, such as potters and others [producing] jars, cloths, carts, and so forth; and in some cases, even multiple agents produce a single effect, such as a multitude of men [working together] to carry a palanquin.

Furthermore, even in the case of a palace or similar structure—which is produced by many architects and others—it is not observed that their activity therein must necessarily be regulated by a single master-builder; for there is no contradiction in their carrying out the work even when they have distinct intentions, provided they are regulated by a single master-builder. Thus, a single creator is not established for the earth and other such things. For this very reason, it is also not logical to establish his omniscience based on that [creatorship].
