Thus, since there is no possible inference that establishes the full range of specific qualities such as eternity and so forth, and since there exists a *prasaṅga* argument that establishes the opposite of those qualities, how could there not be room for a "contradiction of the specific" (*viśeṣaviruddha*)? Now, if the state of being an effect were observed in the earth and other things as being pervaded by having an intelligent cause possessed of a body and so forth, then, if that [cause] were established therein on that basis, it would be established as being exactly of that nature; thus, the state of being an effect and so forth would indeed be contradictory.

Because it proves the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhyaviparyayasādhanāt*). And since such a thing does not exist there, how can there be contradiction (*viruddhatā*)? No; for the designation of contradiction is made by relying on the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) as established by the opponent, and by relying on the pervasion of the opposite (*viparyayavyāpti*). However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it has been demonstrated that the specific quality of "being an effect" (*kāryatvaviśeṣa*) is unestablished (*asiddhatva*) in the case of the earth and so forth, whereas its general form (*tatsāmānya*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*).

Since the defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) are common to all the inferences put forward to prove the existence of God (*īśvara*), those [other arguments] are also refuted by the very refutation of the argument from "being an effect" (*kāryatva*); therefore, they are not refuted here by being restated individually. Furthermore, the proponents of God accept that He is eternal; however, we shall demonstrate that the existence of a non-momentary entity is impossible.

And as for the argument that the great elements, such as earth and the rest, proceed in their respective activities only when presided over by an intelligent cause because they are impermanent, like an axe or similar tools—in that case, since the reason characterized by impermanence exists even in the intellect of a potter and others, it would follow that even that [potter's intellect] must be presided over by another intelligent cause. If one accepts that, then since the impermanence of the intellect of Maheśvara is likewise established, that too must be presided over by another intelligent being; and the same would apply to that intellect as well.

[The opponent objects: There would be an infinite regress. If, despite the impermanence of the intellect (*buddhi*), it were not the case that [the world] is presided over by an intelligent agent (*buddhimad-adhiṣṭhitatva*), then the reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*). Furthermore, this [objection] is not to be suspected here, because it has already been refuted. Moreover, whatever refutation was leveled against the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), such as its being unestablished (*asiddhatva*), applies equally here as well. To explain: the kind of impermanence established in the case of axes and the like as being presided over by an intelligent agent is not established in the case of bodies and so forth. Since a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established for mere impermanence, there is inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*).

If a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is admitted, there is the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddhatva*), because it proves the opposite of what is intended. There is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*) in the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the property to be proven—namely, being presided over by a single, eternal intelligent being—is not established. If the probandum is stated in general terms, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); if it is stated in specific terms, there is inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*), because a different state is observed in the case of jars and other such things. This same reasoning should be applied to all the reasons (*hetu*) adduced for the purpose of proving the present probandum.

Regarding the proof stated as "because [the cause] acts after having remained," another refutation must also be voiced: since all entities perish immediately upon their arising, there is no stability even for a single moment; thus, how could there be activity after having remained? Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the opponent, and it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to Īśvara himself; for he too acts after having remained toward successive effects, yet he is not presided over by another conscious being, lest there be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, if the reason is stated with a qualification as "being insentient," as proposed by Praśastamati, even so, its inconclusiveness remains unavoidable because its exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa) is doubtful. For only that qualification which actually excludes the reason from the counter-example is logical; however, a qualification that does not remove doubt regarding the counter-example is as good as non-existent even if it is employed. Furthermore, the previously mentioned fault of being unestablished (asiddhatā) remains in the very same state even when the reason is qualified.

As for what was stated regarding "the conventional usage at the beginning of creation" and so forth, even there, the qualification "of those awakened at a later time" is unestablished. For instance, in our view, at the time of dissolution, persons do not remain with their knowledge and memory obliterated and devoid of bodies and instruments; rather, they are reborn among the classes of gods in the Ābhāsvara and other realms, who possess an excellence of clear cognition.

However, it is held that those whose karma is conducive to the ripening of specific hells and so forth are reborn in other world-systems. Furthermore, even at the time of cosmic evolution (*vivarta-kāla*), beings arise here having passed away from the Ābhāsvara heaven and so forth with their knowledge and mindfulness unimpaired; therefore, the qualification "for those who awaken at a later time" is unestablished (*asiddha*). Moreover, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because its exclusion from the contrary case (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

Furthermore, if the probandum is merely "having been preceded by the instruction of another," then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it is accepted by all that beginningless linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by the instruction of another. If, however, what is being proved is "having been preceded by the instruction of a person characterized as God (*īśvara*)," then there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), since linguistic usage is possible otherwise [i.e., without such a person], and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the probandum. This general refutation regarding other reasons has been stated previously.

Furthermore, the reason is contradictory and the thesis is sublated by what has been accepted, because it is impossible for one who is faceless to be a teacher. If the worldly practice of instruction were preceded by God, then the reason would not be contradictory; however, since he is faceless, it is not logical for him to be a teacher. That facelessness follows from his being bodiless, and that in turn follows from his being devoid of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Thus, as Uddyotakara stated: "Just as there is no possibility of proof for the intelligence of God..."

"There is no such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the eternity of dharma and so forth" [NV 464,14]. Therefore, since it is impossible for God to be a teacher, the fact that linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by His instruction is not established; rather, it is preceded by the instruction of another person distinct from God. Consequently, because it subverts what is intended [to be proven], the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*). Alternatively, if God’s status as a teacher is accepted, then the previously admitted [attribute of His] being turned away [from worldly activity] is abandoned; thus, there is a contradiction with what has been accepted (*abhyupetabādha*).

In this same way, regarding other reasons that establish [the existence of] omniscience and its specific attributes, one should mentally infer the web of fallacies—such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), or contradictory (*viruddha*)—since the present effort is intended merely to provide a general indication. For this very reason, [it is argued]: "The seven worlds were created by a single intellect, because they are contained within a single entity, like the various rooms contained within a single house."

Just as it is observed that the various inner chambers within a single dwelling are produced by the intellect of a single architect, so too the seven worlds contained within this one world [are likewise]; therefore, it is determined that these also are produced by a single intellect.

As for the arguments proposed by Praśastamati and others—such as "those things which are fashioned by intelligence are [the work] of that Blessed Lord Maheśvara, the sole architect of the entire world"—in these cases too, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). For there is no such thing as a single world or a single dwelling-place and so forth; this designation was applied to many things merely for the sake of linguistic convenience. Consequently, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is also devoid of the probandum (*sādhanavikala*);
furthermore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since one observes that rooms and other parts contained within a single mansion, for instance, are constructed by more than one architect.

Furthermore, from Brahmā down to the Piśācas, all possess a single point of dependence, because they exist in a state of mutual superiority; for it is observed in this world that those who exist in a state of mutual superiority are dependent upon a single authority—just as in this world the lords of houses, villages, towns, and regions are dependent upon one universal sovereign—and likewise, there is a state of mutual superiority among the Bhujangas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and so forth.

By this we consider that even for them there is dependence upon a single Lord; however, if the intended meaning to be proven by this is that "they are governed by a single presiding Lord," then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established due to the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary. Furthermore, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

If it is then argued that [the world] is "endowed with a presiding deity" merely by virtue of having a presider, then this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For the sons of the Sugata accept that the entire world is indeed presided over by the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the crest-jewel of all the worlds, through the power of his compassion; it is by his influence that caravans of virtuous people even today attain the perfection of worldly prosperity and the ultimate good.

Moreover, regarding all the proofs for an omniscient being proposed by others, if what you intend to prove is merely that "some [person] is omniscient" in a general sense, then this proof of yours does not shine before us due to the fault of proving what is already established; rather, it is only effective against those such as the Jaiminīyas or the Cārvākas who deny the existence of an omniscient being.

If an omniscient Lord were to be established as the object of proof, then, according to the method already stated, the logical reasons (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the failure to establish the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). As for the remainder of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), it has been disregarded due to its lack of substance. Therefore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish either the Lord or His attributes such as eternity, the entire position beginning with "The Lord is a particular *puruṣa* untouched by afflictions, actions, their ripening, and latent dispositions" [Yogasūtra 1.24] remains untenable.

Therefore, because they have conquered passion and other defilements which are the causes of existence, the Jinas—the propounders of the teaching—are established as perfected beings. Consequently, it is well-established that this teaching belongs to those who are victorious over existence. Now, an objection may be raised: if they possess the quality of being conquerors of passion and other defilements that bind one to existence, then their status as propounders of the teaching would be untenable; for immediately after conquering them, liberation (apavarga) would be attained, and in the absence of a body, the capacity for speech would be impossible. Alternatively, if liberation is not attained immediately after the destruction of passion and so forth, then the conquest of passion and the rest cannot be the cause for attaining liberation, which is characterized by the exhaustion of existence.

For indeed, when something does not arise even though another thing is present, it is impossible to establish that the latter is its complete cause, just as a barley seed is not the cause of a rice sprout. Now, if it is argued that there is no fault because he attained liberation (*apavarga*) precisely before becoming the author of that [scripture] due to having conquered all passion (*rāga*) and other defilements without exception—the Master [Haribhadra], anticipating the objection that the authority of this teaching would not be absolute since it was composed by a person still bound by the stains of passion—just like the teachings composed by persons such as Kapila—states: "Having attained the station of incomparable bliss."

The intention here is as follows: although the Jinas possess the perfection of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*)—which has destroyed the four types of destructive karma (*ghātikarma*) that obstruct omniscience—they nevertheless possess a small amount of residual karma bound to the body that sustains existence (*bhavopagrāhi*). Because of this, it is not the case that they cannot be the authors of the teaching due to the absence of a body and so forth; nor is the scripture composed by them invalid due to the presence of even a trace of passion and other defilements, because the destructive karmas, which are the cause of error, have been utterly destroyed.

Nor can the non-occurrence of subsequent karma result from the exhaustion of [past] karma alone, because the karma that sustains existence (*bhavopagrāhikarma*) has not yet been entirely exhausted; and since liberation occurs immediately upon that exhaustion, it is the exhaustion of karma itself that constitutes the unimpeded cause for attaining liberation.

The meaning of the individual components (*avayavārtha*) is as follows: "Sthāna" refers to the distinguished field characterized as the summit of the world (*lokāgra*), wherein pure souls (*śuddhātman*) abide, having attained the destruction of all karma and being occupied by infinite knowledge and bliss. "Upama" means that whose bliss—consisting of the nature of *ānanda*—has no comparison (*upamā*) because it transcends all other happiness due to its natural, absolute, and entirely painless state. "Upagata" refers to those who have gone to or attained that [state] in proximity of time (*kālasāmīpyena*). Alternatively, "upa" is a prefix (*upasarga*).

It is also observed in the sense of excellence (*prakarṣa*), as in the expression "with passion fully risen" (*upoḍharāgeṇa*). Therefore, the phrase "those who have gone to the state of incomparable bliss" refers to those who have reached that state in its highest degree. According to the logical principle that words employed for the sake of another meaning convey that meaning even without the suffix *-vat*, they are said to have "gone there" as if they had actually gone, despite the presence of a mere trace of the karma of the name "Tīrthakṛt" (Ford-maker) still being experienced. Consequently, their status as the promulgators of the teaching in that state is indeed established.

Or, regarding the claim that "the liberated ones abide everywhere like space, free from all suffering," the Master (Sūri) spoke in order to refute this erroneous doctrine: *ṭhāṇam aṇovamasuham uvagayāṇaṃ*. Here, "place" (*ṭhāṇam*) refers to incomparable bliss (*aṇovamasuham*). It should be explained as "of those who have gone" (*uvagayāṇaṃ*), meaning those who have reached [that state] pre-eminently and without returning.

Alternatively, in order to exclude the view that "liberation of the self is the absolute destruction of the nine specific qualities, such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth," the Teacher has presented the aphorism: *ṭhāṇam aṇovamasuham uvagayāṇaṃ*.

And this is its meaning: *sthiti* (abiding) means the state (*sthāna*), which is the attainment of one's own essential nature (*svarūpaprāpti*). *Upa* refers to that incomparable bliss for those who have gone to—that is, attained—it immediately after the destruction of all karma. This means: for those who have attained the essential nature of the self, which consists of infinite bliss, which is the object to be acquired in the final moment of the *śaileśī* state, and which is in some sense non-different from [the self].
